items: [A | guideline supported] The AACE/ATA 2012 guideline abstract states that serum TSH is the single best screening test for primary thyroid dysfunction in most outpatient situations. This is the only initial laboratory work-up element stated in the available text. The abstract does not specify history, examination or other laboratory elements. - PMID:23246686

[B | guideline supported] Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined biochemically as elevated TSH with normal free T4, so evaluation needs both TSH and free T4 to distinguish it from overt disease. Guidelines differ on whether to treat subclinical disease. The BMJ panel strongly recommends against thyroid hormones in adults with it, whereas the AACE/ATA guideline says treatment should be individualized when TSH is below 10 mIU/L. - PMID:22954017, PMID:31088853
[B | guideline supported] Referral to a specialist is recommended in guidelines when conservative therapy fails or when steppage gait is present. - PMID:34205193

[B | evidence supported] Red flags differ widely between low back pain guidelines, and evidence for their diagnostic accuracy is lacking. Any lab-triggering criteria are therefore not firmly evidence-based. - PMID:27376890

[B | guideline supported] The abstract of the 2012 AACE/ATA guideline identifies serum TSH as the single best screening test for primary thyroid dysfunction in most outpatient situations and says treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH <10 mIU/L should be individualised. It gives no specific history, physical examination or anti-TPO antibody recommendations. (verified with caveat) - PMID:22954017

[C | guideline supported] The AACE/ATA adult hypothyroidism guideline names serum TSH as the single best screening test for primary thyroid dysfunction in most outpatient situations. It also identifies L-thyroxine as the standard treatment. (verified with caveat) - PMID:22954017

[C | guideline supported] A systematic review of clinical practice guidelines reports consistent 'should do' physical-examination elements for radicular pain from disc disease: straight leg raise, crossed straight leg raise, mapping pain distribution, gait assessment, and congruence of signs and symptoms. Only 6 of 23 guidelines addressed physical examination. (verified with caveat) - PMID:34205193

[C | guideline supported] Guidelines consistently advise against routine imaging in primary care or without red flags, and against routine CT/MRI in the first 4-6 weeks. Imaging is advised when history and examination are consistent with disc herniation and certain triggers apply. (verified with caveat) - PMID:34205193

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review states that a detailed history and careful physical examination, supplemented if necessary by MRI, can differentiate a herniated lumbar disc from low back strain and other causes. It also states that initial screening for serious pathology and monitoring for neurological deficits, cauda equina syndrome or refractory pain are essential. - PMID:10029785

[C | evidence supported] Nearly all spontaneous (presumed autoimmune) primary overt hypothyroidism is antibody-positive, and TPOAb is more often detectable than TgAb. A TPOAb result would therefore mainly confirm or refute an autoimmune etiology rather than redirect therapy. - PMID:17060029, PMID:9594622

[C | evidence supported] Management of Hashimoto's-related hypothyroidism is described as treating hypothyroidism, not the autoimmune process, with levothyroxine adapted to TSH. This implies that antibody status does not by itself drive routine dosing or monitoring. One review does state that treatment depends on both TSH and the presence or absence of anti-TPO antibodies, but this appears to be a broad thyroiditis summary and gives no detail. - PMID:32107053, PMID:42278392

[C | evidence supported] Anti-TPO titers during levothyroxine treatment vary. The effect of levothyroxine on antibody levels is described as inconclusive and variable between individuals, and titers can fall without normalizing. Serial antibody titers are therefore unlikely to serve as a reliable treatment-monitoring marker on this evidence. - PMID:42278392, PMID:8088002

[C | evidence supported] Guidelines consistently advise against routine imaging in primary care or when red flags are absent. Imaging (MRI, or CT) is advised when history and examination fit disc herniation and radiculopathy persists, surgery is considered, or severe or progressive neurological signs are present. The excerpt does not list the red flags themselves. - PMID:34205193
[C | evidence supported] Specialist referral is recommended when conservative therapy fails or when steppage gait is present. - PMID:34205193

[C | evidence supported] Individual examination tests have limited accuracy. The SLR is highly sensitive but poorly specific in surgical populations, and the crossed SLR is highly specific but insensitive. Most other tests (weakness, wasting, reflexes, sensory deficits) performed poorly in isolation, and combining positive tests increased specificity. - PMID:20166095, PMID:23499340

[C | emerging] A clinical classification study identified history and examination items that predicted radicular pain caused by lumbar disc herniation: monoradicular leg pain distribution, unilateral leg pain, positive SLR below 60° (or femoral stretch test), unilateral motor weakness and asymmetric ankle reflex. - PMID:28483706

[C | evidence supported] A guideline-based review (German National Disease Management Guideline) emphasises history, exclusion of neurological deficits and red flags, and no initial imaging when no specific cause is found. The excerpted abstract does not recommend routine laboratory tests. Further testing is reserved for suspected fracture, infection or tumour. - PMID:27120496

[C | evidence supported] The general diagnostic approach is to screen for red flags in the history and examination. Imaging is of limited value without them. The abstract does not recommend routine baseline blood tests. - PMID:15949776, PMID:25398569

[C | emerging] In patients with chronic low back pain or radiculopathy due to disc and degenerative causes, ESR and hsCRP were generally not raised. This suggests that routine inflammatory markers add little in uncomplicated chronic disc-related pain, but the study was not designed to evaluate screening. - PMID:20556218

[C | emerging] In ED patients with spinal pain who underwent MRI, low ESR and CRP values helped rule out infectious spinal pathology. This is a rule-out application in a setting where infection was already a concern, not baseline testing for suspected disc disease. - PMID:40689404

[C | emerging] In a retrospective single-centre study of euthyroid, levothyroxine-treated patients with overt primary hypothyroidism, antibody-positive patients needed higher mean daily levothyroxine doses than antibody-negative patients. TPOAb and TgAb titers correlated weakly with dose. This is an association, and dose also correlated with weight and BMI. - PMID:28578356

[C | emerging] A retrospective study in hypothyroid women with Hashimoto's thyroiditis found that more than half needed higher levothyroxine doses postpartum than before pregnancy. Women whose dose had to be increased stepwise through gestation were far more likely to need a dose at least 20% above baseline at 3 months postpartum. The authors attributed this to thyroid functional reserve and progression of autoimmune destruction. - PMID:20615129

[C | emerging] Among euthyroid TPOAb-positive women trying to conceive, about 7% developed subclinical or overt hypothyroidism within a year. Higher baseline TSH and TPOAb titers were associated with developing hypothyroidism. Regular thyroid function monitoring is suggested for TPOAb-positive women trying to conceive. - PMID:36103260

[C | emerging] Euthyroid TPOAb-positive women likely have a higher risk of miscarriage and preterm birth. It is unknown whether this works through the thyroid or through general autoimmune susceptibility. Available data do not support a recommendation for or against gestational levothyroxine in this group. - PMID:35798546

[C | emerging] Smaller prospective studies in euthyroid TPOAb-positive pregnant women reported fewer miscarriages and preterm deliveries with levothyroxine. The meta-analysis of RCTs did not confirm these effects. - PMID:16621910, PMID:27879326

[C | emerging] In Hashimoto's thyroiditis, anti-thyroid antibody levels were negatively correlated with quality of life, whereas TSH and thyroid hormone levels showed no consistent association. This is an association only, and some studies did not confirm it. - PMID:41766594

[C | evidence supported] Dietary fibre, certain foods and mineral supplements can significantly reduce levothyroxine absorption. This is a non-immunological factor that could affect dose requirement or TSH stability, independent of TPOAb status. - PMID:42278392

[C | emerging] An audit in subclinical hypothyroidism supported cascade anti-TPO testing, because TPOAb positivity predicts progression to overt disease and was used to guide thyroxine prescribing. This applies to untreated subclinical disease, not to established treated hypothyroidism. - PMID:15117432

[C | evidence supported] Systematic reviews in the sources show that individual physical examination tests have limited or variable diagnostic accuracy for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy. They give indirect context for examination, but they are not the NASS recommendations. - PMID:20166095, PMID:23499340

[C | emerging] The 2025 Korean LDH-with-radiculopathy guideline, as described in its abstract, organises its key clinical questions around treatment (surgical, interventional, physical/exercise). No diagnostic or initial-evaluation question is listed in the available text. - PMID:40625002

[C | evidence supported] In emergency-department patients with spine pain and a risk factor for spinal epidural abscess (a red-flag context), ESR had high sensitivity and moderate specificity. This supports ESR/CRP when serious infection is suspected. It does not address routine testing without red flags. - PMID:21417700

[C | evidence supported] A 2025 international consensus on pyogenic spondylodiscitis states that ESR and CRP remain the most reliable diagnostic tests. This applies to suspected spinal infection, not to non-specific back pain without red flags. - PMID:42678285

[D | guideline supported] The ENDO-ERN congenital hypothyroidism consensus recommends confirmatory serum free T4 and TSH measurement after an abnormal screen. This is the only source that explicitly names baseline confirmatory tests, and it applies to neonates. (verified with caveat) - PMID:33272083

[D | emerging] A narrative review in patients with vitiligo suggests TSH is the practical initial test, with further laboratory evaluation guided by clinical presentation and risk factors. It lists anti-TPO antibodies as a marker that may identify thyroid autoimmunity before overt dysfunction. - PMID:42542894

[D | guideline supported] Guidelines differ on the preferred imaging modality. CT is described as a consistent 'should do' when history and examination fit disc herniation after 4-6 weeks of pain, if surgery is considered, or with severe or progressive neurological signs. MRI is described as a common 'should do' under similar triggers, including when an epidural steroid injection is being considered. (verified with caveat) - PMID:34205193

[D | emerging] Suspected cauda equina syndrome is a red-flag presentation that requires emergent assessment. A case report states emergent MRI followed by decompression is the standard of care, and notes that a full infectious workup, including inflammatory markers and cultures, was useful in an atypical cystic and infectious presentation. - PMID:42677046

[D | guideline supported] The guideline abstract states that the decision to treat subclinical hypothyroidism when TSH is below 10 mIU/L should be tailored to the individual patient. A secondary study reports that the guideline lists TPO antibody positivity, cardiovascular risk factors and symptoms or signs of hypothyroidism as factors to consider. This is the only place anti-TPO antibodies appear in the sources, and it concerns treatment decisions in subclinical disease rather than initial work-up. (verified with caveat) - PMID:22954017, PMID:23627903

[D | emerging] A positive TPOAb marks increased risk of hypothyroidism in euthyroid people. Sources suggest TPOAb or TSH testing in women planning pregnancy or at higher risk, and describe fertility and pregnancy benefits of levothyroxine in hypothyroid women with HT. This is indirect evidence that antibody status may matter for pregnancy-related counselling and TSH surveillance, though in this patient hypothyroidism is already treated. - PMID:15826919, PMID:23214065, PMID:42278392

[D | emerging] Vitamin D supplementation is reported to lower thyroid antibodies only in euthyroid TPOAb-positive patients with baseline deficiency, with diminished efficacy in overt hypothyroidism. RCTs are mixed, including a double-blind RCT with no antibody improvement. Knowing TPOAb status would therefore be unlikely to justify supplementation to lower antibodies in a patient who is already treated for hypothyroidism. - PMID:40822954

[D | emerging] ESR/CRP testing appears in the sources only when red flags or infection risk factors are present, as part of a screening pathway for spinal epidural abscess or as a listed red flag. This is not baseline testing in uncomplicated disc disease. - PMID:21417700, PMID:25057398

[D | guideline supported] The AACE/ATA hypothyroidism guideline abstract names serum TSH as the best screening test and says treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH below 10 mIU/L should be individualised. The abstract does not mention TPOAb testing or any action based on it. The full-text recommendations were not supplied, so no inference can be drawn about them. (verified with caveat) - PMID:22954017

[D | hypothesis] A narrative review on PCOS and thyroid disorders recommends regular screening for thyroid function and thyroid autoantibodies in women with PCOS, especially before and during pregnancy. The patient has no recorded PCOS diagnosis. - PMID:37635968

[D | hypothesis] An immune checkpoint inhibitor review lists baseline thyroid autoantibodies as a consideration for risk stratification before therapy. It notes this is rarely done in practice. This is a practice-gap comment rather than a formal recommendation, and the patient has no recorded ICI exposure. - PMID:42820064

[D | guideline supported] An overview of 15 primary-care guidelines for non-specific low back pain lists history/examination for red flags, neurological testing, selective imaging and psychosocial assessment as diagnostic recommendations. Its abstract does not mention routine laboratory tests such as ESR/CRP. It does not name NICE, ACP or NVL, so it cannot confirm what those guidelines say about labs. (verified with caveat) - PMID:29971708

(verified with caveat) - PMID:22954017

[D | hypothesis] A narrative review on PCOS and thyroid disorders recommends regular screening for thyroid function and thyroid autoantibodies in women with PCOS, especially before and during pregnancy. The patient has no recorded PCOS diagnosis. - PMID:37635968

[D | hypothesis] An immune checkpoint inhibitor review lists baseline thyroid autoantibodies as a consideration for risk stratification before therapy. It notes this is rarely done in practice. This is a practice-gap comment rather than a formal recommendation, and the patient has no recorded ICI exposure. - PMID:42820064

[C | evidence supported] Systematic reviews in the sources show that individual physical examination tests have limited or variable diagnostic accuracy for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy. They give indirect context for examination, but they are not the NASS recommendations. - PMID:20166095, PMID:23499340

[D | guideline supported] An overview of 15 primary-care guidelines for non-specific low back pain lists history/examination for red flags, neurological testing, selective imaging and psychosocial assessment as diagnostic recommendations. Its abstract does not mention routine laboratory tests such as ESR/CRP. It does not name NICE, ACP or NVL, so it cannot confirm what those guidelines say about labs. (verified with caveat) - PMID:29971708

[C | evidence supported] In emergency-department patients with spine pain and a risk factor for spinal epidural abscess (a red-flag context), ESR had high sensitivity and moderate specificity. This supports ESR/CRP when serious infection is suspected. It does not address routine testing without red flags. - PMID:21417700

[C | evidence supported] A 2025 international consensus on pyogenic spondylodiscitis states that ESR and CRP remain the most reliable diagnostic tests. This applies to suspected spinal infection, not to non-specific back pain without red flags. - PMID:42678285

[B | guideline supported] Cervical cancer screening with cervical cytology alone every 3 years is recommended for women aged 21 to 29 years (USPSTF grade A). This is a general preventive service not covered by hypothyroidism or disc care. (verified with caveat) - PMID:30140884

[B | guideline supported] Adults who have never received Tdap are recommended to receive one Tdap dose. After Tdap, adolescents and adults are recommended a Td booster every 10 years. Tdap is also recommended in each pregnancy, although she is not currently pregnant. (verified with caveat) - PMID:29702631

[C | evidence supported] A review of USPSTF recommendations for women of reproductive age lists routine primary-care screening for obesity and other cardiovascular risk factors, depression, intimate partner violence, cervical cancer, HIV, hepatitis C virus, tobacco use, and unhealthy alcohol and drug use. It recommends that physicians focus on USPSTF grade A and B recommendations. - PMID:22393182, PMID:33587575

[C | evidence supported] Sexually active women younger than 25 should be screened routinely for gonorrhea and chlamydia. Syphilis and hepatitis B screening should be individualized. A JAMA syphilis review separately recommends syphilis screening at least once for sexually active people aged 15 to 44. - PMID:33587575, PMID:41100079

[C | evidence supported] Immunizations against influenza, tetanus, measles/mumps/rubella, varicella, meningococcus and human papillomavirus are described as particularly important for women of reproductive age. The excerpts give no schedules or catch-up rules for influenza, MMR, varicella, meningococcal or HPV vaccines. - PMID:33587575

[C | evidence supported] General health maintenance for premenopausal women includes preconception counseling and contraception as needed, which may be relevant for a woman of reproductive age on levothyroxine. This older source also advises screening for obesity and elevated blood pressure. - PMID:23317023

items: [C | emerging] In people taking oral thyroxine replacement, total T4 can be supraphysiological. In one 1984 series, total T4 above 150 nmol/l occurred in treated subjects, which suggests an elevated total T4 on levothyroxine may reflect the replacement itself rather than intrinsic thyroid disease. Dose adequacy cannot be judged from total T4 alone. - PMID:6548596

[C | emerging] Free T4 measurement may separate dysfunction from normality better than total T4 when binding proteins vary, but free T4 assays also give discrepant results in some extrathyroidal states (TBG deficiency/excess, late pregnancy, serious illness, T4 administration). Both measures therefore have limitations. - PMID:23301702, PMID:6818530

[C | evidence supported] Thyroid status in the sources is classified using TSH together with free T4, not total T4 alone. Monitoring of treated hypothyroidism interpreted against this framework would need TSH and free T4 results, with the assay and its reference range noted. - PMID:38243784

[C | evidence supported] Total and free T4 rise transiently after an oral levothyroxine dose, so random (post-dose) samples read higher than trough samples; in one outpatient study the average excess was about 8-9% for total T4 and about 13-15% for free T4. - PMID:8369656

[C | evidence supported] The post-dose rise in free T4 is consistent across studies, peaking about 2-4 h after record (about +15-25%) and returning toward baseline within 24 h. Total T4 and free T4 are elevated within about 1 h and remain elevated for at least 6 h. - PMID:36762702, PMID:3766048, PMID:6627702

[C | evidence supported] The size of the post-dose rise appears to depend on dose and baseline level: patients with higher basal levels and higher replacement doses had the largest rises. Supranormal values after a dose occurred only at the highest dose tested in one study. A rise can move a value from the reference range into the abnormal range. - PMID:6621483

[C | evidence supported] TSH responds less consistently to dose timing than T4. One study found TSH about 19% lower in random than trough samples in replacement patients. Others found no significant change over 8 h, with large intra-individual TSH variability. TSH is therefore not a clean marker of the T4 timing artefact. - PMID:3359603, PMID:6463564, PMID:8369656

[C | evidence supported] In the sources, over-replacement was identified by the combination of suppressed TSH and raised free T4, not by T3. T3 testing added little: normal T3 was seen in over-replaced patients. No source supplies a total T4 cut-off for over-replacement. - PMID:26738396

[C | evidence supported] High free T4 with a TSH that is not suppressed is common in levothyroxine users and was mainly explained by levothyroxine record and blood-draw timing, not assay faults. Elevated T4 values in clinically euthyroid levothyroxine users are also reported with older analog methods and in TSH-suppression settings. - PMID:2588121, PMID:36762702

[C | evidence supported] Authors recommend accounting for dose timing, with trough sampling (before the daily dose) preferred, to avoid unnecessary dose changes. One study concluded strict timing was probably unnecessary. - PMID:36762702, PMID:6463564

[C | emerging] In a small double-blind RCT of adults with subclinical hypothyroidism (not on levothyroxine), 8 weeks of ashwagandha root extract was associated with lower TSH and higher T3 and T4 than placebo. - PMID:28829155

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of 30 human studies reported no serious adverse events, but it noted increased T4 with the root in some studies. The same review reported no changes in biochemical parameters. This is a general-safety statement and is not specific to thyroid disease or levothyroxine. - PMID:32201301

[C | evidence supported] FDH is typically seen as raised total T4 with normal TSH in a clinically euthyroid person. A normal sensitive TSH with euthyroidism separates it from thyrotoxicosis. Demonstrating excess T4 binding to albumin establishes the diagnosis and separates it from thyroid hormone resistance. - PMID:15251607

[C | evidence supported] The differential for euthyroid hyperthyroxinaemia includes assay interference from heterophile antibodies, biotin and anti-analyte antibodies. The review cites biotin-loaded supplements as an emerging interference. The patient's supplement composition is unverified. - PMID:34374345

[C | emerging] In a single-centre retrospective study, TT4/TT3 and FT3/ULN ratios and a somatostatin analogue test helped distinguish FDH from thyroid hormone resistance and TSHoma. The authors state that validation in larger cohorts is needed. - PMID:41920220

[C | evidence supported] In adults on levothyroxine, random-time samples showed total T4 about 8-9% higher than trough samples (more than 22 h post-dose). The rise was larger for free T4, at about 13-15%. So the relative post-dose excursion is smaller for total T4 than for free T4. - PMID:8369656

[C | evidence supported] In a dose-ranging study (100-300 ug), total T4, free thyroxine index and free T4 rose significantly by 1 h and stayed elevated for at least 6 h. Supranormal values occurred only after the highest dose. TSH and T3 did not change significantly. - PMID:6627702

[C | emerging] One observational study used an operational definition of levothyroxine over-replacement: fully suppressed TSH (<0.02 mU/L) with free T4 above the reference range (>27 pmol/L). Patients with low but measurable TSH and normal free T4 were used as the comparison group. The definition was applied to clinic samples and was not validated against outcomes or taken at a defined trough. - PMID:26738396

[C | evidence supported] Sampling time relative to the levothyroxine dose affects the results. Random clinic samples had higher total and free T4 and lower TSH than trough samples (>22 h after the dose). Free T4 stayed elevated for about 9 h after a dose. A high free T4 or lower TSH on a post-dose sample can therefore overstate over-replacement, so trough sampling is needed to separate true over-replacement from a timing artefact. - PMID:8369656

[C | emerging] T3 measurement is of doubtful value for identifying over-replacement. No patient in the over-replaced group had a raised T3, and T3 discriminated poorly (sensitivity 58%, specificity 71%). A normal T3 therefore does not exclude over-replacement. - PMID:26738396

[C | evidence supported] Reviews recommend adjusting levothyroxine so TSH, measured by sensitive assays, lies within the normal range, and warn that over-replacement is common and linked to atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis. Suppressed TSH is the central biochemical signal of over-replacement. The specific TSH targets proposed differ between sources. - PMID:22191793, PMID:3059080

[C | emerging] In an 8-week pilot RCT in untreated subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4.5-10 µIU/L), ashwagandha root extract lowered TSH and raised T3 and T4 compared with placebo. This is the only direct human trial of ashwagandha's effect on thyroid tests in hypothyroid-range patients in the sources. It did not include people on levothyroxine. - PMID:28829155

[C | emerging] For interpreting thyroid tests during supplement use, one review notes that TSH should be assessed together with free T3 or free T4 rather than total hormone levels. Free fractions are the biologically active ones. - PMID:41454558

[C | evidence supported] Biotin supplementation is a documented cause of analytical interference in streptavidin-biotin-based immunoassays, the formats commonly used for thyroid hormone measurement. It can produce false positive or false negative results and a seemingly coherent but spurious hormonal profile, including a false biochemical picture of hyperthyroidism. - PMID:27732554

[C | evidence supported] Thyroid function immunoassays (TSH, free T4, free T3) are vulnerable to six main interference types: macro-TSH, biotin, anti-streptavidin antibodies, anti-ruthenium antibodies, thyroid hormone autoantibodies and heterophilic antibodies. Reported interferences often led to misdiagnosis or inappropriate management. Suspicion should be raised when clinical and biochemical findings are discordant, and identification relies on additional laboratory work-up. - PMID:29982406

[C | evidence supported] The only general prevalence figure in the sources is about 1 in 10,000 in Caucasian populations. One review notes that prevalence can be much higher in some ethnic groups, but no South Asian figure is given. - PMID:29163366

[C | evidence supported] In FDH, total T4 is consistently elevated, and free T4 by direct immunoassay is frequently falsely elevated. Free T4 by direct dialysis with tandem mass spectrometry is usually normal. This was shown in euthyroid, untreated individuals, so it is indirect evidence for a levothyroxine-treated patient. - PMID:3111180, PMID:31822224

[C | evidence supported] Susceptibility of free T4 immunoassays to FDH interference varies by platform. One study found all assays except Ortho VITROS gave raised FT4 and found no consistent link to one-step versus two-step architecture. A study of the R222I variant reported more abnormal values in one-step than two-step assays, with an exception for Beckman Access. Some genetically affected relatives had normal FT4 on certain assays. - PMID:24646103, PMID:32213658

[C | evidence supported] Reference-method free hormone measurement (equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration with LC-MS/MS) is considered more accurate and robust than immunoassays. It is the approach used to resolve FDH discordance, but it is not available in many laboratories. - PMID:38716305

[C | evidence supported] Because TSH is not suppressed in FDH, TSH can distinguish FDH from true thyrotoxicosis in untreated patients. A general review notes TSH can be misleading when thyroid status is unstable on levothyroxine (first months of treatment or altered dose). That review states only free hormone measurements are reliable in that setting. This creates a practical tension for interpreting an FDH patient on levothyroxine. - PMID:12915350, PMID:3111180

[C | evidence supported] Factors that can raise TSH or cause apparent levothyroxine refractoriness, such as malabsorption from dietary fibre or soy, may confound interpretation of thyroid tests on treatment. They are independent of FDH assay artefact. - PMID:37067253

[C | evidence supported] Biotin at elevated serum concentrations interferes with biotin-streptavidin immunoassays. Competitive formats (typically FT4, FT3) show falsely increased results, and sandwich formats (typically TSH) show falsely decreased results. - PMID:35953126, PMID:37370185

[C | evidence supported] Over-the-counter biotin doses (5-20 mg/day) have been reported to interfere with thyroid function tests. A review states that 24-72 hours off biotin is often sufficient for OTC doses, with longer intervals possibly needed for high-dose therapy. Another review cites more than 48 hours. - PMID:30872068, PMID:42933321

[C | evidence supported] Susceptibility is assay- and platform-dependent. On one Beckman analyzer, TSH and total T4 (non-biotin-based) were unaffected while FT4, FT3 and total T3 showed positive interference. A reformulated Beckman FT4 assay showed negligible biotin interference. - PMID:32567529, PMID:36889777, PMID:40064456

[C | guideline supported] The ETA 2026 guideline recommends considering assay interference when thyroid function tests are incongruent with the clinical picture or with each other. It also recommends clinical review including medication history for suspected interference. Its abstract lists pharmaceutical causes such as displacing agents and biotin. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42466561

[C | evidence supported] Undetected interference has led to misdiagnosis and inappropriate management. Reviewers specifically flag the risk in patients on levothyroxine whose dose is titrated by thyroid function tests. - PMID:29982406, PMID:37370185

[D | emerging] Altered serum protein binding of T4 can produce a high total T4 and a high free T4 index with a normal free T4 and normal T3 in euthyroid people. An inherited increase in the affinity of T4 for binding proteins has been described, and it is a recognised confounder when only total T4 is measured. - PMID:85873

[D | hypothesis] Total T4 immunoassay results depend on which binding protein carries T4 and vary substantially between assays. Values were under-represented when T4 was bound to TBG and over-represented when bound to albumin or transthyretin, so a single total T4 value may not reflect true hormone concentration. - PMID:15687815

[D | emerging] A secondary analysis of thyroid indices in a bipolar-disorder RCT found numerically higher free T4 with ashwagandha but no statistically significant difference between groups. The authors suggested ashwagandha may increase thyroxine and that vigilance for hyperthyroidism may be warranted. - PMID:25624699

[D | hypothesis] A case report describes thyrotoxicosis, confirmed by laboratory assessment, in a healthy woman taking an ashwagandha extract. It resolved after the capsules were stopped. - PMID:16355578

[D | hypothesis] Rodent studies report that ashwagandha root extract raises circulating T4 (and T3 in male mice) and, in PTU-induced hypothyroid rat models, restores thyroid hormones and lowers TSH. This provides a mechanistic hypothesis for the human findings. - PMID:10619390, PMID:9811169

[D | emerging] Recent narrative reviews describe ashwagandha as increasing T3/T4 and lowering TSH, and flag people with thyroid disorders as a group potentially at risk. They also link its endocrine activity to reports of thyrotoxicosis. - PMID:38003702, PMID:41454545, PMID:41502355

[D | evidence supported] Reported FDH prevalence ranges widely, from 0.01% to 1.8% depending on the population. It may be underestimated because TSH-only screening misses it. No South Asian-specific figure is given in the supplied sources. - PMID:33728390

[D | evidence supported] In FDH, free T4 is normal by equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration but can be artefactually high on analogue immunoassays. Reference methods (equilibrium dialysis, LC-MS/MS) can be used to confirm the true free T4 when a binding abnormality is suspected. - PMID:3111180, PMID:33728390

[D | emerging] Immunoassay free T4 interference in FDH differs by platform and by ALB variant. Abbott ARCHITECT showed the least interference in several reports, but it is prone to substantial interference with the p.Arg242Pro variant. Even 2-step assays can be affected. - PMID:41799632

[D | emerging] Genetic confirmation by ALB hotspot sequencing (the Arg242His variant is the commonest reported) is suggested as a simple alternative to complex laboratory and imaging tests. FDH is autosomal dominant and generally benign, but misdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary treatment. - PMID:38736368

[D | emerging] Where FDH coexists with primary hypothyroidism, one source advises titrating levothyroxine by TSH rather than free T4 to avoid undertreatment. Counselling and family screening are suggested to avoid unnecessary hyperthyroidism treatment. - PMID:33728390

[D | hypothesis] Elevated total T4 or free T4 with normal T3 is common in clinically euthyroid patients taking levothyroxine, so a raised T4 or free T4 alone is an unreliable marker of over-replacement. In one study, 41-63% of euthyroid patients on L-thyroxine had free T4 in the hyperthyroid range depending on the analog assay, and TSH was lower than in controls. A smaller study found suppressed TSH response to protirelin and shortened systolic time intervals in patients with high T4 and normal T3, which the authors interpreted as possible subclinical hyperthyroidism. - PMID:2495780, PMID:2588121

[D | emerging] A hospital chart review used TSH <0.1 µU/mL as inappropriately suppressed on levothyroxine. It found this in 12.2% of 905 patients, 7% with no indication for suppression, and 2.5% overtly thyrotoxic. This shows that suppressed TSH is frequent in routine care. The review does not define a free T4 pattern. - PMID:9625507

[D | emerging] Case reports describe thyrotoxicosis (suppressed TSH, raised fT4) during ashwagandha supplement use. It resolved after the supplement was stopped. A causal relationship has not been established. - PMID:16355578, PMID:41454558

[D | hypothesis] One case report describes a woman who stopped levothyroxine, which she had taken for 2 years for hypothyroidism, and replaced it with ashwagandha. Her TSH was then below the normal range with normal fT4 and T3. After ashwagandha was stopped she returned to a mildly hypothyroid state. This is the only treated-hypothyroidism report in the sources. It describes substitution rather than use alongside levothyroxine. - PMID:41454558

[D | emerging] In an 8-week RCT in bipolar disorder, thyroid indices were measured only as a safety check. In this small set of abnormal results, the three ashwagandha-treated patients' T4 rose from baseline and most placebo patients' T4 fell. The authors advise vigilance for hyperthyroidism. - PMID:25624699

[D | hypothesis] Rodent studies found that ashwagandha root extract raises serum T3 and T4, with evidence of increased thyroid activity. In propylthiouracil-induced hypothyroid rats, extracts lowered TSH and restored T3 and T4. These findings are mechanistic or hypothesis-level and do not support clinical recommendations. - PMID:9811169

[D | hypothesis] Ashwagandha interferes with some immunoassays, but not with the thyroid assays in the supplied sources. It produced assay-dependent apparent digoxin concentrations (probably through structurally similar alkaloids) and negative interference in an IL-6 assay, with no effect on CRP or on the digoxin assay in the IL-6 study. These data do not establish interference in TSH, FT4 or T3 assays. - PMID:17683192, PMID:35414513

[D | emerging] Reported thyroid abnormalities after ashwagandha use are described as true physiological or drug-induced effects, not analytical artefact. A case of painless thyroiditis was supported by scintigraphy showing deficient uptake, and thyrotoxicosis resolved after discontinuation in a second case. A randomized trial in hypothyroidism is cited (secondhand, within the case report) as showing improved TSH, T3 and T4 versus placebo. A raised or lowered thyroid test in a patient taking ashwagandha could therefore be real, but the sources do not allow real changes to be distinguished from artefact in this patient. - PMID:16355578, PMID:38559552

[D | emerging] Discordant thyroid function results across analytical platforms can indicate assay interference in a patient with treated hypothyroidism. One case report describes falsely elevated free T4 by immunoassay, resolved by interference work-up, which avoided unnecessary investigation and treatment. This case was not attributed to a supplement. - PMID:19225029

[D | emerging] A family of Bangladeshi extraction had FDH caused by a novel ALB variant (R218S, also written p.Arg242Ser with the signal peptide counted). Two family members were affected. - PMID:24494774

[D | hypothesis] The only treated-hypothyroid FDH evidence is a single case report. After starting T4, equilibrium-dialysis FT4 rose to hyperthyroid levels with TSH suppression, and the patient was intolerant of treatment. This was attributed to a putative inhibitor of T4 binding. This is not generalisable, but it suggests free T4 behaviour on replacement may be unpredictable in FDH. - PMID:8929830
[E | hypothesis] The supplied sources do not compare post-dose total T4 rises across assay methods or platforms. Dependence on assay method cannot be assessed from this evidence. - PMID:8369656

blocks.text: Verified research findings (91)

items: [A | evidence supported] Motor control exercise (MCE) is not clinically more effective than other forms of exercise for chronic non-specific LBP at any follow-up period (including long-term, 12 months or more). Choice of exercise may therefore reasonably depend on preference, training, cost and safety rather than on exercise type. - PMID:26742533

[B | guideline supported] High-quality guidelines on low back pain (mostly nonspecific LBP) list exercise among the management options for chronic LBP, alongside education, manual therapy and multimodal rehabilitation. The evidence is indirect for LDH specifically. - PMID:27712027

[B | evidence supported] Meta-analyses of RCTs in adults with LDH report that exercise therapy reduces pain and disability, with pain SMD about -0.68. Heterogeneity is substantial, and the authors note that no specific recommendations exist for exercise intensity, frequency or type. - PMID:40224631, PMID:42215311

[B | evidence supported] A head-to-head RCT of motor control exercises versus graded activity found no significant differences between groups at any time point up to 12 months for pain, function, disability, global change or quality of life. A separate RCT of high-load lifting versus low-load motor control exercise found no difference through 24 months. - PMID:22135712, PMID:27097785

[B | evidence supported] Psychologically informed care delivered with physiotherapy (mainly structured exercise) appears more effective than psychological intervention alone. Cognitive behavioural therapy and mindfulness probably reduce pain and disability at long-term follow-up (moderate certainty). Behavioural therapy with physiotherapy maintained clinically important pain effects to mid-term follow-up. - PMID:35354560, PMID:40449512

[C | emerging] A review of air pollution and biological aging reports that system-level composite clinical biomarker measures (KDM biological age, PhenoAge) showed the most robust associations with exposure, while epigenetic clock findings were inconclusive at meta-analytic level. This is not about hypothyroidism. - PMID:42617978

[C | emerging] In a small case-control study of end-stage renal disease, epigenetic age estimators showed accelerated aging, and an inflammatory-profile clock (ipAGE) was more sensitive. This illustrates that clock behaviour is studied disease by disease; no equivalent hypothyroidism data were provided. - PMID:35237926

[C | emerging] One cross-cohort study found that adding epigenetic age (especially GrimAge) to creatinine-based eGFR models improved mortality prediction in the UK Biobank and NHANES general populations. Thyroid status was not reported in the provided abstract. - PMID:42165591

[C | evidence supported] A general-adult guideline recommends a diet emphasising vegetables, fruits, nuts, whole grains, lean protein and fish, and minimising trans fats, processed meats, refined carbohydrates and sweetened beverages. It is for cardiovascular prevention and not specific to hypothyroidism or disc disease. - PMID:30879339

[C | evidence supported] The same guideline recommends at least 150 min/week of moderate-intensity (or 75 min/week of vigorous) physical activity for all adults. Whether and how this applies to chronic low back pain from L4-L5 disc compression is not addressed in the sources. - PMID:30879339

[C | evidence supported] The same guideline recommends assessing tobacco use at every healthcare visit and advising those who use tobacco to quit. The patient's smoking status is not recorded. - PMID:30879339

[C | evidence supported] Higher ultra-processed food exposure is associated with higher risks of adverse cardiometabolic, mental-health and mortality outcomes. The evidence is observational, mostly low or very low GRADE certainty, and association is not causation. - PMID:38418082

[C | emerging] In NHANES, Hashimoto's thyroiditis (HT) was associated with higher KDM biological age and PhenoAge after adjustment for age, sex, socioeconomic and lifestyle factors. The same direction appeared in two clinical discovery cohorts. Associations were also seen in euthyroid HT, and were larger in subclinical hypothyroid HT. Elevated estimates therefore are not limited to biochemically overt hypothyroidism, and may reflect autoimmunity, inflammation or other correlates. This is an association, not evidence of causation. - PMID:42434311

[C | emerging] In NHANES, phenotypic age (and its age gap) was associated with thyroid indices and thyroid disease. TSH and FT4 had U-shaped relationships with phenotypic age, and the age gap was positively associated with TSH. Subclinical hypothyroidism and TPOAb/TGAb positivity were associated with higher phenotypic age. Mediation modelling (in the direction aging to thyroid disease) found that MCV mediated 10% of the association between phenotypic age and overt hypothyroidism, and lymphocyte percentage had a negative mediation effect (-26%) for subclinical hypothyroidism. This indicates that components of the PhenoAge formula track with thyroid status, but it does not show that thyroid dysfunction changes the components. - PMID:40687584

[C | emerging] Biological-age algorithms are validated for mortality prediction in general or diabetic populations, and disease states shift the estimates. KDM predicted mortality better than chronological age in NHANES III. In diabetes, KDM-based biological age was substantially higher than in people without diabetes. – of the supplied sources validated PhenoAge or KDM specifically in treated or untreated hypothyroidism, so the interpretability of these measures in this setting is unverified. - PMID:23213031

[C | emerging] Motor control training for symptomatic LDH improved pain and function versus TENS in the short term in non-surgical patients. Certainty of evidence was very low to low, and most trials were at high risk of bias. - PMID:35701082

[C | emerging] A large meta-analysis of conservative physiotherapy for LDH found large pooled effects, but the authors state that the wide confidence intervals for exercise and manipulation cross the null. They also report that shorter follow-up was associated with larger effects, which suggests overestimation of benefit. - PMID:41209688

[C | emerging] For lumbar radiculopathy, a narrative systematic review of 19 RCTs found short-term improvements with conservative interventions, including exercise-based combinations. It concluded that firm conclusions on comparative effectiveness cannot be drawn. - PMID:42434659

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of human adult studies found most reported increased arterial stiffness biomarkers in hypothyroidism, even in subclinical and mild forms. Heterogeneity of methods and designs prevented a definitive conclusion. - PMID:35683533

[C | evidence supported] Endothelial dysfunction, measured by flow-mediated dilation (FMD), is reported in subclinical and overt hypothyroidism. A cited meta-analysis of 10 studies found lower endothelial function in subclinical hypothyroidism, and individual studies including young women support this. - PMID:23776901, PMID:25563466, PMID:40390147

[C | emerging] Evidence for increased carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) is less consistent. Some studies found higher IMT or carotid stiffness in hypothyroid or subclinical hypothyroid patients, while another small study found no difference in CIMT or aortic distensibility in subclinical hypothyroidism despite impaired FMD. - PMID:15740929, PMID:21111945, PMID:23776901

[C | emerging] Severity of thyroid dysfunction (TSH) relates to the degree of vascular stiffening. TSH independently correlated with PWV in women with hypothyroidism, and mild stiffness changes were seen even at TSH 2.01-4.0. Age independently predicts stiffness, adding about 0.068 m/s PWV per year in the meta-regression. - PMID:16061115, PMID:31557076, PMID:35284772

[C | emerging] Small uncontrolled before-and-after studies report improvement of arterial stiffness, IMT and endothelial dysfunction after levothyroxine-restored euthyroidism. A narrative review notes that only some studies have shown improved vascular function on levothyroxine, and the authors call for RCTs. - PMID:15740929, PMID:25563466, PMID:40390147

[C | emerging] Causality and magnitude of vascular risk remain uncertain. A review states that the causal link between subclinical hypothyroidism and cardiovascular outcomes is unclear, and that associations are stronger in younger people and diminish in older adults because TSH rises physiologically with age. No source directly tests 'accelerated vascular ageing' (vascular age vs chronological age) in treated hypothyroidism. - PMID:40255342

[C | emerging] Measures that capture vascular involvement: PWV is described as the gold-standard method for aortic stiffness and is consistently elevated. FMD is a dynamic functional measure that may be abnormal when structural measures (CIMT, aortic distensibility) are normal. - PMID:23776901, PMID:35284772

[C | evidence supported] A 2024 primary-care cohort states that clinical practice guidelines recommend TSH/thyroid function testing every 6-12 months for long-term management of treated hypothyroidism. The guidelines themselves are not supplied, so this is a secondary statement. - PMID:39462347

[C | guideline supported] The ETA 2013 guideline on subclinical hypothyroidism recommends re-checking TSH 2 months after starting L-thyroxine and monitoring at least annually thereafter. It aims for a stable TSH in the lower half of the reference range for most adults. - PMID:24783053

[C | emerging] Retrospective cohorts suggest that less frequent testing (18 months to 2 years) may be acceptable in selected stable patients. The selection criteria were a TSH well within range, a dose at or below 125 µg/day, age under 60 years, and robust follow-up systems. - PMID:17605766, PMID:24333203

[C | evidence supported] Sources support waiting several weeks after a levothyroxine dose change before re-testing TSH or adjusting the dose. Dose changes are advised no more often than every 4-6 weeks or after 6-12 weeks. TSH can take several weeks to normalise after therapy begins. - PMID:2208954, PMID:26594730

[C | evidence supported] TSH is the primary monitoring test. No supplied source gives a guideline interval for routine free T4 in stable treated hypothyroidism. A study of older primary-care patients found that many free T4 tests were done without indication when TSH was normal. - PMID:16608134, PMID:2208954, PMID:26594730

[C | emerging] HT is associated with higher biological age on clinical-biomarker clocks (KDM biological age, PhenoAge), including in euthyroid and subclinical hypothyroid stages. These are blood-chemistry-based clocks, not DNA methylation clocks, so they do not answer the question directly. Results for overt hypothyroid HT were imprecise. - PMID:42434311

[C | evidence supported] Thyroid hormones affect DNA methylation, and many AITD methylation studies have not addressed confounding by reverse causation. Many findings are unreplicated and lack functional support. Any observed epigenetic-clock difference in thyroid disease would therefore be hard to attribute to the disease itself rather than to thyroid hormone state or treatment. - PMID:36420742

[C | evidence supported] Blood cell composition explains a large part of the variation in DNA methylation age (up to 53%) and a smaller part of age acceleration (up to 21%). Clock results in thyroid disease should therefore be interpreted with cell counts in mind, since autoimmune and inflammatory states can alter leukocyte subsets. - PMID:42823742

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review found limited evidence that coffee, soy products, fibre, calcium or iron supplements and enteral nutrition reduce levothyroxine absorption. Maintaining a time interval between levothyroxine and these items was proposed as a way to avoid the interaction. - PMID:33801406

[C | evidence supported] A review recommends separating levothyroxine from interfering foods or medications by 3 to 4 hours. It lists fibres, espresso coffee, grapefruit juice, and calcium and iron salts as interfering agents. - PMID:41109285

[C | emerging] Small observational and pharmacokinetic studies on fibre conflict. In hypothyroid patients requiring high doses, dietary fibre supplements were linked to higher T4 requirements through nonspecific adsorption of T4 to fibre. Two pharmacological fibre supplements (calcium polycarbophil, psyllium) did not cause detectable malabsorption in 8 volunteers. A review states the effect of dietary fibre remains incompletely understood. - PMID:28153426, PMID:8636317, PMID:9737361
[C | emerging] A small before/after study of 37 hypothyroid patients linked long-term tea consumption to reduced levothyroxine absorption, similar to coffee. - PMID:36171905

[C | evidence supported] Time of dosing (morning versus bedtime) is reported as comparably effective in a meta-analysis cited by a systematic review. A narrative review reports crossover studies where non-fasting dosing was associated with higher TSH. It concludes that the main variable is whether the stomach contains food or other substances at dosing. - PMID:33801406, PMID:34671932

[C | emerging] In a cross-sectional study, Hashimoto's thyroiditis was associated with higher clinical-biomarker biological age (KDM biological age, PhenoAge) and higher metabolic age acceleration. This is the only direct human evidence in the sources for accelerated ageing in autoimmune thyroiditis. The measures are blood-biomarker and metabolomic ageing indices, not epigenetic clocks, and the design cannot show causation. - PMID:42434311

[C | evidence supported] Anti-TPO is not specific to Hashimoto thyroiditis. It is found in most patients with Graves' disease, in some people with non-thyroid autoimmune disease and in some normal subjects. A positive result therefore does not by itself establish Hashimoto aetiology. - PMID:10483258

[C | evidence supported] Anti-TPO antibodies above an assay-dependent cut-off are a risk factor for later hypothyroidism in euthyroid people. This is the main evidence that antibody status carries prognostic information. - PMID:15826919

[C | emerging] A systematic review of population-based studies found no statistically significant association between TPO antibody positivity and anxiety disorders. The authors conclude the evidence is inconclusive. A review of euthyroid Hashimoto thyroiditis suggests affective and cognitive symptoms may be linked to TPO antibody levels, but it is mechanistically speculative. - PMID:24685840, PMID:42569470

[C | emerging] A systematic review found that, in most included studies, poorer sleep quality and/or shorter sleep duration correlated with subclinical hypothyroidism. This is an association with the thyroid condition, not with fatigue or sleepiness, and the direction of causality is unresolved. - PMID:38548514

[C | emerging] A narrative review of commonly prescribed medications reports that levothyroxine does not significantly disrupt sleep, and that evening administration may enhance hypothyroidism management. This suggests levothyroxine itself is an unlikely main cause of sleep disruption, but the review gives no fatigue or sleepiness outcomes. - PMID:40318905

[C | emerging] A prospective study of 92 patients with primary hypothyroidism found that levothyroxine reduced fatigue in most patients. Higher pre-treatment fatigue scores and diabetes predicted persistent fatigue; sleep was not reported as a predictor. - PMID:36979787

[C | emerging] Persistent or new symptoms, with fatigue the most constant, were reported in about 1 in 4 levothyroxine-treated patients with normal TSH in a retrospective chart review. The cause was described as unclear. The abstract does not examine sleep as a contributor. - PMID:37913925

[C | emerging] A narrative review of narrow practical scope advises excluding non-thyroid causes (other autoimmune conditions, anemia, mental health disorders) in symptomatic patients on adequate levothyroxine. It does not list sleep disorders explicitly in the abstract. - PMID:33112818

[C | emerging] In small before-and-after cohorts of adults with SCH, LT4 treatment was followed by lower hs-CRP, a low-grade inflammation marker linked to cardiovascular risk. A meta-analysis found a favourable effect of LT4 on CRP, mainly in overt hypothyroidism. This is a surrogate marker, and an RCT found no CRP change in SCH. - PMID:32880055, PMID:38249164

[C | emerging] Lipid and CK responses to LT4 differ by severity. In one cohort, LT4 did not change TC, HDL-c, LDL-c, CK or creatinine in SCH, but lowered these markers in overt hypothyroidism. Another before-and-after study of untreated primary hypothyroidism found improved lipid parameters and fasting insulin, with no significant change in HOMA-IR or QUICKI. - PMID:42827785

[C | evidence supported] Bladder or bowel dysfunction from lumbar disc herniation (cauda equina syndrome) is an absolute surgical emergency and should prompt immediate evaluation. Acute conus/cauda symptoms occur in roughly 1-1.5% of patients with disc herniation. - PMID:38835174, PMID:42384175

[C | evidence supported] Clinical history and physical examination are the core of monitoring, and red flags are what trigger further imaging. Screening for serious pathology and watching for neurological deficit, cauda equina syndrome or refractory pain are described as essential parts of management. - PMID:10029785, PMID:42384175

[C | evidence supported] New neurological deficit or worsening pain is an indication for early surgical assessment. Greater weakness and longer symptom duration are associated with poorer neurological recovery. - PMID:38835174

[C | evidence supported] Most symptomatic herniations improve with conservative care. Reassessment and escalation are tied to failure to improve over about 6-12 weeks, or to the presence of a corresponding neurological deficit with imaging confirmation. - PMID:2139310, PMID:38835174

[C | emerging] In a longitudinal within-person analysis (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging), thyroid hormone use was associated with lower values of some phenotypic-aging markers (body composition, neuroplasticity/neurodegeneration). In fully adjusted models it was not associated with PhenoAge. This is general medication-category data, not hypothyroid-specific or euthyroid-restoration data. It is also not a treatment-effect estimate for levothyroxine on PhenoAge or KDM. - PMID:40498559

[C | emerging] Cross-sectional data associate Hashimoto's thyroiditis with higher KDM biological age and PhenoAge, including in euthyroid HT, compared with controls. This shows the age estimates differ in autoimmune thyroid disease at a single time point. It does not show whether treatment or normalising TSH changes them. - PMID:42434311

[C | guideline supported] Several co-administered substances can reduce oral levothyroxine absorption (for example dietary fibre such as wheat bran, per the guideline table). This could affect whether euthyroidism is actually achieved and so how any biological-age change should be interpreted. This is indirect and does not address biological age itself. - PMID:40622204

[C | emerging] Some exercise trials suggest benefits persisting beyond one year: a small RCT of supervised home exercise reported lower pain at 5 years than controls, and a graded stabilising exercise RCT showed reduced disability at 12 months, although the pain benefit was seen only immediately post-intervention. A meta-analysis found low-certainty evidence that exercise might reduce disability at very long-term (≥2 years) follow-up. - PMID:17849435, PMID:19179916, PMID:40449512

[C | emerging] Exercise therapy and manual therapy are not clearly different for chronic LBP: a small long-term disability benefit favouring exercise was non-clinically relevant and based on very low certainty evidence. - PMID:40747709

[C | emerging] In small studies, arterial stiffness measures (baPWV, carotid stiffness beta) fell after levothyroxine normalised thyroid function in hypothyroid or subclinical hypothyroid patients. This includes women with autoimmune thyroiditis. In the randomized study the change in baPWV did not correlate with change in TSH, so a TSH dose-response relationship was not shown. - PMID:15740929, PMID:19114542

[C | emerging] In thyroidectomised adults on long-term levothyroxine targeting TSH in the reference range, carotid-femoral PWV and central hemodynamics did not differ from matched controls. This suggests arterial stiffness need not be abnormal when TSH is kept in range. - PMID:27029953

[C | emerging] In young adults with congenital hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine since the first month of life, FMD and brachial artery distensibility were impaired versus controls. Higher mean TSH and undertreatment episodes predicted worse vascular function, suggesting TSH exposure over time may influence residual vascular abnormalities. - PMID:19903797

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of arterial stiffness in thyroid disease found most studies reported increased stiffness biomarkers in hypothyroidism, including subclinical forms, but heterogeneity of methods and designs prevented a definitive conclusion. Evidence for subclinical hypothyroidism was described as conflicting and heterogeneous. - PMID:35683533

[C | evidence supported] Whether levothyroxine replacement improves cardiovascular outcomes in subclinical thyroid dysfunction remains uncertain because adequately powered RCTs are lacking. Therefore, improvements in surrogate vascular markers cannot be taken to show clinical benefit. - PMID:41996368

[C | guideline supported] The 2013 ETA guideline on subclinical hypothyroidism says TSH should be re-checked about 2 months after starting L-thyroxine, with dose adjustment, and then monitored at least annually. This is the only guideline-level interval in the supplied sources, and it applies to subclinical hypothyroidism rather than to treated primary hypothyroidism in general. - PMID:24783053

[C | guideline supported] The ETA 2025 levothyroxine guideline excerpt lists dietary fibre and whey/soy protein supplements as interfering with oral L-thyroxine bioavailability, with advice to separate record by several hours. The excerpt gives no TSH re-check interval after such changes. - PMID:40622204

[C | emerging] In an NHANES 2007-2012 validation cohort, HT was associated with higher KDM biological age and PhenoAge than healthy controls after adjustment for demographic and lifestyle factors. The comparator was healthy controls, not non-autoimmune hypothyroidism. The listed covariates did not include TSH or levothyroxine treatment, so the question's contrast is not answered. - PMID:42434311

[C | emerging] The association with higher biological age was also seen in euthyroid HT (normal thyroid function), which suggests it is not explained solely by thyroid hormone dysfunction. Associations were larger in subclinical hypothyroid HT. Overt hypothyroid HT results were mostly non-significant, with wide confidence intervals and small numbers. - PMID:42434311

[C | emerging] In the general NHANES population, higher phenotypic age was associated with higher odds of TPOAb and TGAb positivity. This is an association between biological age and antibody positivity in a general population sample, not a comparison within hypothyroid patients. - PMID:40687584

[D | hypothesis] In CKD populations, meta-analyses of exercise RCTs show benefit for functional capacity, blood pressure, inflammation markers and mortality (mainly in dialysis). This is indirect evidence, as the patient has no documented CKD. - PMID:41980883

[D | hypothesis] In the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, use of thyroid hormones was associated with reductions in domain-specific Klemera-Doubal phenotypic aging markers (body composition and neuroplasticity/neurodegeneration). These markers are not the standard clinical-chemistry PhenoAge or KDM panel. The finding is observational and potentially confounded by indication, so it provides only indirect, hypothesis-level information about levothyroxine and biological-age estimates. - PMID:40498559

[D | hypothesis] For persistent pain, a narrative review proposes sensitisation-informed management in which graded, time-contingent exercise and pain neuroscience education target pain-related cognitions. This is a mechanism-based proposal rather than proven efficacy in LDH. - PMID:42512439

[D | emerging] A 1990 review recommends that once the optimal replacement dose is determined, monitoring can be yearly or even every two years, depending on patient education and compliance. A 192-patient series concluded that a yearly baseline TSH seems sufficient when there are no intercurrent events. - PMID:1287777, PMID:2208954

[D | emerging] Genome-wide methylation profiling in blood from HT patients (10 matched pairs) showed an overall reduction in methylation, with 283 differentially methylated positions. Epigenetic clocks were not calculated, and the sample was small. - PMID:38075038

[D | emerging] In lymphocytes, patients with autoimmune hypothyroidism and those with positive thyroid autoantibodies had no difference in global DNA methylation versus healthy controls. Levothyroxine replacement for 3 months did not change methylation in these cells. Newly diagnosed Graves' disease (hyperthyroid) did show hypomethylation. This suggests global methylation changes are not a consistent feature of autoimmune hypothyroidism and not clearly altered by levothyroxine, but it is not a clock measurement. - PMID:29336230

[D | hypothesis] A bidirectional Mendelian randomization study found that genetically predicted PhenoAge acceleration (PhenoAA) was associated with higher subacute thyroiditis risk (borderline significance). Subacute thyroiditis was associated with lower intrinsic epigenetic age acceleration (IEAA). Subacute thyroiditis is a transient inflammatory condition, not chronic hypothyroidism, and Hashimoto's or non-autoimmune hypothyroidism was not studied. - PMID:39300457

[D | hypothesis] Human thyroid tissue transcriptomes show age-related downregulation of mitochondrial and proteasomal genes and upregulation of immune-process genes that overlap with those in lymphocytic thyroiditis. This supports a mechanistic link between thyroid ageing, mitochondrial dysfunction and autoimmune inflammation within the gland. It does not show that hypothyroidism causes systemic mitochondrial dysfunction or inflammation. - PMID:29652618

[D | hypothesis] Single-cell human thyroid data identified a senescent epithelial cell subgroup with a senescence-associated secretory phenotype that increases with age. Thyroid-specific Bmal1 knockout in mice and cell-line experiments suggest circadian-gene downregulation accelerates thyroid cellular senescence and impairs hormone synthesis. This is cellular-senescence evidence in the thyroid itself, mostly preclinical. - PMID:40434135

[D | hypothesis] A hypothesis paper proposes that telomere shortening links autoimmune thyroiditis, thyroid dysfunction and parity. The abstract states autoimmune thyroiditis shows some degree of telomere shortening, but it presents no new data in the abstract. - PMID:29857903

[D | hypothesis] Some sources point the opposite way from accelerated ageing: subclinical hypothyroidism has been paradoxically associated with longevity in some centenarian cohorts, possibly via reduced oxidative metabolism. Higher adipose TSHB expression correlated with fewer senescence markers and longer telomeres in euthyroid subjects. Higher cord-blood TSH correlated with shorter relative telomere length in neonates. The direction of any thyroid-ageing association is therefore inconsistent across tissues, ages and study types. - PMID:30448824, PMID:38326475, PMID:40921197

[D | emerging] One review addresses antibody testing for associated autoimmune conditions and recommends using such tests in patients with autoimmune thyroid disorders. Its abstract states that large trials of cost-benefit are lacking and that clinicians must use individual judgement, so the evidence for routine associated-condition screening is weak. The abstract does not show which tests it recommends. - PMID:15826920

[D | hypothesis] A two-patient case report describes improved excessive daytime sleepiness and shorter sleep times after 8 weeks of levothyroxine in idiopathic hypersomnia with mildly raised TSH (subclinical hypothyroidism). This shows an association between thyroid status and sleepiness in these patients but cannot establish causation. - PMID:19269544

[D | hypothesis] A narrative review of Ayurveda-based interventions reports that studies of ashwagandha showed improved sleep quality and reduced fatigue. The patient is listed as taking ashwagandha, so this is a possible confounder and not evidence of benefit. - PMID:42183570

[D | hypothesis] One small study of SCH patients with a mean age of about 50 reported that LT4 reduced carotid intima-media thickness, independently of lipid change. It had no effect on hs-CRP or paraoxonase-1. - PMID:20037493

[D | emerging] Recurrence at the same level can occur months to years after treatment, in up to about 10% of patients. A programme of weight control, exercise and posture correction is suggested to reduce recurrent symptoms. This is low-grade, dated evidence. - PMID:22124958, PMID:8465710

[D | hypothesis] In adolescents, imaging-based disc degeneration progressed over 1 year despite near-complete symptom resolution after endoscopic discectomy. This is a possible dissociation between structural and clinical outcome in young patients with long expected lifespans. It is from a single case series within a review, in a surgically treated paediatric cohort. - PMID:42829654

[D | hypothesis] A narrative review proposes that mechanism-based approaches (pain neuroscience education plus graded, time-contingent exercise) may suit people with a sensitised pain phenotype and a mismatch between imaging and symptoms, as in disc herniation. This is a conceptual proposal, not proven durable benefit for any exercise type. - PMID:42512439

[D | emerging] Endothelial function (FMD) was lower in subclinical hypothyroidism than in controls and increased after 2 months of levothyroxine, with TSH falling to the normal range. Carotid IMT did not change. This was a small quasi-experimental study without a placebo group. - PMID:27099851

[D | hypothesis] Evidence on whether autoimmune thyroiditis itself, independent of thyroid hormone status, raises arterial stiffness is mixed. Euthyroid Hashimoto patients had higher carotid-femoral PWV than controls, attributed to a direct effect of the disorder. In another study, levothyroxine-treated Hashimoto patients had higher carotid pulsatility index than untreated euthyroid Hashimoto patients, and the authors concluded hypothyroidism, not autoimmunity per se, influences stiffness. - PMID:19348585, PMID:25671800

A 1990 narrative review adds that monitoring may be yearly or less often depending on patient education and compliance. A case series of 192 patients found the dose requirement stable over time. - PMID:1287777, PMID:2208954

[D | hypothesis] Levothyroxine corrects hypothyroidism but does not block the autoimmune process. This gives a plausible reason why autoimmune and non-autoimmune hypothyroidism could differ biologically even when TSH is normalised. This is a narrative statement and was not tested against PhenoAge or KDM. - PMID:41704486

[D | emerging] In NHANES, the association between FT3 and phenotypic age acceleration differed by age: higher FT3 was linked to more acceleration in people under 60. This suggests that thyroid hormone levels, and so possibly treatment-related hormone levels, may independently relate to PhenoAge acceleration. - PMID:40332749

items: [A | guideline supported] AACE/ATA guidelines state that serum TSH (thyrotropin) is the single best screening test for primary thyroid dysfunction in most outpatient situations. TSH is the core laboratory test for evaluation. - PMID:22954017, PMID:23246686

[A | established] The ATA task force concluded that levothyroxine monotherapy should remain the standard of care for hypothyroidism. It found no consistently strong evidence that alternatives such as LT4/LT3 combination or thyroid extract are superior. It also noted a research need for better biomarkers of euthyroidism to supplement TSH measurement. - PMID:22954017, PMID:25266247

[A | guideline supported] For subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, normal free T4), the 2019 BMJ GRADE guideline issues a strong recommendation against thyroid hormones. It recommends monitoring progression or resolution instead. It does not apply to women trying to become pregnant or to TSH above 20 mIU/L, and may not apply to people with severe symptoms or young adults (about 30 years or under). AACE/ATA state that treatment decisions when TSH is below 10 mIU/L should be individualised. - PMID:22954017, PMID:31088853
[A | established] Levothyroxine monotherapy is the guideline-endorsed standard of care for treating hypothyroidism in adults. - PMID:25266247, PMID:26654514, PMID:40622204

[A | guideline supported] LT4+LT3 combination therapy, thyroid extracts and other alternative preparations have not shown consistent superiority over LT4 monotherapy and are not recommended for routine use. Two European guidelines allowed combination therapy only in certain circumstances and as an experimental treatment. A 2025 pooled analysis found no significant difference in fatigue between LT4 and LT4+LT3, with a small significant heart-rate difference. - PMID:25266247, PMID:26654514, PMID:40699541
[A | guideline supported] Treatment guidance for subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH) differs between guidelines.
A 2019 GRADE guideline strongly recommends against thyroid hormones in adults with SCH. It found no clinically relevant benefit for quality of life, fatigue or depressive symptoms.
That guideline excludes TSH >20 mIU/L and women trying to become pregnant, and may not apply to adults aged 30 or younger.
AACE/ATA state that the decision to treat SCH when TSH is below 10 mIU/L should be individualised. - PMID:23246686, PMID:31088853

[A | established] Levothyroxine remains the standard of care for hypothyroidism. The ATA found no consistently strong evidence that alternative preparations (e.g., combination with liothyronine, or thyroid extract) are superior. For untreated subclinical hypothyroidism, the BMJ guideline advises monitoring progression or resolution rather than routine treatment. That guideline explicitly excludes women trying to become pregnant and patients with TSH >20 mIU/L. - PMID:25266247, PMID:31088853

[A | guideline supported] Congenital hypothyroidism (primary or central, permanent or transient) is a separate category in the differential. It is detected by neonatal TSH-based screening, with central forms needing FT4 measurement. It is unlikely to be relevant to adult-onset diagnosis but is part of the full disease spectrum. - PMID:22570946, PMID:33272083

[A | guideline supported] In subclinical hypothyroidism, symptoms occur as often as in euthyroid people. A guideline strongly recommends against thyroid hormones for adults with subclinical hypothyroidism because there are no clinically relevant benefits for quality of life or symptoms such as fatigue. These findings concern untreated subclinical disease and do not tell us whether this patient's symptoms are thyroid-related. - PMID:31088853

[A | guideline supported] Guideline-level evidence finds no consistently strong evidence that alternatives to levothyroxine monotherapy (including LT4+LT3) improve health outcomes. A narrative review likewise concludes that adjusting treatment to a low T3 level does not seem to improve outcomes. - PMID:25266247, PMID:37419564

[B | evidence supported] A systematic review of 12 studies found that levothyroxine at replacement doses had a very low risk of cardiac, neuropsychiatric and musculoskeletal adverse events. Adverse events occurred mainly when TSH was suppressed, and blinded placebo-controlled trials in euthyroid patients showed no significant differences. Some subjective symptoms may be placebo or nocebo effects. - PMID:41559017

[B | evidence supported] A systematic review of RCTs reports that B vitamins and vitamin D may be effective, well-tolerated adjuncts for depression and anxiety. For anxiety specifically, the available RCT results were limited to adjuvant vitamin D therapy, so there is no RCT-level support for B12 either causing or treating anxiety. - PMID:35156551

[B | evidence supported] A systematic review found that adverse events attributed to levothyroxine, including neuropsychiatric events such as headache, occurred mainly when TSH was suppressed. In euthyroid patients in blinded placebo-controlled trials there was no significant difference. The pattern suggests thyroid status (over-replacement versus normal TSH) is the main discriminator for a drug-related headache. - PMID:41559017

[B | evidence supported] The same review lists headache among reported neuropsychiatric adverse events but concludes most comparisons were nonsignificant and not clinically meaningful at replacement doses. It notes that subjective symptoms may reflect placebo or nocebo effects. A subjective headache therefore cannot by itself be attributed to the drug. - PMID:41559017

[B | guideline supported] The 2025 South Korean evidence-based guideline for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy is organised around surgical, interventional and physical/exercise treatment questions. It gives exercise therapy a grade A recommendation, higher than the NASS guideline. The excerpt contains no diagnostic or monitoring key question. - PMID:40625002

[B | guideline supported] Exercise therapy received a grade A recommendation in a 2025 Korean LDH-with-radiculopathy guideline, partly because of minimal risk and low cost. An earlier Korean CPG strongly recommended exercise and traction despite moderate-level evidence. Across international guidelines, clinician-guided exercise and physical therapy were recommended by most but not all. - PMID:31201860, PMID:40625002, PMID:40625005

[B | guideline supported] Short-term epidural steroid injections (transforaminal, interlaminar, caudal) show definite cross-guideline consensus in favour, and the transforaminal approach is favoured over caudal. However, the 2025 Korean CPG assigned ESIs a lower grade than NASS. - PMID:31201860, PMID:40625002, PMID:40625005

[B | guideline supported] For patients refractory to nonoperative care, discectomy is the most common surgery. Open discectomy/microdiscectomy was recommended by 8 guidelines and microendoscopic discectomy by 5. A 2025 Korean CPG upgraded endoscopic procedures to grade B. - PMID:34637405, PMID:40625002, PMID:40625005

[B | evidence supported] Hypothyroidism can plausibly account for fatigue and dry skin, but its symptoms are non-specific. No single symptom reliably identifies thyroid disease, and persistent symptoms in levothyroxine-treated patients are hard to attribute to thyroid status. This supports checking whether current thyroid replacement is biochemically adequate while keeping non-thyroid causes open. - PMID:25305308, PMID:36814580

[B | emerging] A small double-blind placebo-controlled RCT of intramuscular B12 in chronic mechanical low back pain or sciatic neuritis found a statistically significant between-group advantage for active treatment on pain (VAS) and disability, and less paracetamol use. Both groups improved sharply, and the participants had no signs of nutritional deficiency. - PMID:11558625

[B | emerging] A phase 3 RCT of injectable hydroxocobalamin + thiamine + pyridoxine added to NSAIDs in chronic mechanical low back pain showed a higher proportion with ≥30% NRS reduction at day 28 than placebo + NSAIDs. Adverse events were more frequent with treatment, with no significant difference in serious events. The effect cannot be attributed to B12 alone. - PMID:41604864

[B | emerging] In euthyroid HT (not levothyroxine-treated specifically), a meta-analysis of case-control/cross-sectional studies found higher odds of anxiety disorders than in controls, and the authors link thyroid antibodies to anxiety and depression. Because the patients were euthyroid, this suggests an association not explained by overt thyroid dysfunction. The data are observational, heterogeneous and cannot establish causation. - PMID:39717384

[B | emerging] A meta-analysis restricted to population-based studies found no statistically significant association between TPO antibodies and anxiety disorders. The authors judge the overall evidence inconclusive: small positive associations are likely but small protective effects are also compatible with the data. - PMID:42569470
