[B | evidence supported] Adding T3 to levothyroxine did not improve depression, fatigue, pain, anxiety or anger scores on average in a meta-analysis of 18 studies, although patients preferred combination therapy. Narrative review evidence indicates that baseline serum T3 and on-treatment T3 changes did not predict who responds. - PMID:32636887, PMID:35445422

[B | emerging] The only RCT of ashwagandha on thyroid indices (50 adults with subclinical hypothyroidism, 600 mg/day for 8 weeks) reported significantly improved TSH, T3 and T4 versus placebo. Ashwagandha can therefore shift thyroid function tests in people with a mild hypothyroid state. Participants were not described as taking levothyroxine, so the result cannot be extrapolated directly to treated hypothyroidism. - PMID:28829155

[B | evidence supported] In a systematic review of 12 studies, adverse events with levothyroxine, including neuropsychiatric ones such as anxiety, occurred mainly when TSH was suppressed. In euthyroid patients, blinded placebo-controlled trials showed no significant differences. This points to thyroid status (over-replacement) rather than the act of starting the drug as the relevant driver. The review does not give onset timing for anxiety. - PMID:41559017

[B | evidence supported] About 10-15% of levothyroxine-treated patients have persistent symptoms despite normalised thyroid hormone levels. A systematic review found no high-quality evidence supporting any intervention for these symptoms. - PMID:38622434, PMID:39368843

[C | guideline supported] The ETA guideline frames the therapeutic goals of levothyroxine therapy as symptom relief and serum TSH control. It notes that patients frequently fail to reach these goals in real-life use. It discusses nutritional, pharmacological and pathological factors that can increase levothyroxine requirement. - PMID:40622204

[C | guideline supported] The ETA guideline lists foods and supplements that interfere with oral levothyroxine bioavailability. These include dietary fibre (suggested LT4 at least 4 h before) and over-the-counter whey and soy protein supplements (suggested separation of more than 4 h; avoid if possible). Its drug table lists medicines that alter LT4 bioavailability or TSH, many with a 'thyroid function monitoring' suggestion. - PMID:40622204

[C | guideline supported] Guidelines treat pregnancy and pregnancy planning as a distinct context. The BMJ subclinical-hypothyroidism recommendation explicitly excludes women trying to become pregnant, and AACE/ATA and LATS cover pregnancy in separate sections. The pregnancy-specific recommendations themselves were not shown in the provided sources. - PMID:22954017, PMID:23828433, PMID:31088853

[C | guideline supported] AACE/ATA state that appropriate treatment requires an accurate diagnosis and is influenced by coexisting medical conditions. Evaluation therefore includes establishing the aetiology. The provided excerpts do not state specific recommendations on thyroid antibody testing. - PMID:22954017

[C | guideline supported] The 2025 Chinese OSA guideline lists hypothyroidism among OSA-related comorbidities that define high-risk individuals. It recommends OSA screening for high-risk people with typical symptoms, which include excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headaches and non-restorative sleep. It recommends STOP-Bang for screening and objective sleep testing for diagnosis. - PMID:41820035

[C | emerging] Anxiety is common in levothyroxine-treated hypothyroidism even when TSH is normal. In one Spanish case-control study of women, those treated with levothyroxine had about twice the odds of anxiety compared with women without hypothyroidism. TSH did not correlate with anxiety. This suggests the anxiety may reflect the underlying condition, or residual factors, rather than the drug, but a drug effect cannot be excluded. - PMID:31795239

[C | emerging] Persistent emotional symptoms in Hashimoto's thyroiditis may relate to inflammation rather than TSH, levothyroxine use or antibody levels. In 80 patients with free hormones in range, higher IL-6 was independently associated with anxiety and depressivity. Another cross-sectional study found that a lower FT3/FT4 ratio, but not TSH, was associated with more anxiety in levothyroxine-treated patients. These are associations and are not specific to this patient's autoimmune status, which is not recorded. - PMID:42313710, PMID:42942548
[C | emerging] LT3 monotherapy is investigational. In one crossover RCT of 69 women with persisting symptoms despite optimal LT4, fatigue scores were better on LT3 than on LT4. - PMID:40699541

[C | guideline supported] Under- and over-replacement with thyroid hormone are common and are associated with adverse cardiovascular or metabolic consequences. Many patients do not reach the goals of symptom relief and TSH control on LT4. - PMID:28327186, PMID:40622204
[C | guideline supported] Many foods, supplements and drugs reduce LT4 bioavailability or alter TSH. The ETA 2025 guideline gives separation timings for each, including:
fibre and whey/soy protein supplements;
coffee;
calcium and iron;
PPIs.

blocks.text: It also notes that estrogens increase LT4 requirement. - PMID:40622204

items: [C | emerging] Supervised discontinuation of thyroid hormone leaves about 37% of patients euthyroid (41% after SCH, 11% after overt hypothyroidism). Autoantibody positivity, heterogeneous ultrasound findings and higher baseline TSH are associated with restarting therapy. Adverse events were uncommon. - PMID:42969098

[C | guideline supported] In pregnancy the approach differs: LT4 has been recommended for SCH diagnosed in pregnant women. Pregnancy and preconception management is covered by a separate ATA guideline. - PMID:31088853, PMID:42800939

[C | evidence supported] B12 deficiency, not excess, is the more established link to anxiety. It is described as having a possible etiological role in anxiety and other neuropsychiatric presentations. Plasma MMA and homocysteine are named as diagnostic aids alongside serum B12. This is a competing explanation for the symptom and shows how deficiency can be distinguished from a supplement effect. - PMID:35337631

[C | evidence supported] Congenital and dyshormonogenic hypothyroidism arises from defects in genes for iodide transport and organification or iodotyrosine recycling (e.g. SLC5A5, SLC26A4, TG, TPO, DUOX2, DUOXA2). Thyroid dysgenesis can arise from defects in thyroid transcription factors or in TSH receptor function. - PMID:31301652, PMID:35999191

[C | evidence supported] Thyroid hormone action depends on deiodinase conversion of T4 to active T3 (DIO1/DIO2, selenocysteine enzymes) and on T3 binding to the nuclear receptors TRα/TRβ, which regulate transcription. TRβ mutations cause resistance to thyroid hormone. - PMID:20051527, PMID:35999191

[C | evidence supported] Levothyroxine replacement is the treatment of choice in these sources, and optimal substitution restores biochemical euthyroidism. Excessive replacement may cause atrial arrhythmia and osteoporosis, particularly in postmenopausal or elderly patients, and maintaining TSH within the reference range is advised. In secondary (central) hypothyroidism, corticotropin deficiency should be excluded before starting replacement. - PMID:17077946, PMID:35726428

[C | evidence supported] Hypothyroidism is linked to dyslipidaemia, blood pressure changes, endothelial dysfunction and arrhythmia. Overt hypothyroidism is considered a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor, and Mendelian randomization suggests causal effects of Hashimoto's thyroiditis on cardiovascular traits. - PMID:41996368, PMID:42527560
[C | evidence supported] Levothyroxine is reported to restore muscle function in hypothyroidism once euthyroidism is achieved. - PMID:41649890
[C | emerging] Micronutrient status is relevant to thyroid function.
Excess iodine (total record around 800 µg/day) was associated with subclinical hypothyroidism in a randomized trial in euthyroid adults.
Iron deficiency was associated with lower FT4.
A narrative review emphasises iodine, iron, selenium and vitamin D. - PMID:41498438

[C | evidence supported] Several endocrine society guidelines, as summarised by a review, recommend treating subclinical hypothyroidism when TSH is above 10 mIU/L. The benefit is clearer in younger people. - PMID:38887272

[C | emerging] Fatigue is a typical symptom of hypothyroidism, and in a prospective study levothyroxine reduced fatigue in most patients. Fatigue on levothyroxine is therefore more often a marker of inadequate or incomplete treatment or of other causes than a drug effect. Persistent fatigue was associated with higher pre-treatment fatigue scores and with diabetes. - PMID:36979787

[C | evidence supported] Overtreatment with levothyroxine (low TSH) is a recognised cause of symptoms and harm. Reviews advise checking for over-the-counter products containing thyroid hormone and considering lower doses when TSH is low. The harms listed in the sources are cardiovascular, cognitive and skeletal; fatigue is not specifically listed. Most of this evidence concerns older adults. - PMID:28336049, PMID:40900603, PMID:42768899

[C | evidence supported] Symptoms, including fatigue, can persist despite normal TSH on levothyroxine. About 1 in 4 treated patients with normal TSH had persistent or new symptoms, and about 10% had persistent ill-health despite normal thyroid function tests. The cause is unclear, so fatigue with normal TSH does not itself point to a levothyroxine effect. - PMID:37913925, PMID:39368843

[C | evidence supported] When TSH remains elevated or symptoms persist on levothyroxine, a review lists a differential of causes: inadequate dose, absorption problems (including interfering supplements and drugs such as calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate), gastrointestinal malabsorption, non-adherence, and concurrent autoimmune disease such as Addison's disease. A case report describes persistently raised TSH on levothyroxine revealing autoimmune adrenal insufficiency, but in an adolescent with positive adrenal antibodies and marked electrolyte abnormalities. - PMID:28336049, PMID:42684977

[C | emerging] In a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, hypothyroidism (overt or subclinical) was associated with significantly higher cardiovascular mortality versus euthyroid controls. It was not significantly associated with incident cardiovascular events. The association was concentrated in acute or high-risk cardiac settings such as acute coronary syndrome, acute heart failure and CABG. - PMID:42603211
[C | evidence supported] Maternal overt hypothyroidism during pregnancy is associated with:
miscarriage;
gestational hypertensive disorders;
postpartum haemorrhage.

blocks.text: Children of mothers with inadequately controlled hypothyroidism are at higher risk of lower IQ, neurodevelopmental disorders and ADHD. In the congenital hypothyroidism literature, poorly controlled thyroid function may also lead to higher infertility rates. - PMID:40570035

items: [C | guideline supported] A descriptive review of major guidelines (Endocrine Society, ETA, RANZCOG, ATA, ACOG) found agreement on several points:
Overt hypothyroidism should be treated during pregnancy and also before conception, with similar management and treatment targets.
Universal screening is discouraged, and targeted TSH screening of high-risk patients is supported.

blocks.text: The 2026 ATA guideline provides updated recommendations on thyroid function testing and hypothyroidism management across preconception, pregnancy and postpartum. Its specific recommendations were not in the supplied abstract. - PMID:34994394, PMID:42219800

items: [C | evidence supported] Thyroid autoimmunity (e.g., TPO antibodies) is associated with miscarriage, preterm delivery, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and postpartum thyroiditis, even in euthyroid women. It is also an independent predictor of developing hypothyroidism during pregnancy. Guidelines summarised in the review favour targeted screening and close biochemical monitoring over universal intervention. - PMID:42602420

[C | evidence supported] Overtreatment is a recognised treatment-related complication. TSH below the reference range is associated with atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis and should be avoided. In primary care, both overtreatment and undertreatment are common:
Overtreatment is linked to suppressed TSH during follow-up.
Undertreatment is linked to inadequate follow-up.
Symptoms attributed to hypothyroidism often have non-thyroidal causes. - PMID:33543160, PMID:42249773

[C | emerging] Headache can be a symptom of hypothyroidism itself. In a prospective cohort, about one third of recent-onset hypothyroid patients had headache attributed to hypothyroidism, with a prior migraine history more frequent in those patients, and most reported fewer headaches after levothyroxine treatment. Not all patients responded. Persistent headache may therefore reflect under-treatment, a coexisting primary headache disorder, or another cause rather than a drug effect. - PMID:27390121

[C | emerging] A systematic review of low-dose levothyroxine in patients with subclinical hypothyroidism and migraine found a trend toward fewer migraines that did not reach statistical significance in the random-effects model. The evidence for levothyroxine improving migraine is therefore uncertain. - PMID:40329276

[C | emerging] Headache was among the mild adverse events in healthy volunteers given a supraphysiologic levothyroxine regimen that produced full TSH suppression and subclinical thyrotoxicosis. This is consistent with over-replacement being a plausible mechanism for headache. - PMID:28741453

[C | evidence supported] Primary and secondary (central) hypothyroidism are distinguished by the TSH-FT4 pattern. In primary hypothyroidism TSH is raised, with low FT4 (overt) or normal FT4 (subclinical). In central hypothyroidism FT4 is low while TSH is normal or decreased. A raised TSH almost always signals primary hypothyroidism. - PMID:20596261, PMID:32628881

[C | evidence supported] The differential for the cause of primary hypothyroidism includes the following: chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, the most common cause in adults; insufficient iodine record; prior treatment of hyperthyroidism (radioiodine or thyroidectomy); and drug-induced hypothyroidism, e.g. tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Antithyroid antibodies, history and examination ordinarily separate these causes. - PMID:20596261, PMID:3085076, PMID:32628881, PMID:35235282

[C | evidence supported] Self-limited destructive thyroiditis is an important differential because the hypothyroidism may be transient. Subacute (painful) thyroiditis has anterior neck pain, a tender goitre, fever, raised inflammatory markers and a triphasic course (thyrotoxicosis, then hypothyroidism, then recovery). Painless, pregnancy-associated (postpartum) and therapy-related forms also occur. Levothyroxine in subacute thyroiditis is described as selective and time-limited, with follow-up to identify the minority who develop permanent hypothyroidism. - PMID:3085076, PMID:42741759

[C | evidence supported] Thyroid function tests can be altered by factors other than thyroid disease. Acute illness, diet and drugs may change values. Reference-interval interpretation is especially difficult in aging, pregnancy, non-thyroidal illness and central hypothyroidism. These are important pseudo-hypothyroid or confounding states in the differential. - PMID:35235282, PMID:36814580

[C | evidence supported] Hypothyroid symptoms (fatigue, lethargy, dry skin) are non-specific. In a population study, people with subclinical hypothyroidism reported thyroid-related symptoms at similar rates to people with normal thyroid function. Persistent symptoms in levothyroxine-treated patients may come from other factors, including autoimmunity or another chronic disorder. Non-thyroidal causes of these symptoms therefore belong in the differential. - PMID:36814580

[C | evidence supported] Whether hypothyroidism is overt or subclinical matters. The review states all patients with overt hypothyroidism should be treated. Patients with subclinical hypothyroidism do not always benefit, especially the elderly and those with baseline TSH below 10 mU/L. Thyroid hormone discontinuation with maintained normal thyroid function has been reported in about one third of treated patients, suggesting overdiagnosis in some. - PMID:32628881, PMID:36814580

[C | emerging] A systematic review and an RCT suggest B12-containing regimens may reduce migraine. The review reports an overall favourable safety profile, with gastrointestinal events the most common adverse events and headache not listed among them. This argues against B12 being a frequent cause of headache at supplement doses, but it does not exclude individual reactions. - PMID:32279306, PMID:38011468

[C | emerging] Low B12 status, rather than B12 supplementation, is associated with headache in several observational studies. A new or persistent headache may therefore reflect an underlying B12 deficiency or insufficiency. Serum B12 and MMA could help distinguish this, but the sources do not give a validated diagnostic pathway for headache. - PMID:31471907, PMID:38743602, PMID:39903066

[C | evidence supported] Initial evaluation of suspected lumbar disc herniation relies on a detailed history and careful physical examination, supplemented by MRI only if necessary, to distinguish it from low back strain and other causes. Early screening for serious pathology, followed by monitoring for complications (neurological deficits, cauda equina syndrome, refractory pain), is described as essential. - PMID:10029785

[C | evidence supported] Reviews describe first-line management of lumbar disc herniation as conservative: analgesics or NSAIDs, activity modification, physical therapy or rehabilitation, and exercise. Surgery is indicated for patients who fail conservative treatment or who develop neurological deficits. Monitoring therefore centres on symptom response and the emergence of neurological deficits. - PMID:34637405, PMID:41487424

[C | evidence supported] In a surgical cohort, MRI showed excellent reliability for identifying herniation level and neural compression (level correctly identified in all 47 patients). However, it significantly underestimated bilateral foraminal and lateral recess stenosis compared with intraoperative findings, so MRI findings need to be integrated with clinical assessment. - PMID:41959992

[C | evidence supported] The natural history of lumbar disc herniation is generally favourable: most patients recover within weeks (reported as within 4 weeks, or significant relief within 6 to 8 weeks). Persistent symptoms beyond this are what typically trigger further evaluation. - PMID:10029785, PMID:41487424

[C | evidence supported] Conservative management is described as guideline-recommended first-line therapy for LDH: NSAIDs/oral analgesics, physical rehabilitation, functional exercise and activity modification. Surgery is reserved for failure of conservative care or neurological deficit. - PMID:34637405, PMID:41487424

[C | guideline supported] NSAIDs were recommended by 9 of the guidelines reviewed, and cognitive behavioural therapy by 5. However, systematic-review evidence suggests the effect of NSAIDs is limited, and some high-quality guidelines advise against routine NSAID use for acute radiculopathy. An older systematic review found little evidence that drug treatments are effective for herniated disc. - PMID:19445754, PMID:40625005, PMID:41487424

[C | evidence supported] Surgical safety concerns in these sources include the following. Open surgery is limited by invasiveness, long recovery and higher complication risk. Rare but serious postoperative spinal infection is documented: a case of L4-L5 microdiscectomy followed by Mycobacteroides abscessus osteomyelitis/discitis. Transforaminal endoscopic surgery for far-lateral herniation carries a risk of aggravated leg pain and ganglion compression injury. - PMID:25102508, PMID:41487424, PMID:42597783

[C | emerging] A Korean-medicine CPG recommends acupuncture, alone or with conventional therapy, for overall LHIVD symptoms and describes it as low clinical risk. However, the evidence was downgraded for high heterogeneity in some comparisons. - PMID:35206861

[C | evidence supported] Clinical red flags for infection or malignancy should prompt targeted laboratory and imaging investigation in degenerative spine presentations. In vertebral infection, early tissue diagnosis is associated with better outcomes. - PMID:42597783, PMID:42849905

[C | evidence supported] Genetic factors are reported to contribute substantially to intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) risk. A narrative review cites about 75% of aetiology. IVDD is described as multifactorial, combining genetic and environmental factors. - PMID:27617275, PMID:27917384

[C | emerging] Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with IVDD risk are reported in several gene groups. These include structural matrix genes (COL1A1, COL9A3, COL11A1, COL11A2, ACAN, CHST3), the vitamin D receptor gene, ECM-degrading enzyme genes (MMP-1, -2, -3, -9, -14, ADAMTS-4, -5), apoptosis genes (CASP9, TRAIL, DR4) and growth factor genes (GDF5, VEGF). Some effects are limited by sex and population. - PMID:27917384

[C | emerging] A systematic review of spinal stenosis mechanisms reports that intervertebral disc herniation is associated with mutations in the type I collagen genes (COL1A1/COL1A2) and the resulting protein dysregulation. It cautions that most publications lack direct mutation-to-pathology data. - PMID:36362274

[C | emerging] Proposed molecular mechanisms of disc degeneration include inflammation, oxidative stress, cell injury and dysregulated ECM metabolism. Mechanical loading is described as a main driver that promotes matrix metalloproteinase production, along with nucleus pulposus cell death (pyroptosis, apoptosis, ferroptosis, senescence) and cartilage endplate destruction. - PMID:31435545, PMID:38626521, PMID:39379638

[C | emerging] The sources identify no established disease-modifying drug target. Current management is described as symptomatic or palliative. Most regenerative and biomaterial strategies remain at preclinical validation. - PMID:38626521, PMID:42964622
[C | evidence supported] Lumbar disc degeneration lacks reliable early biomarkers, and diagnosis currently relies on imaging. - PMID:41769000

[C | emerging] In degenerative lumbar spine disease, stenosis can lead to neurogenic claudication or radiculopathy. When radicular or claudicatory symptoms predominate, a coexisting condition such as lumbar spinal stenosis should be considered. - PMID:42849905

[C | emerging] After L4-L5 lumbar fusion, cranial adjacent segment disease is described as a dreaded long-term complication. At 5 years, 10.8% of the control-technique group had undergone revision surgery for it. - PMID:37632571

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review states that history, physical examination and, if necessary, MRI can differentiate a herniated lumbar disc from low back strain and other causes of similar symptoms. It also says that screening for serious pathology and monitoring for complications (neurologic deficits, cauda equina syndrome, refractory pain) are essential in managing lumbar disc herniation. - PMID:10029785

[C | evidence supported] Thyroid function tests must be interpreted carefully because acute illness, diet and drugs may alter values. Levothyroxine should be titrated to goal TSH, symptoms and adverse effects. Both under- and over-replacement and test interference are therefore part of the thyroid-related differential. - PMID:35235282

[C | emerging] Fibromyalgia / chronic primary pain is a differential for the combination of widespread pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance and cognitive symptoms. It is diagnosed clinically using ACR criteria (widespread pain index plus symptom severity score, generalized pain in at least four of five body regions, symptoms for at least 3 months). The review states that a thorough differential diagnosis against rheumatic, neurological, endocrine and psychiatric disorders is required, and that the 2016 criteria allow diagnosis regardless of coexisting conditions. - PMID:42764960

[C | emerging] Fatigue in primary care has a broad differential including depression, situational stress, postviral or drug-induced fatigue, endocrine disorders, sleep disorders, infections, autoimmune disorders and neurological disease. Endocrine and metabolic causes (thyroid, pituitary, parathyroid, adrenal, glucose, lipids, gonadal) need to be differentiated from psychiatric causes, and diagnosis of endocrinopathy depends on laboratory values rather than self-report. A small prospective case series found a medical disorder in about half of patients with persistent fatigue, depression in about a fifth and no definitive diagnosis in about a third. - PMID:11430174, PMID:1524082, PMID:20656620

[C | emerging] A narrative review concluded that clinical trials provide some evidence for B12 in low back pain and neuralgia, but the data are limited and optimal regimens are unknown. It suggested B12 may be an adjunctive option with low side-effect incidence. - PMID:30700078

[C | emerging] In an observational case-control study of chronic nonspecific low back pain, pain sensitivity correlated negatively with record of anti-inflammatory nutrients, including B12. This is an association with dietary record, not serum B12, and does not show causation. - PMID:37659446

[C | emerging] In the only clinical trial directly studying ashwagandha's effect on thyroid function, a 50-patient placebo-controlled pilot RCT in subclinical hypothyroidism found that TSH fell toward normal and T3/T4 rose after 8 weeks. The review authors conclude ashwagandha interferes with the thyroid hormone system in mildly hypothyroid people. - PMID:41454558, PMID:42183570

[C | emerging] A narrative review reports no indication that ashwagandha raises thyroid hormones above normal in people with normal thyroid function treated for up to 12 months. However, it calls for more long-term studies. - PMID:41454558, PMID:41830041

[C | emerging] Ashwagandha products vary in plant part and composition, and root products are documented as adulterated with leaf and stem. This makes the thyroid-relevant exposure from any given supplement uncertain. - PMID:34254920, PMID:42835472

[C | emerging] A systematic review notes ashwagandha-associated hepatotoxicity warrants liver enzyme monitoring during prolonged use. Another review states plant-based approaches should be supportive rather than substitutive to standard endocrine therapy, with attention to interactions and monitoring. - PMID:41798846, PMID:42858054

[C | emerging] A small case-control study reported higher lifetime depressive and anxiety disorders in euthyroid-phase Hashimoto disease but not in euthyroid goitre. The authors interpret this as independence from thyroid function measured by routine tests and a link to thyroid autoimmunity. - PMID:16285879

[C | evidence supported] Guideline comparison (pregnancy context only): neither the ATA nor the Endocrine Society recommends TPOAb screening in pregnancy to prevent miscarriage or preterm delivery. Both recommend that TPOAb-positive euthyroid women not receiving LT4 be monitored for hypothyroidism during pregnancy. No provided source gives a guideline recommendation on TPOAb testing in established, treated adult primary hypothyroidism. - PMID:23738229

[C | evidence supported] TPOAb is the most sensitive of the thyroid autoantibodies for chronic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis. It is present in almost all patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis and in more than 70% with Graves' disease, so it is a marker of autoimmune cause rather than a specific diagnosis. - PMID:10483258, PMID:9594622

[C | evidence supported] In a population-based cohort of new overt hypothyroidism, more than 99% of spontaneous cases were thyroid-antibody positive, and TPOAb was measurable more often than TgAb (95.9% vs 80.7%). Autoimmunity therefore appears to underlie almost all spontaneous hypothyroidism in that population. - PMID:17060029

[C | evidence supported] TPOAb positivity depends on assay-specific cut-offs, and reported thresholds vary widely across assays (for example 200 units/ml in one assay, and a proposed 17 IU/ml in another study). Highly sensitive assays detect low titres in nearly everyone. In autoimmune hypothyroidism, TPOAb levels vary inconsistently during T4 substitution, so serial titres may not track treatment. - PMID:15826919, PMID:28954485, PMID:8088002

[C | emerging] A population-based meta-analysis found no statistically significant association between TPOAb positivity and anxiety disorders (OR 1.47, 95% CI 0.73-2.94); the authors judged the evidence inconclusive. - PMID:42569470

[C | emerging] In levothyroxine-treated adults (Hashimoto or post-thyroidectomy) and comparison participants, a lower FT3/FT4 ratio and lower FT3, but not TSH, were associated with worse thyroid-related quality of life and more anxiety and depression symptoms. The ratio association persisted when all three tests were in range. - PMID:42942548

[C | emerging] An older, larger cohort of patients on thyroid hormone replacement found that fT4 and TSH, but not fT3 or the rT3-based ratios, correlated with general psychological well-being (GHQ-12). Correlations were not seen with anxiety/depression scale scores. This partly conflicts with the FT3-ratio finding. - PMID:16804044

[C | hypothesis] Symptoms on levothyroxine with normal TSH are common and have no reliable tissue-level biomarker. Reviews describe a lower T3:T4 ratio as a proposed mechanism ('peripheral hypothyroidism'), while noting that markers of tissue thyroid status are lacking. - PMID:39368843, PMID:43005807

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review recommends preconception care for women with known hypothyroidism to ensure euthyroidism from the onset of pregnancy, with a TSH target below 2.5 mIU/L. - PMID:32616466

[C | emerging] In a small retrospective study of women on levothyroxine with preconception TSH <2.5 mIU/L, a higher preconception TSH was associated with needing a dose increase in pregnancy. Half of women with TSH 1.2-2.4 mIU/L needed an increase, versus 17.2% with TSH <1.2 mIU/L. The authors suggested a preconception TSH of no more than about 1.2. - PMID:20860419

[C | evidence supported] Most women with hypothyroidism need a levothyroxine dose increase after conception. A review states that an empirical dose increase of 30-50% may be considered as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, with doses then titrated against trimester-specific TSH ranges. - PMID:20860419, PMID:32616466

[C | evidence supported] TSH thresholds in pregnancy should be gestational-age specific. Reference ranges differ by trimester and are important for accurate interpretation and treatment. - PMID:17868484

[C | evidence supported] Levothyroxine requirement may increase postpartum compared with pre-pregnancy in Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Limited data show no adverse infant effects of replacement doses during breastfeeding. - PMID:30000062

[C | emerging] In hypothyroid women with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the disease is linked to adverse fertility and pregnancy outcomes, and levothyroxine treatment has been associated with improved fertility and pregnancy outcomes. - PMID:42278392

[C | evidence supported] Dietary fibre, soy/whey protein supplements, and calcium and iron salts can reduce levothyroxine absorption. Separating their record by about 3-4 hours is recommended. Impaired absorption can make TSH targets harder to achieve, especially when tight preconception or pregnancy targets apply. - PMID:41109285, PMID:42278392

[C | emerging] In a randomized trial of ashwagandha in bipolar disorder, thyroid indices were measured as a safety parameter. Only 10 of 60 patients had abnormal values. Subtle T4 increases were seen in 3 ashwagandha-treated patients, and the authors suggested vigilance for hyperthyroidism may be warranted. The data are too sparse to confirm an effect. - PMID:25624699

[C | emerging] A review of ashwagandha's adverse effects reports that its endocrine-modulating activity has been implicated in thyrotoxicosis and adrenal suppression. This supports treating it as a thyroid-active supplement. - PMID:41502355

[C | evidence supported] Methodologically, thyroid effects of an exogenous compound are best judged by measuring TSH together with a free hormone (fT3 or fT4), since TSH is a sensitive marker and the free fractions are the biologically active ones. This frames which tests are informative if ashwagandha exposure is suspected to affect results. - PMID:41454558

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review lists anxiety among the adverse effects of levothyroxine over-replacement, alongside muscle wasting, osteoporosis and atrial fibrillation. It gives no time course. - PMID:15663347

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review states that TSH should be monitored 6 to 8 weeks after starting levothyroxine or changing the dose, to avoid over- or under-treatment. This defines a standard biochemical checkpoint against which new or changing symptoms can be assessed. It does not describe anxiety trajectories. - PMID:40900603

[C | emerging] In a small double-blind pilot RCT in adults with untreated subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4.5-10), 8 weeks of ashwagandha root extract significantly improved TSH, T3 and T4 versus placebo. This indicates ashwagandha can measurably alter thyroid function tests in a mildly hypothyroid state. - PMID:28829155, PMID:41454558

[C | emerging] One review states there are no indications that ashwagandha raises thyroid hormones above normal in euthyroid volunteers treated for up to twelve months. It also notes the rare hyperthyroid cases normalized after withdrawal and advises using only well-standardized root products. - PMID:41830041

[C | emerging] A narrative review proposes four non-exclusive explanations for persistent symptoms despite normal thyroid biochemistry: low tissue T3, coexisting somatic symptom and related disorders, autoimmune neuroinflammation, and comorbidities or psychosocial factors. The review states that the low-T3 line of investigation has not translated into patient benefit. - PMID:33783849

[C | emerging] A systematic review found that thyroid autoimmunity is associated with persisting symptoms or lower quality of life in biochemically euthyroid Hashimoto's disease patients. Causality is unproven, and the larger population-based studies were more often negative. - PMID:34027377

[C | evidence supported] Persistent hypothyroid-like symptoms are non-specific and common in euthyroid people. A narrative review advises checking for non-thyroid causes (other autoimmune conditions, anemia, mental health disorders) and for treatment-related causes (underdosing, poor adherence, interactions with food or drugs, malabsorption). - PMID:33112818

[C | hypothesis] A reduced serum T3:T4 ratio on levothyroxine monotherapy has been proposed to cause tissue-level hypothyroidism despite normal serum T4, T3 and TSH. The evidence is inconsistent: one cited study found free T3 did not correlate with symptom scores, and the contribution of the ratio to differences from the general population remains unclear. - PMID:43005807

[C | emerging] In a double-blind placebo-controlled study of one month of high-dose B12 in young adults, B12 produced no adverse anxiety signal. The B12 group showed a non-significant trend toward reduced anxiety, and the interaction was not significant. This is the opposite direction to the case report. - PMID:35851507

[C | emerging] Anxiety is reported as a manifestation of B12 deficiency rather than excess. A review states B12 deficiency can have an etiological role in presentations including anxiety. This is a confounder when interpreting anxiety in someone taking B12 with unverified status. - PMID:35337631

[C | guideline supported] The ETA 2025 guideline lists dietary fibre (wheat bran) and over-the-counter whey and soy protein supplements as interfering with oral LT4 bioavailability. It suggests taking LT4 at least 4 h before fibre, delaying protein supplements by more than 4 h after LT4, and avoiding them if possible. No quantitative TSH effect is given in the excerpt, and the proposed mechanisms for protein supplements are marked as uncertain. - PMID:40622204

[C | emerging] In 8 volunteers given a single 600 µg LT4 dose, absorption was 89% alone, 86% with calcium polycarbophil and 80% with psyllium (absorption peak delayed to 240 min). The authors concluded these pharmacological fibre supplements are unlikely to cause detectable LT4 malabsorption. TSH was not an outcome. - PMID:9737361

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of 63 studies found limited evidence on LT4 interactions with soy products and fibre, though these interactions were associated with decreased LT4 absorption. It identified separating LT4 from food record as an effective way to eliminate such interactions. A separate review states that the effect of dietary fibre on LT4 absorption is not fully understood, and that soy has among the greatest impact on reducing absorption. - PMID:28153426, PMID:33801406

[C | evidence supported] For an LT4-treated adult with TSH above target despite reported adherence, a published decision tree advises the physician to review medications and medical history, check serum free T4 (FT4), and consider further absorption work-up. The review notes that dietary fibre and mineral supplements can reduce or slow LT4 absorption. - PMID:34671932

[C | evidence supported] TPOAb is present in almost all patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis but also in other autoimmune conditions and some normal subjects. It is therefore supportive but not specific for an autoimmune aetiology, and it does not by itself explain symptoms. - PMID:10483258, PMID:15826919

[C | emerging] In euthyroid women undergoing thyroidectomy for benign goiter, anti-TPO levels above a cut-off were associated with a higher symptom load and lower quality of life, with no difference in TSH. This suggests TPOAb or Hashimoto thyroiditis may relate to symptoms independently of thyroid hormone status. - PMID:21186954

[C | emerging] A two-sample MR study (European-ancestry GWAS data) reported a suggestive association between genetically predicted higher serum B12 and anxiety disorders (OR 1.34) and bipolar disorder (OR 1.85). It found no association with depression, OCD or schizophrenia. The authors state horizontal pleiotropy cannot be excluded. - PMID:38999734

[C | emerging] A Danish MR study in 4126 participants found no evidence for a causal effect of circulating B12 or folate on depression or anxiety. It could not exclude small to moderate effects. - PMID:28656970

[C | emerging] Observational data on B12 and mood or anxiety mostly point to LOW B12 as the risk marker. In adolescents with anxiety or depressive symptoms, lower B12 correlated with a higher risk of severe symptoms. In a population cohort (Hordaland), low B12 was not significantly related to depression, and none of the investigated parameters were significantly related to anxiety. - PMID:12796225, PMID:37056916

[C | emerging] In outpatients with major depressive disorder, higher baseline and follow-up B12 levels were associated with better six-month treatment outcomes, independent of adjustment variables. No patients had a low B12 at baseline. - PMID:14641930

[C | evidence supported] High serum B12 is a nonspecific marker. In hospital patients it was associated with alcoholism, liver disease and cancer, and a review states that functional B12 deficiency can occur at any serum level. A high B12 with neuropsychiatric symptoms may therefore reflect an underlying condition or functional deficiency, not a direct effect of B12. - PMID:23029349, PMID:23447660

[C | emerging] An RCT of one month of high-dose B12 versus placebo in young adults found only trends towards changes in anxiety, with no clear effect. High-dose B6 reduced self-reported anxiety. - PMID:35851507

[D | hypothesis] A small uncontrolled 30-day study of 24 adults with primary hypothyroidism given a fixed 75 mcg/day dose reported frequent side effects, including anxiety/agitation, after starting levothyroxine despite hormonal balance. Anxiety/agitation correlated with hs-CRP, and other side effects correlated with hydroperoxides. The authors proposed oxidative stress as a mechanism. This is an association only and conflicts with the systematic review. - PMID:22108484

[D | emerging] Observational data suggest anxiety may be a feature of untreated or under-treated hypothyroidism that improves with levothyroxine. A rural Nepalese cross-sectional study reported a large retrospective reduction in HAM-A anxiety scores after starting levothyroxine. A TriNetX study in children and adolescents with hypothyroidism and anxiety disorders found levothyroxine treatment associated with lower SSRI use and lower recorded suicidal ideation/self-harm. This argues against a net anxiogenic effect of treatment in many patients. - PMID:41111734, PMID:42074695

[D | hypothesis] Even with supraphysiologic levothyroxine doses, an RCT in refractory bipolar depression did not find greater anxiety than placebo. In contrast, a single case report describes psychiatric symptom exacerbation, including suicidal ideation, after an accidental prolonged overdose (300 mcg). Overall, the evidence suggests anxiogenic effects, if present, are likely tied to marked over-replacement and to individual vulnerability rather than to usual replacement dosing. - PMID:31583561, PMID:37809152

[D | hypothesis] One case report describes anxiety, with palpitations, akathisia, headache and insomnia, after repeated high oral cyanocobalamin doses in a young woman with severe pernicious anemia. Symptoms resolved after the drug was stopped. This is a hypothesis-level signal of a possible dose-related effect, not evidence of a general effect. - PMID:31018715

[D | hypothesis] The Mutanex published evidence links anxiety and vitamin B12 through a SIDER-derived relation that may be either a recorded drug effect or an indication. The record alone does not show direction or dose, and it cannot confirm that B12 causes anxiety. - DB:7059b87fa5005f87

[D | hypothesis] In an uncontrolled real-world cohort of adults with anxiety/depression receiving personalised nutraceutical treatment (including B12), psychological distress fell on average and no serious adverse events were identified. Serum B12 rose significantly. This gives no signal of B12-related worsening in that cohort but cannot isolate B12's effect. - PMID:42738962

[D | hypothesis] Hashimoto's (autoimmune) hypothyroidism has a strong polygenic basis. The largest multi-ancestry GWAS highlights immune-cell, and especially T-cell, pathways. Implicated genes include cytokine-signalling genes (IL2RA, IRF4, IRF5, JAK1, PTPN2, STAT4, TYK2), T-cell activation genes (CD28, CTLA4, CD247) and multiple HLA class I/II genes, as well as thyroid hormone synthesis genes (TPO, TG, PDE8B). - PMID:42527560

[D | hypothesis] The genetic evidence base for autoimmune hypothyroidism is predominantly European-ancestry. Several loci show ancestry heterogeneity, mostly in the MHC region, and six loci were European-specific. - PMID:42527560

[D | hypothesis] A hypothyroidism GWAS with Mendelian randomization identified 139 loci enriched for lymphocyte function. Drug-gene analysis supported increased hypothyroidism risk with immune checkpoint inhibitors and tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and the authors proposed potential drug targets. - PMID:36093044

[D | hypothesis] Hashimoto's thyroiditis is characterised by autoantibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin. Animal models implicate CD4+/CD8+ T cells, Th1/Th2/Th17 cytokines, regulatory T-cell loss and B cells. In NOD mice, iodide exposure induces thyroiditis, and anti-CD20 B-cell depletion reduces disease severity. - PMID:36980259

[D | emerging] In patients on levothyroxine for thyroid carcinoma, drug-induced subclinical hyperthyroidism was associated with a higher degree of fatigue and worse muscle function than in euthyroid subjects. This suggests fatigue can accompany over-replacement. It is an association in a cross-sectional study of suppressive therapy and cannot be applied directly to replacement dosing. - PMID:22643561

[D | hypothesis] A published evidence record links fatigue and levothyroxine as 'drug effect' (SIDER). The record does not distinguish an adverse effect from an indication-related symptom, and gives no dose, frequency or causality. - DB:7059b87fa5005f87

[D | emerging] Rare case reports describe intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) with headache associated with levothyroxine, in one case shortly after a dose increase, with resolution after dose reduction or discontinuation. This is a rare, causally uncertain signal. A physician would look for features such as papilloedema or visual symptoms in a persistent or severe headache. - PMID:25266827, PMID:34747819

[D | hypothesis] The Mutanex published evidence record (SIDER) lists headache as linked to levothyroxine, but the relation type is ambiguous between a recorded drug effect and an indication. It supports a labelled association only and gives no frequency, dose or causality information. - DB:7059b87fa5005f87

[D | emerging] Hypothyroidism can itself be missed because it masquerades as other conditions. Reported examples are cardiac disease (myocardial dystrophy, coronary disease, myocarditis), hypertension and oedema. Severe decompensated hypothyroidism (myxedema coma) can resemble more common causes of altered mental status and depressed vital signs, and TSH and free T4 should be obtained when it is considered. - PMID:33039222, PMID:8644032

[D | emerging] A case report describes headache, with anxiety, palpitations, insomnia and other symptoms, after repeated high oral cyanocobalamin doses in a patient with severe pernicious anemia. The symptoms improved after the drug was stopped. This is the only direct report of B12 as a drug causing headache in the sources, and it concerns a much higher cumulative dose than is known for this patient. - PMID:31018715

[D | hypothesis] The Mutanex published evidence (SIDER-derived) has a record linking headache and vitamin B12 as a drug effect or an indication. The record does not distinguish which, or give frequency or dose. - DB:7059b87fa5005f87

[D | hypothesis] Headache with hyperhomocysteinemia and low B12 has been reported in case reports of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, including after nitrous oxide misuse. These reports are a reminder that headache can have other causes linked to B12 metabolism and need clinician assessment for red-flag features, rather than being assumed to be a vitamin side effect. - PMID:34515072, PMID:39034579

[D | emerging] Clinical red flags for infection or malignancy should prompt targeted laboratory and imaging investigations. Case reports show that L4-L5 spondylodiscitis with epidural abscess, for example secondary to infective endocarditis, can present at the lumbar spine. - PMID:42005267, PMID:42849905

[D | emerging] Investigational biological therapies are described as having potential, but their clinical translation remains an unresolved challenge. These include PRP, bone marrow aspirate concentrate, chemonucleolysis and mesenchymal stem cells. Regenerative therapies appeared in only one of 12 guidelines reviewed. - PMID:40625005, PMID:41487424

[D | hypothesis] Novel needle-based interventions are supported only by single case reports. These are ultrasound-guided Shinbaro 2 pharmacopuncture with motion-style acupuncture, and paraspinal hook-needle intervention. The hook-needle report itself cautions that spontaneous herniation resorption cannot be excluded and that causality or efficacy is not established. - PMID:42494667, PMID:42793488

[D | hypothesis] Only a single case report links a COL1A1 frameshift mutation in osteogenesis imperfecta to multilevel lumbar disc herniation despite mild disc degeneration. It suggests that type I collagen defects may increase susceptibility to herniation. - PMID:40760627

[D | hypothesis] Piezo1, a mechanosensitive ion channel, is proposed as a core transducer linking abnormal mechanical load to inflammation (NF-κB, NLRP3) and to ECM catabolism. Its inhibition has been tested only in cell, ex vivo and animal models, with major barriers to drug delivery and safety. - PMID:41769000
[D | hypothesis] GDF-5 is proposed as a biological therapy that could slow disc degeneration. The supporting data shown are mesenchymal stem cell culture experiments. - PMID:35754493

[D | hypothesis] Mast cells are found in disc tissue and are reported to be elevated in degenerative disc conditions. Mast cell stabilisers such as ketotifen are proposed for investigation, but the authors state the supporting data are incomplete. Efficacy evidence exists only in other connective tissues, mostly in animals. - PMID:41898664

[D | hypothesis] Transcriptomic and database analyses propose ELMO1, CKAP4 and SACM1L as highly expressed in degenerated disc tissue. They also propose diagnostic models and drug candidates derived from the Connectivity Map (CMap). Separately, network analysis predicts regulatory hubs such as miR-193b-3p, CRNDE, E2F1 and E2F4. - PMID:32538749, PMID:41381667

[D | emerging] Recurrence after percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy is described as a major problem. In a small retrospective L4/5 cohort, no dural tear, disc-space infection or nerve injury occurred. - PMID:41102838

[D | emerging] After endoscopic (AUSS) discectomy for single-level herniation, reported complications included postoperative infection, incisional haematoma with vertebral infection, and cerebrospinal fluid leak. The leak resolved with conservative treatment, and one patient underwent revision surgery. - PMID:42996711

[D | evidence supported] Cauda equina syndrome is a red-flag presentation. A case report describes emergent MRI followed by decompression as the standard of care in suspected cauda equina syndrome. Several of the mimics in these sources (discal cyst or infection, intradural disc, ligamentum flavum hematoma, brucellar abscess) presented with cauda equina compression or bilateral deficits. - PMID:30459862, PMID:42677046

[D | emerging] Intradural disc herniation is a differential for a large central L4-L5 disc. Suggestive MRI features are displacement of traversing roots with a 'crumble disc' sign, a Y-sign in the ventral dura, and a hypointense intradural structure not continuous with the disc. Sudden lower-limb weakness with cauda equina syndrome should raise suspicion. - PMID:30459862

[D | emerging] Ligamentum flavum hematoma can mimic disc herniation, with low back or radicular pain and neurological deficits. It is favoured when a posterolateral extradural lesion at a degenerative segment shows MRI features of acute haemorrhage. Facet joint, synovial and ligamentum flavum cysts are the main cystic mimics; they are mostly found at L4/5 in degenerative spines and usually present with radicular pain. - PMID:42888559

[D | emerging] An intervertebral disc cyst is a rare ventral extradural lesion that communicates with the disc and can cause L5 radiculopathy at L4-L5. The case report states it should be in the differential of any ventral extradural intraspinal mass, with discography and post-discography CT confirming the diagnosis. - PMID:14589206

[D | emerging] Spinal infection, such as discitis or epidural abscess, can mimic an L4-L5 disc extrusion or discal cyst. Case reports describe MRI features that favour infection: heterogeneous peripheral diffusion restriction, thick peripheral enhancement, and interval vertebral marrow oedema on short-interval follow-up. Infectious causes should be considered when findings are atypical. - PMID:42677046, PMID:42810754

[D | emerging] A systematic review of 28 published cases found that Mycobacteroides abscessus complex vertebral osteomyelitis is rare and diagnostically challenging. It usually presented with back pain, and most patients were immunocompetent. Early tissue diagnosis and combined medical-surgical management were associated with better outcomes. - PMID:42597783

[D | emerging] An L4-L5 foraminal herniation can compress the exiting L4 root and cause L4 crural (anterior thigh) neuralgia. This is conventionally attributed to L3-L4 disc herniation, so the herniation's location within the canal versus the foramen affects which root is involved. In an older surgical series, foraminal L4-L5 hernias outnumbered L3-L4 hernias as the cause. - PMID:3704529

[D | hypothesis] A single case report describes an L4-L5 disc herniation compressing the L4 root that presented as chronic right lower abdominal pain. The spinal origin was confirmed by a selective nerve root block. This shows that disc compression can produce atypical referred pain that mimics visceral disease. - PMID:41998714

[D | emerging] Autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is diagnosed using clinical features plus thyroid antibodies (thyroperoxidase and thyroglobulin). A case report describes hypothyroidism from Hashimoto's thyroiditis presenting as low back pain, myalgia and cramps that improved within eight weeks of levothyroxine. Hypothyroid myopathy or myalgia could therefore overlap with, or be mistaken for, the patient's chronic disc-related back pain. Muscle pain and exercise intolerance in thyroid dysfunction are proposed to relate to mitochondrial and carnitine changes. - PMID:38738164

[D | hypothesis] Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), which the patient reportedly takes, is reported in a systematic review of mostly small trials to cause mainly mild adverse events, including somnolence and, less commonly, drowsiness and giddiness. The same review notes that some studies reported mild CNS depression and an increase in thyroxine (T4) levels. The supplement is therefore a possible modifier of daytime sleepiness and a possible confounder of thyroid function interpretation in a levothyroxine-treated patient. This is a hypothesis for clinician review, not evidence of causation in this patient. - PMID:32201301

[D | hypothesis] The published evidence record is a database-level ASSOCIATED_WITH link from Open Targets meaning medicine and symptom are linked (a recorded drug effect, or an indication). It does not state the effect size, population or direction, so it is a pointer to the literature and not clinical evidence. - DB:90c7ce597c4c69c9

[D | emerging] An RCT of nucleotides + B12 versus B1/B6/B12 for low back pain had no placebo arm, so no B12-specific effect can be derived. Both arms improved. The nucleotides+B12 arm had greater VAS reduction at 30 days, equivalence at 60 days, and fewer adverse events and discontinuations. - PMID:33116795

[D | hypothesis] Proposed mechanisms (nerve regeneration, cyclooxygenase inhibition, other pain-signalling pathways) come from animal studies. They are hypothesis-level and are not treatment recommendations. - PMID:30700078

[D | hypothesis] Case reports show that B12 deficiency can present with low back pain and neurological symptoms (e.g., nitrous-oxide-induced deficiency), which resolved with B12 replacement. These cases show a deficiency pathway and not B12 treatment benefit in non-deficient chronic low back pain. - PMID:41804043

[D | hypothesis] Four case reports describe thyrotoxicosis (very low TSH, high fT4 or elevated thyroid hormones) in people taking ashwagandha supplements. Hormone levels normalized after discontinuation, which suggests an association, but causality was not established. - PMID:41454558, PMID:41502355, PMID:41830041

[D | hypothesis] The only levothyroxine-related evidence is one case report. A 73-year-old woman who replaced her levothyroxine with ashwagandha had TSH below the normal range; after stopping ashwagandha she returned to a mildly hypothyroid state. No source studied ashwagandha taken together with levothyroxine or any pharmacokinetic interaction. - PMID:34254920, PMID:41454558

[D | hypothesis] In propylthiouracil-induced hypothyroid rats, ashwagandha extract decreased TSH and increased T3/T4, comparable to a standard thyroxine drug. This mechanistic signal supports a possible thyroid-stimulating effect. - PMID:42183570

[D | hypothesis] A narrative review proposes that the autoimmune process itself may directly contribute to persistent symptoms in some levothyroxine-treated HT patients. This is a hypothesis and does not specifically address anxiety or inflammatory markers. - PMID:33332019

[D | emerging] Case reports describe thyrotoxicosis (low TSH, high fT4) in people using ashwagandha supplements. Thyroid indices normalised after discontinuation in the reported cases, which suggests an association, although causation was not established. - PMID:16355578, PMID:38559552, PMID:41454558

[D | emerging] One case report concerns a woman with levothyroxine-treated hypothyroidism who replaced levothyroxine with ashwagandha. Her TSH fell below range while fT4 and T3 appeared normal. After she stopped ashwagandha she returned to a mildly hypothyroid state. This is a replacement scenario rather than concurrent use, so it does not show an interaction with levothyroxine. - PMID:41454558

[D | hypothesis] In female mice, ashwagandha root extract increased serum T4. This supports a biologically plausible thyroid-stimulating effect but is animal data and not a basis for any recommendation. - PMID:10619390

[D | emerging] In a cross-sectional study of 101 treated hypothyroid patients in rural Nepal, post-treatment anxiety scores (HAM-A) were significantly lower than pre-treatment scores. This suggests anxiety symptoms often improve with levothyroxine over the long term (median treatment duration 5 years). The study gives no information on how quickly improvement occurs. - PMID:41111734

[D | emerging] A retrospective TriNetX cohort of children and adolescents with hypothyroidism and anxiety disorders found levothyroxine treatment was associated with lower use of SSRIs, fewer psychiatric consultations and lower recorded suicidal ideation or self-harm. The authors state causality cannot be inferred. No timing of symptom change is reported. - PMID:42074695

[D | hypothesis] A single case report describes anxiety-like symptoms in a 32-year-old woman that were misdiagnosed as generalized anxiety disorder for 10 months before hypothyroidism was identified. This illustrates that anxiety symptoms can be a manifestation of untreated or inadequately treated hypothyroidism rather than a drug effect. - PMID:39991346

[D | hypothesis] In a bipolar disorder RCT where thyroid indices were safety measures, all three ashwagandha-treated patients with abnormal indices had T4 increases (7-24%), and one had baseline subclinical hypothyroidism that normalized. The authors suggest vigilance for hyperthyroidism. - PMID:25624699

[D | hypothesis] Case reports describe thyrotoxicosis, including painless thyroiditis, during ashwagandha use, with normalization after it was stopped. One report involved a woman who replaced her levothyroxine with ashwagandha: TSH was suppressed while on it, and she reverted to hypothyroidism after stopping. Causality was not established. - PMID:38559552, PMID:41454558

[D | hypothesis] Rat studies show ashwagandha root extract lowers TSH and restores T3/T4 in drug-induced hypothyroidism. A review proposes central regulatory pathways rather than direct receptor binding as the likely mechanism. - PMID:41454558, PMID:42005335

[D | emerging] Documented adverse effects of cyanocobalamin in the supplied sources include rare hypersensitivity, such as anaphylaxis after intramuscular injection. These are case reports and do not mention anxiety as a reported effect. Parenteral and oral exposure should be distinguished when assessing any reaction. - PMID:29984124

[D | emerging] A case series reported that hypothyroid patients needing disproportionately high LT4 doses while taking a dietary fibre supplement had a lower LT4 requirement or lower TSH after the fibre was withdrawn. In vitro, wheat bran adsorbed LT4 in a dose-dependent way. The abstract reports no numeric TSH change. - PMID:8636317

[D | hypothesis] A single case report describes a woman with stable TSH on LT4 who developed elevated TSH and mild symptoms after starting an over-the-counter whey protein supplement. TSH returned to normal (1.7 mIU/L) 6 weeks after stopping the supplement at an unchanged LT4 dose. The authors note there was no prior literature on protein supplements and LT4 absorption. - PMID:34280893

[D | hypothesis] In one case, a woman taking a soy protein supplement immediately after LT4 needed unusually high LT4 doses. Separating the two in time allowed target free T4 and TSH levels to be reached on lower LT4 doses. - PMID:11421567

[D | emerging] A narrative review reports that in women with persistent hypothyroid symptoms despite appropriate levothyroxine therapy, restoring serum ferritin above 100 µg/l ameliorated symptoms. Patients with autoimmune thyroid disease are described as frequently iron-deficient. Non-antibody contributors to persistent symptoms are therefore relevant when interpreting any TPOAb result. - PMID:30208979

[D | hypothesis] High serum B12 was higher in neurodevelopmental disorders than in healthy controls or schizophrenia. This suggests a possible disorder-specific feature, but the mechanism is unknown and it is not evidence of an anxiety link. - PMID:32323402

[E | hypothesis] No supplied source evaluates a pharmacokinetic or absorption interaction between ashwagandha and levothyroxine, or ashwagandha's thyroid effects in patients already on levothyroxine. Only one clinical study directly examined ashwagandha's effect on thyroid hormones in humans. - PMID:38003702, PMID:41454558

[C | evidence supported] Celiac and thyroid autoimmunity are linked by a shared genetic background, notably HLA DQ2 and DQ8. This provides a mechanistic basis for co-occurrence but not a patient-level risk estimate. - PMID:30316996

[D | emerging] Genetic confirmation by ALB hotspot sequencing (the Arg242His variant is the commonest reported) is suggested as a simple alternative to complex laboratory and imaging tests. FDH is autosomal dominant and generally benign, but misdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary treatment. - PMID:38736368

[D | emerging] A family of Bangladeshi extraction had FDH caused by a novel ALB variant (R218S, also written p.Arg242Ser with the signal peptide counted). Two family members were affected. - PMID:24494774

[D | hypothesis] Hashimoto's (autoimmune) hypothyroidism has a strong polygenic basis. The largest multi-ancestry GWAS highlights immune-cell, and especially T-cell, pathways. Implicated genes include cytokine-signalling genes (IL2RA, IRF4, IRF5, JAK1, PTPN2, STAT4, TYK2), T-cell activation genes (CD28, CTLA4, CD247) and multiple HLA class I/II genes, as well as thyroid hormone synthesis genes (TPO, TG, PDE8B). - PMID:42527560

[D | hypothesis] The genetic evidence base for autoimmune hypothyroidism is predominantly European-ancestry. Several loci show ancestry heterogeneity, mostly in the MHC region, and six loci were European-specific. - PMID:42527560

[C | evidence supported] Congenital and dyshormonogenic hypothyroidism arises from defects in genes for iodide transport and organification or iodotyrosine recycling (e.g. SLC5A5, SLC26A4, TG, TPO, DUOX2, DUOXA2). Thyroid dysgenesis can arise from defects in thyroid transcription factors or in TSH receptor function. - PMID:31301652, PMID:35999191

[D | hypothesis] A bidirectional Mendelian randomization study found that genetically predicted PhenoAge acceleration (PhenoAA) was associated with higher subacute thyroiditis risk (borderline significance). Subacute thyroiditis was associated with lower intrinsic epigenetic age acceleration (IEAA). Subacute thyroiditis is a transient inflammatory condition, not chronic hypothyroidism, and Hashimoto's or non-autoimmune hypothyroidism was not studied. - PMID:39300457

[C | evidence supported] Genetic factors are reported to contribute substantially to intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) risk. A narrative review cites about 75% of aetiology. IVDD is described as multifactorial, combining genetic and environmental factors. - PMID:27617275, PMID:27917384

[C | emerging] Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with IVDD risk are reported in several gene groups. These include structural matrix genes (COL1A1, COL9A3, COL11A1, COL11A2, ACAN, CHST3), the vitamin D receptor gene, ECM-degrading enzyme genes (MMP-1, -2, -3, -9, -14, ADAMTS-4, -5), apoptosis genes (CASP9, TRAIL, DR4) and growth factor genes (GDF5, VEGF). Some effects are limited by sex and population. - PMID:27917384

[C | emerging] A systematic review of spinal stenosis mechanisms reports that intervertebral disc herniation is associated with mutations in the type I collagen genes (COL1A1/COL1A2) and the resulting protein dysregulation. It cautions that most publications lack direct mutation-to-pathology data. - PMID:36362274

[D | hypothesis] Only a single case report links a COL1A1 frameshift mutation in osteogenesis imperfecta to multilevel lumbar disc herniation despite mild disc degeneration. It suggests that type I collagen defects may increase susceptibility to herniation. - PMID:40760627

[C | emerging] A two-sample MR study (European-ancestry GWAS data) reported a suggestive association between genetically predicted higher serum B12 and anxiety disorders (OR 1.34) and bipolar disorder (OR 1.85). It found no association with depression, OCD or schizophrenia. The authors state horizontal pleiotropy cannot be excluded. - PMID:38999734

[C | emerging] A Danish MR study in 4126 participants found no evidence for a causal effect of circulating B12 or folate on depression or anxiety. It could not exclude small to moderate effects. - PMID:28656970

[C | evidence supported] AITD susceptibility genes fall into immune-regulatory genes (including HLA, CTLA4, PTPN22, CD40, CD25/IL2RA, FCRL3) and thyroid-specific genes (TG, TSHR). Each has a modest effect, and none is essential for disease. This is consistent with a polygenic mechanism involving T-cell regulation and IL-2 receptor signalling, but it is an association-level inference. - PMID:22530160

[C | emerging] The strongest thyroid-specific locus, TSHR, was associated with Graves' disease but not with autoimmune hypothyroidism in two Caucasian cohorts. The proposed TSHR mechanism (reduced thymic TSHR expression leading to central tolerance failure and escape of TSHR-reactive T cells) was developed for Graves' disease and is not demonstrated for hypothyroidism. - PMID:16106256, PMID:26361261

[D | hypothesis] In one early-onset familial Hashimoto's thyroiditis pedigree, affected members had high polygenic risk scores, and rare structural variants were enriched in hypothyroidism GWAS loci. This is consistent with a multi-hit polygenic model, but the data are exploratory and come from a single family. - PMID:42938419

[C | evidence supported] Inactivating TSHR variants cause TSH resistance with a wide phenotypic range. Biallelic disrupting variants cause the more severe, recessively inherited forms. Milder forms occur with monoallelic defects, some with dominant-negative effects on wild-type receptor. - PMID:20083154

[C | evidence supported] Heterozygous TSHR LOF variants can cause non-autoimmune subclinical hypothyroidism or fluctuating TSH elevation, often clustering in families, and expressivity varies between carriers. - PMID:12050212, PMID:16060907, PMID:17526952

[D | emerging] In consanguineous families with TSHR-related congenital hypothyroidism, expression varied within and between families. The authors suggest co-existing variants in other thyroid genes (for example SLC26A7) may modify severity, pointing to possible oligogenic inheritance. - PMID:40391015

[D | hypothesis] The common TSHR intronic SNP rs2268458 was reported as possibly associated with non-autoimmune hypothyroidism in a small Indian study. After age and sex adjustment the genotype association was not statistically significant. - PMID:42605379

[C | evidence supported] Pendred syndrome is autosomal recessive and caused by biallelic SLC26A4 variants. The hallmark is hearing impairment with inner-ear malformation (enlarged vestibular aqueduct), plus goiter and an iodide organification defect, with or without hypothyroidism. The thyroid phenotype is variable and may be modified by nutritional iodine record. - PMID:28648509, PMID:34345941

[C | evidence supported] SLC26A4 is listed among genes whose mutations cause congenital dyshormonogenetic hypothyroidism (iodine organification defect), alongside TPO, DUOX2 and DUOXA2. Consensus guidelines for congenital hypothyroidism recommend genetic counseling for affected families. - PMID:25231445

[D | emerging] Homozygous SLC26A4 missense variants were reported in two patients with apparent thyroid dysgenesis (hypoplastic thyroid). One of the two also had severe hearing problems. This extends the phenotypic spectrum beyond dyshormonogenesis. - PMID:24248179

[D | hypothesis] In a small Indian study of 127 non-autoimmune, non-congenital adult hypothyroid patients without Pendred features, heterozygous SLC26A4 variants were found in about 20% and were proposed to be linked to the hypothyroidism. Controls showed fewer variant types. This is association only, with no demonstrated causation. - PMID:28718179

[D | hypothesis] SLC26A4 variants have been linked to autoimmune thyroid disease. Heterozygous variants were seen in Graves' disease patients, and a case report describes a child with two pathogenic variants, hearing loss and positive TPO antibody. The authors suggest screening thyroid autoantibodies in patients with pathogenic SLC26A4 variants. This is hypothesis-generating only. - PMID:21045265, PMID:39359669
[C | evidence supported] Thyroid diseases are polygenic. No single gene has been found to be specifically causal, and many genes and variants interact. - PMID:31301652

[C | evidence supported] Congenital hypothyroidism has two broad genetic mechanism classes. Dysgenesis involves TSHR, PAX8, NKX2-1, FOXE1 and NKX2-5. Dyshormonogenesis involves iodide transport (SLC5A5), organification (TPO, DUOX2, DUOXA2, SLC26A4), thyroglobulin synthesis or transport, and iodotyrosine deiodinase (IYD) deficiency. - PMID:25231445

[D | hypothesis] In a paediatric dyshormonogenesis cohort, 3.13% of patients carried candidate TSHR variants. Functional cAMP-response reporter assays showed the variants to be totally, partially or mildly deleterious, with genotype-phenotype correlation in the patients studied. - PMID:39337518

[C | evidence supported] Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) TG mutations cause autosomal recessive permanent congenital hypothyroidism, typically with goiter. - PMID:21372558, PMID:42378173

[D | emerging] Genotype-phenotype relations are not clean: single-allele TG variants have been reported in families with a typical phenotype, and TG mutations have also been linked to euthyroid simple goiter. - PMID:20093166, PMID:23164529, PMID:29275168

blocks.text: Database associations and enrichment are hypotheses about mechanism, not proof of causality.
