items: [B | evidence supported] CTLA4 +49A/G (rs231775) is associated with increased HT risk in a meta-analysis of 14 studies. The association was significant in Asian subgroups but not in Caucasians in that analysis. - PMID:23860622

[B | evidence supported] A second meta-analysis (18 case-control studies, >4,600 subjects) found CTLA4 +49 G carriers had higher HT risk in both Asian and Caucasian populations. The authors caution that the results were less stable on sensitivity analysis. - PMID:23677500

[C | evidence supported] AITD susceptibility genes fall into immune-regulatory genes (including HLA, CTLA4, PTPN22, CD40, CD25/IL2RA, FCRL3) and thyroid-specific genes (TG, TSHR). Each has a modest effect, and none is essential for disease. This is consistent with a polygenic mechanism involving T-cell regulation and IL-2 receptor signalling, but it is an association-level inference. - PMID:22530160

[C | evidence supported] The HLA-DR (class II) locus was the first AITD susceptibility locus identified. HLA-C alleles (class I) are proposed, together with TSHR/Tg, to direct a general autoimmune propensity toward the thyroid. HLA-DR, CTLA-4, PTPN22, FCRL3 and probably the IL-2 receptor are also associated with other autoimmune disorders, which suggests a lowered general threshold for autoimmunity. - PMID:17824829, PMID:19343617

[C | emerging] Immune-regulatory risk loci (HLA, CTLA4, PTPN22) are described as general autoimmune risk loci encoding molecules vital to immune function, which supports the T-cell regulation component of the proposed mechanism. The functional link to hypothyroidism specifically is not shown in these sources. - PMID:20083159

[C | emerging] The strongest thyroid-specific locus, TSHR, was associated with Graves' disease but not with autoimmune hypothyroidism in two Caucasian cohorts. The proposed TSHR mechanism (reduced thymic TSHR expression leading to central tolerance failure and escape of TSHR-reactive T cells) was developed for Graves' disease and is not demonstrated for hypothyroidism. - PMID:16106256, PMID:26361261

[C | evidence supported] Reviewers conclude that genetic profiling of AITD patients is unlikely to be clinically useful in the near term, because contributing genes vary between patients and populations and the environment and epigenetics also act. - PMID:22530160

[C | evidence supported] Inactivating TSHR variants cause TSH resistance with a wide phenotypic range. Biallelic disrupting variants cause the more severe, recessively inherited forms. Milder forms occur with monoallelic defects, some with dominant-negative effects on wild-type receptor. - PMID:20083154

[C | evidence supported] Heterozygous TSHR LOF variants can cause non-autoimmune subclinical hypothyroidism or fluctuating TSH elevation, often clustering in families, and expressivity varies between carriers. - PMID:12050212, PMID:16060907, PMID:17526952

[C | evidence supported] In a cohort of 367 Chinese patients with congenital hypothyroidism, TSHR variants were found in 12.3%, and biallelic variants in 4.9%. Many variants were of uncertain significance. Patients with TSHR biallelic variants had a relatively mild phenotype. Hormone levels and initial levothyroxine dose did not differ between those with and without TSHR variants. - PMID:38433572

[C | emerging] In patients with HT, thyroid self-antigens (TPO, thyroglobulin) skewed T-helper differentiation toward Th17 in ex vivo human cell studies. IL-6 and TGF-β1 were higher at baseline and FOXP3Δ2 (a splice variant that does not inhibit Th17 differentiation) was more highly expressed. This supports Th17 involvement in HT pathogenesis as an association from small ex vivo studies. - PMID:26836805

[C | emerging] The evidence does not show loss of regulatory B or T cells in HT. B10 (IL-10-producing B cell) frequencies were not decreased in HT or Graves' disease. Patients were not impaired in producing IL-10 in response to thyroglobulin. Baseline FOXP3 mRNA was similar to healthy donors, although FOXP3Δ2 was higher. This argues against a simple 'regulatory cell loss' model and favours qualitative skewing of the response. - PMID:26836805

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review states that thyroid-infiltrating activated T cells lead to cell-mediated immunity, thyroid injury and eventually hypothyroidism. Humoral immunity via TSHR-stimulating antibodies may give rise to hyperthyroidism. It also notes that genetic polymorphisms in thyroid genes (TG, TSHR) and immunoregulatory genes (HLA, CTLA4, PTPN22, CD40, FCRL3, IL2RA, FOXP3) contribute most of the susceptibility. - PMID:25231450

[C | evidence supported] TSHR autoantibodies are reported to cause Graves' disease and, in some cases, primary hypothyroidism. This supports a possible antibody-mediated contribution beyond TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies. - PMID:12186499

[C | evidence supported] Pendrin is an anion exchanger (chloride, iodide, bicarbonate) expressed on the apical thyroid cell membrane. It is proposed to mediate iodide efflux into the follicular lumen, a step in thyroid hormone synthesis. Other transporters such as ANO1 may also contribute, so the exact thyroid role is still debated. - DB:952a18c1d24b268e, PMID:28648509

[C | evidence supported] Pendred syndrome is autosomal recessive and caused by biallelic SLC26A4 variants. The hallmark is hearing impairment with inner-ear malformation (enlarged vestibular aqueduct), plus goiter and an iodide organification defect, with or without hypothyroidism. The thyroid phenotype is variable and may be modified by nutritional iodine record. - PMID:28648509, PMID:34345941

[C | evidence supported] SLC26A4 is listed among genes whose mutations cause congenital dyshormonogenetic hypothyroidism (iodine organification defect), alongside TPO, DUOX2 and DUOXA2. Consensus guidelines for congenital hypothyroidism recommend genetic counseling for affected families. - PMID:25231445
[C | evidence supported] Thyroid diseases are polygenic. No single gene has been found to be specifically causal, and many genes and variants interact. - PMID:31301652

[C | evidence supported] Congenital hypothyroidism has two broad genetic mechanism classes. Dysgenesis involves TSHR, PAX8, NKX2-1, FOXE1 and NKX2-5. Dyshormonogenesis involves iodide transport (SLC5A5), organification (TPO, DUOX2, DUOXA2, SLC26A4), thyroglobulin synthesis or transport, and iodotyrosine deiodinase (IYD) deficiency. - PMID:25231445

[C | evidence supported] Biallelic inactivating TSHR mutations cause TSH resistance and congenital hypothyroidism. Phenotype depends on residual receptor activity: nonfunctional alleles give thyroid hypoplasia with overt hypothyroidism, and hypomorphic alleles give a normal-sized gland with preserved hormone output (compensated resistance). - PMID:25797365

[C | evidence supported] The thyroid dysgenesis transcription factors (Ttf-1, Ttf-2, Pax8) and Tshr act at early thyroid development. Mutations occur in only some TD cases, and familial screening excluded these genes in some families, implying genetic heterogeneity. - PMID:15539794

[C | evidence supported] In a targeted NGS panel study of 106 Chinese CH patients, DUOX2, TG, TPO and TSHR variants were among the most frequent. No SLC5A5 or IYD mutations were found, so the iodide-transport and iodotyrosine-recycling mechanisms had no supporting variants in that cohort. - PMID:30022773

[C | evidence supported] Transient congenital hypothyroidism has both genetic (DUOX2/DUOXA2) and environmental (iodine deficiency or excess, anti-TSHR antibodies, antithyroid or iodine-rich medications) causes. Genotype alone cannot predict duration. If TCH is genetically mediated, long-term monitoring for recurrent dysfunction is advised, particularly in pregnancy. - PMID:35588090

[C | evidence supported] Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) TG mutations cause autosomal recessive permanent congenital hypothyroidism, typically with goiter. - PMID:21372558, PMID:42378173

[C | evidence supported] The classic TG-defect phenotype is goiter with high radioiodine uptake, a negative perchlorate discharge test, low serum TG, high TSH and low T4. Serum T3 can be low, normal or high. Severity ranges from euthyroid to severe hypothyroidism. - PMID:20093166, PMID:21372558, PMID:29275168

[C | evidence supported] TG variants impair TG folding, assembly and export from the endoplasmic reticulum, reducing thyroid hormone biosynthesis. Missense variants in the ACHE-like domain or variants affecting cysteines are emphasised as functionally important. - PMID:20093166, PMID:23164529

[C | evidence supported] Pathogenic THRA variants cause RTHα, a distinct inherited disorder of thyroid hormone action. Its clinical picture resembles primary hypothyroidism but without TSH elevation, and it has a characteristic biochemical signature. - PMID:22168587, PMID:42843455

[C | evidence supported] The usual mechanism is a dominant-negative effect. Heterozygous mutant receptors (often impaired in T3 binding) inhibit wild-type THRA activity. This explains tissue-specific hypothyroidism despite near-normal circulating hormones. - PMID:24969835, PMID:42843455

[C | evidence supported] Genotype-phenotype relationships are imperfect. Truncating (frameshift/nonsense) variants tend to cause more severe phenotypes than missense variants. Variability is considerable even with identical mutations, and atypical phenotypes occur, including a gain-of-function variant with mixed hypo- and hyperthyroid features. - PMID:25670821, PMID:34069457, PMID:42843455

[C | emerging] Standard thyroid tests may not reveal RTHα, particularly in adults. Reverse T3, anemia and creatine kinase are described as clues that would warrant THRA sequencing. Reviewers suggest suspecting RTHα in mild hypothyroid features with high/high-normal FT3, low/low-normal FT4 and normal TSH. - PMID:28527577, PMID:32349464

[C | emerging] In a South Indian case-control study of 235 AITD patients (180 HT, 55 GD) and 235 controls, CTLA4 +49 GG was increased and AA decreased in HT. HLA-DRB1*11 and *12 were increased in HT, and DRB1*03 and *10 were decreased (suggesting a protective association). Several DRB1 and CTLA4 genotype combinations were also associated with HT. - PMID:29174716

[C | emerging] Older Caucasian data show only weak HLA class II contributions to HT. A meta-analysis found weak positive associations with DR3 and DR4 and no significant DR5 association. The authors concluded that any HLA contribution is small. - PMID:1356664

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews list HLA-DR, CTLA-4, PTPN22 and FOXP3 as genetic predispositions for thyroid autoimmunity. They note that these genes are shared across other autoimmune disorders and that individual patients have their own cluster of susceptibility factors. - PMID:19343617, PMID:38999993

[C | emerging] In small, selected cohorts of antibody-negative SCH or isolated hyperthyrotropinemia, TSHR variant detection ranged widely depending on selection. It was 4 of 10 in one series. In another series (42 subjects), mutations were found only in members of two familial clusters, and none of 34 sporadic cases carried them. Ages of participants are not stated in the abstracts, so adult-specific prevalence cannot be derived. - PMID:12050212, PMID:15531543

[C | emerging] In a pediatric idiopathic SH cohort selected for features suggesting a genetic cause (neonatal TSH elevation, family history, thyroid in situ, or SH persisting after levothyroxine withdrawal), heterozygous TSHR variants were found in about one third of patients. This figure cannot be extrapolated to adults or unselected antibody-negative disease. - PMID:42246651

[C | emerging] Clinical course and levothyroxine requirement in variant carriers are only partly characterized, and the only follow-up cohort is pediatric. Variant-positive children generally had a stable, compensated phenotype without progression to overt hypothyroidism. Levothyroxine was discontinued in some, but five patients needed it re-started because of rising TSH or symptoms. Lower thyroid volume and additional risk factors were associated with needing treatment. The authors favor a conservative, individualized strategy rather than routine levothyroxine. - PMID:42246651

[C | emerging] A review states that the usefulness of replacement treatment in subclinical hypothyroidism from partial TSH resistance is controversial, because the raised TSH may compensate for the mildly impaired receptor. Early replacement is considered mandatory only in severe congenital hypothyroidism from complete resistance. - PMID:23154162

[C | emerging] HT is associated with increased Th17 cells in blood and thyroid tissue, raised IL-17 and a Th17/Treg imbalance. This is an association; the source does not establish causation. - PMID:38710521

[C | emerging] A systematic review reports that serum and tissue IL-17 correlate positively with TPOAb/TgAb titres and early fibrosis, and that Th17 predominance precedes Th1-mediated tissue destruction. Th1 cells and their cytokines are described as predominant in HT, whereas Th2-mediated humoral responses dominate in Graves' disease. - PMID:41243116

[C | emerging] A review of HT immunology describes the Th1, Th17, Tfh and Tc subsets as increasing while Treg falls. It lists IL-2, IL-12, IL-17, IL-21, IL-22, IFN-γ and TNF-α as increased, and IFN-γ and TNF-α as triggering pyroptosis through the inflammasome. IFN-γ and IL-2 are therefore implicated, but only as a cytokine list, not as demonstrated signalling experiments. - PMID:38999993

[C | emerging] A narrative review reports that vitamin D supplementation in HT has shown promise in reducing antithyroid antibodies and favourably shifting cytokines and T-cell subsets (Th17, Tr1). This supports immunomodulation as a hypothesis, but it does not establish clinical benefit. - PMID:37513592

[C | evidence supported] Targeted NGS panels in CH cohorts identify a candidate variant in roughly 38% to 67% of cases, depending on cohort, gene set and variant-classification threshold. TPO, TSHR, DUOX2, TG and NKX2-1 were among the genes found in a guideline-selected cohort. - PMID:32459320, PMID:34248839, PMID:39378853

[C | emerging] Oligogenic (multi-gene) variant combinations are frequent in CH and are proposed to explain sporadic or variable presentations and phenotypic severity. This supports testing a multigene panel rather than single genes. - PMID:28444304, PMID:34248839

[C | emerging] In consanguineous families, homozygous TSHR variants account for a minority of cases, with other known genes absent in one cohort. Variable expression in TSHR families may be modified by additional variants such as SLC26A7. This supports a multigene panel over TSHR-only testing in consanguineous families. - PMID:20718767, PMID:40391015

[C | emerging] The clinical utility of NGS for treatment decisions or prognosis is not established. Many variants are VUS, and variant detection did not track with initial thyroid function or other clinical features in one cohort. - PMID:32459320, PMID:39378853, PMID:41262259

[C | emerging] IL-17A and IFN-γ mRNA are higher in thyroid tissue and PBMC of HT patients than in controls, and IL-17A and IL-23p19 protein is high in HT thyroid tissue. This suggests a mixed Th17/Th1 response, rather than a pure Th1 profile, in the destructive process. It is an association in a small sample, not proof of causation. - PMID:23090124

[C | emerging] High TPOAb titre was associated with higher frequencies of IFN-γ- and TNF-α-producing T cells in peripheral blood of HT patients on levothyroxine. The authors interpret this as Th/Tc1 cytokines probably responsible for thyroid cell damage. This is a correlation measured in blood, not thyroid tissue, so it does not show that TPOAb itself is pathogenic. - PMID:16060913

[C | guideline supported] The only guideline provided (ETA 2026) addresses assay interference, not TSHR genetic testing. It states that interference must be excluded before diagnosing rare inherited conditions in people with discordant thyroid function tests. It does not recommend TSHR sequencing for suspected TSH resistance. - PMID:42466561

[C | evidence supported] Heterozygous TSHR variants show variable expressivity. A grossly defective single allele invariably led to subclinical hypothyroidism in one cohort, whereas partially functional variants varied between generations. This makes interpretation of a single variant difficult. - PMID:16060907

[C | evidence supported] Some TSH resistance is not explained by TSHR mutations. Dominant familial RTSH has been found without TSHR or TSH-beta defects, and a larger proportion of families express the phenotype without a TSHR defect. A negative TSHR result therefore does not exclude a heritable cause. - PMID:14669836, PMID:9398691

[C | evidence supported] ACMG-based variant classification in the supplied sources comes from a UK Caucasian adult hyperthyroidism cohort studying activating TSHR variants. – were pathogenic; p.Glu34Lys, p.Asp36His and p.Pro52Thr were classed as definitely benign, and p.Ile334Thr as likely benign. This does not address loss-of-function TSH resistance or South Asian populations. - PMID:30372544

[C | evidence supported] A meta-analysis of about 1,100 AITD patients and controls found that Treg proportion among CD4+ T cells was lower in untreated AITD. In the HT subgroup, the CD4+ Treg proportion did not differ clearly (p=0.62), but circulating FoxP3+ Tregs were reduced in untreated HT (p=0.04). The result depends on the marker definition and on treatment status. - PMID:31827051

[C | evidence supported] A meta-analysis of newly diagnosed HT patients (26 case-control articles in total across HT and Graves' disease) reported lower peripheral Treg levels, lower FoxP3 mRNA, and higher Th17 levels than in healthy people. This points to a Th17/Treg imbalance. The authors suggest this imbalance may contribute to AITD, but case-control data cannot establish this. - PMID:36332627

[C | emerging] Genetic evidence is directionally consistent with a protective role for Tregs. Two-sample Mendelian randomization identified several Treg phenotypes that causally protect against HT risk in the European cohort. Separately, a case-control study found that the FOXP3 rs3761548 CC genotype was more frequent in HT patients and was associated with higher anti-TPO titres. These findings concern susceptibility and Treg-related genetics, not measured Treg function in patients. - PMID:32377237, PMID:38524638

[C | evidence supported] The clinical phenotype linked to NIS iodide transport defect is a variable degree of congenital hypothyroidism and goiter with low to absent radioiodide uptake on scintigraphy. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. - PMID:21565787, PMID:28648508

[C | evidence supported] SLC26A4-related Pendred syndrome and DFNB4 are autosomal recessive and caused by biallelic variants, with the thyroid iodine organification defect distinguishing PS. A single VUS therefore does not by itself establish either condition. - PMID:34345941

[C | evidence supported] Hearing loss and inner-ear malformation (especially EVA) are described as near-constant in PS, and one case report argues there is no compelling reason to consider PS when only goiter is present. This makes PS less likely in a patient with hypothyroidism and no hearing loss, though the sources do not directly test this. - PMID:25960948, PMID:39359669

[C | evidence supported] Patients with a single mutant SLC26A4 allele are reported to have normal iodide organification and normal thyroid gland volume, in contrast to patients with two mutant alleles. This suggests a monoallelic variant is unlikely to cause a thyroid biochemical defect, but all these patients had EVA and hearing loss. - PMID:25960948

[C | evidence supported] SLC26A4-related thyroid disease is variable. The organification defect occurs with or without goiter, and hypothyroidism is described as less common. Some biallelic patients have normal thyroid function at assessment. Hypothyroidism alone is therefore not a specific marker of SLC26A4 pathogenicity. - PMID:21358184, PMID:42231373

[C | evidence supported] The perchlorate discharge test is described as detecting the underlying thyroid biochemical defect and as useful for clinical diagnosis of PS when the SLC26A4 genotype is non-diagnostic, which would apply to a VUS. The sources do not say whether it would be appropriate in a patient without hearing loss. - PMID:21358184

[C | emerging] In a pilot cohort and systematic review of mild isolated hyperthyrotropinemia, monoallelic TSHR and DUOX2 variants were the most frequently reported disease-associated variants. Heterozygous carriers were predominant among untreated patients, which supports the idea that mild genetic forms exist. The cohort was neonatal or pediatric and does not address adult onset. - PMID:41262259

[C | emerging] Reviews describe the Pendred syndrome thyroid phenotype (goiter, hypothyroidism) as variable and possibly modified by nutritional iodine record. Pendred syndrome requires biallelic SLC26A4 mutations. - PMID:18692402, PMID:28648509

[C | evidence supported] Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) TG variants are an established cause of dyshormonogenic hypothyroidism, usually goitrous, with a wide phenotypic range from euthyroid to severe hypothyroidism. - PMID:20093166, PMID:29275168

[C | emerging] Heterozygous TG variants have been found in children with mild or transient congenital hypothyroidism, and in a Spanish cohort some of them had mild permanent hypothyroidism at reevaluation. These authors considered that no TG pathogenic variant was clearly involved in this group, so a causal role remains unproven. - PMID:39040671

[C | emerging] In a pilot cohort of children with mild isolated hyperthyrotropinemia, the contribution of a monoallelic TG variant was judged unclear. The systematic review found few MIH cases with presumed disease-causing variants in TG or TPO, and these were mostly monoallelic. - PMID:41262259

[C | emerging] Reported genetic testing yields come from paediatric, selected cohorts. Guideline-selected familial, dysgenesis or syndromic CH cases gave a variant detection rate of 37.7% of families (TPO was most common, with TG in only 2 families). A Spanish dyshormonogenesis cohort found TG variants that could explain the phenotype in 11.8% of patients. No sources give a yield for adult-onset or unselected hypothyroidism. - PMID:39040671, PMID:39378853

[C | emerging] In a Korean case-control study, a PTPN22 SNP other than rs2476601 (rs12730735) and a five-SNP haplotype were associated with AITD, especially HT. This is the only HT-specific non-rs2476601 PTPN22 signal in the sources, and it is East Asian, not South Asian. - PMID:22069277

[C | emerging] In a Japanese cohort, no individual PTPN22 SNP was associated with AITD. A haplotype showed a protective association, pooled across Graves' disease and HT. One IL2RA SNP (rs3118470) was weakly associated with Graves' disease, not HT. - PMID:20615141

[C | evidence supported] A meta-analysis found the PTPN22 R620W (rs2476601) association with AITD in Caucasians but not in Asians. This supports population-specific effects but does not cover other variants or South Asians specifically. - PMID:33103521

[C | evidence supported] TG variants cause congenital hypothyroidism with autosomal recessive inheritance (homozygous or compound heterozygous). The most frequently identified variants across the literature are p.R277X, p.C1058R, p.C1977S, p.R1511X, p.A2215D and p.R2223H. - PMID:21372558

[C | emerging] In a cohort of 382 Chinese CH patients, TG variants included truncating and missense variants. c.274+2T>G was described as unique to the Asian population and the most common pathogenic variant (allele frequency 0.021). The estimated prevalence of CH due to TG defects in China was about 1/101,000. - PMID:26777470

[C | evidence supported] The TG clinical spectrum is broad, from euthyroid to mild or severe hypothyroidism, typically with goiter and low serum TG. TG defects are therefore not always overt congenital hypothyroidism. - PMID:21372558, PMID:29275168

[C | emerging] The south Indian AITD case-control study reported DRB1*12 and DRB1*11 as risk-associated and DRB1*10 and DRB1*03 as protective alleles, including in the HT subgroup. This is the index finding and has not been independently replicated in the provided sources. - PMID:29174716

[C | emerging] The Japanese cohort found DRB1 alleles for HT (*08:03, *09:01 higher; *13:02 lower) that differ from both the Indian and European findings. This indicates ancestry-specific heterogeneity and cautions against extrapolating HLA associations across Asian populations. - PMID:33386169

[C | emerging] Serum Tg is TSH-dependent and suppressed by exogenous thyroid hormone. Tg elevation tracked TSH in primary hypothyroidism (in patients who were anti-Tg negative). In a patient on levothyroxine, Tg level therefore reflects TSH stimulation and treatment status, and a low or normal Tg on treatment cannot by itself distinguish aetiologies. - PMID:3251664, PMID:6192141

[C | emerging] Levothyroxine may lower anti-thyroid antibody levels (mainly anti-TPO) in women with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, but the effect is inconsistent and varies between individuals. Antibodies measured on treatment may therefore be lower than at baseline, which could reduce their discriminating value. This is an inference from the review rather than a stated conclusion. - PMID:42278392

[C | emerging] RTHα mimics primary hypothyroidism clinically but occurs without TSH elevation. This means a hypothyroid-like picture with normal TSH, rather than the diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism itself, is the setting in which RTHα is raised as a differential. - PMID:28527577, PMID:42843455

[D | hypothesis] In one early-onset familial Hashimoto's thyroiditis pedigree, affected members had high polygenic risk scores, and rare structural variants were enriched in hypothyroidism GWAS loci. This is consistent with a multi-hit polygenic model, but the data are exploratory and come from a single family. - PMID:42938419

[D | hypothesis] TSHR encodes the thyrotropin receptor, which signals through Gs to adenylate cyclase and cAMP/PKA. This drives thyroid hormone biosynthesis and secretion, so reduced receptor function plausibly causes TSH resistance and hypothyroidism. - DB:4417f5a6d496f0c0

[D | emerging] In adults with mild or subclinical hypothyroidism without thyroid autoantibodies, a TSHR LOF variant is an uncommon but reported cause. Case reports include a 59-year-old woman. The authors suggest considering TSHR when autoantibodies are absent and the thyroid gland is normal. - PMID:16320156, PMID:28123504

[D | emerging] In consanguineous families with TSHR-related congenital hypothyroidism, expression varied within and between families. The authors suggest co-existing variants in other thyroid genes (for example SLC26A7) may modify severity, pointing to possible oligogenic inheritance. - PMID:40391015

[D | hypothesis] The common TSHR intronic SNP rs2268458 was reported as possibly associated with non-autoimmune hypothyroidism in a small Indian study. After age and sex adjustment the genotype association was not statistically significant. - PMID:42605379

[D | hypothesis] In mice and cultured cardiomyocytes, TSH signalling through TSHR was linked to impaired myocardial energy metabolism and worse heart-failure remodelling. This is preclinical and is not evidence for any change in patient care. - PMID:42909573

[D | hypothesis] In mice immunised with a TSHR hinge-region peptide, neutral TSHR antibodies were induced. These were accompanied by follicular destruction with apoptosis, M1 macrophage infiltration, thyroglobulin release, induction of thyroglobulin antibodies, and hypothyroidism with raised TSH. This shows a hypothesised antibody/macrophage route to thyroid damage. - PMID:39435685

[D | emerging] Homozygous SLC26A4 missense variants were reported in two patients with apparent thyroid dysgenesis (hypoplastic thyroid). One of the two also had severe hearing problems. This extends the phenotypic spectrum beyond dyshormonogenesis. - PMID:24248179

[D | hypothesis] In a small Indian study of 127 non-autoimmune, non-congenital adult hypothyroid patients without Pendred features, heterozygous SLC26A4 variants were found in about 20% and were proposed to be linked to the hypothyroidism. Controls showed fewer variant types. This is association only, with no demonstrated causation. - PMID:28718179

[D | hypothesis] SLC26A4 variants have been linked to autoimmune thyroid disease. Heterozygous variants were seen in Graves' disease patients, and a case report describes a child with two pathogenic variants, hearing loss and positive TPO antibody. The authors suggest screening thyroid autoantibodies in patients with pathogenic SLC26A4 variants. This is hypothesis-generating only. - PMID:21045265, PMID:39359669

[D | emerging] The hypo-functional or monoallelic SLC26A4 variants seen in single carriers often do not establish pathogenicity. Heterozygous variants can be coincidental polymorphisms, though a single structural variant has been reported with full Pendred phenotype in one case. Copy-number analysis and segregation studies can matter when only one allele appears affected. - PMID:19204907, PMID:40779065

[D | hypothesis] Hearing loss is considered an inevitable symptom of Pendred syndrome, so goiter alone is not a compelling reason to consider the syndrome. Thyroid disease in an SLC26A4 variant carrier with goiter may instead be Hashimoto's thyroiditis, so antibody testing is advised. - PMID:39359669

[D | hypothesis] In a paediatric dyshormonogenesis cohort, 3.13% of patients carried candidate TSHR variants. Functional cAMP-response reporter assays showed the variants to be totally, partially or mildly deleterious, with genotype-phenotype correlation in the patients studied. - PMID:39337518

[D | hypothesis] Curated protein annotation: TSHR couples to Gs proteins and activates adenylate cyclase and cAMP/PKA signalling, which regulates downstream targets in hormone biosynthesis. This is the pathway read out by the cAMP reporter assays used to test TSHR variants. - DB:4417f5a6d496f0c0
[D | hypothesis] TG is the protein substrate on which thyroid hormones T4 and T3 are made, so TG defects can plausibly reduce hormone output. - DB:03a9c1630c194d9f

[D | emerging] Genotype-phenotype relations are not clean: single-allele TG variants have been reported in families with a typical phenotype, and TG mutations have also been linked to euthyroid simple goiter. - PMID:20093166, PMID:23164529, PMID:29275168

[D | hypothesis] Population-database modelling puts the global TG carrier frequency at about 0.46% and the predicted genetic prevalence of autosomal recessive congenital hypothyroidism (12 genes combined) at about 10 per 100,000 births. South Asians are predicted lower than East Asians, and TG-specific South Asian frequencies are not given in the excerpts. - PMID:34200080

[D | emerging] Next-generation sequencing of TG and other dyshormonogenesis genes has been proposed for primary congenital hypothyroidism, and early genetic diagnosis is said to aid counselling and prevention of recurrence. - PMID:23949896, PMID:42378173

[D | hypothesis] A case report describes a homozygous TG deletion with congenital hypothyroidism, goiter and angioinvasive follicular thyroid carcinoma, and proposes a possible predisposition via chronic TSH stimulation. This is a single case. - PMID:42611393

[D | hypothesis] In male mice, induced hypothyroidism increased TG degradation and altered thyroid architecture. This shows that hypothyroidism changes TG handling, which is the reverse direction to TG variants causing hypothyroidism. - PMID:42942112

[D | emerging] Levothyroxine is the only therapy reported for RTHα. Earlier initiation is associated with better neurodevelopmental and growth outcomes, and established skeletal abnormalities are poorly reversible. Responses vary between reports: improvement in some, and no significant benefit with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis at supraphysiological doses in one case. - PMID:24969835, PMID:40734302, PMID:42843455

[D | hypothesis] A THRA-KO mouse hypothyroidism model showed loss of response to thyroxine, and THRA was shown to transactivate GPX4 for myocardial protection. UniProt describes THRA as a high-affinity thyroid hormone receptor acting as transcriptional repressor or activator. These data are mechanistic only. - DB:485e273c90e81dae, PMID:41313662

[D | hypothesis] PTPN22 and IL2RA data are sparse, mostly pooled with Graves' disease, and not HT-specific. In Japanese patients no individual PTPN22 SNP was associated with AITD, although one PTPN22 haplotype was. The IL2RA rs3118470 GG signal was associated with Graves' disease, not HT. The rs2476601 (R620W) variant is reported as nonpolymorphic in Asians. - PMID:20615141

[D | emerging] Carriers of heterozygous TSHR variants show variable expressivity. Some alleles consistently produce SCH, while partially functional alleles produce different phenotypes across family members and generations. A two-brother report shows different severity and levothyroxine need despite the same variant. - PMID:16060907, PMID:23332130

[D | hypothesis] Adult-onset data are limited to isolated case reports. One report describes a loss-of-function TSHR mutation as the potential cause of SH in a 59-year-old woman. The authors describe this as rare. - PMID:28123504

[D | hypothesis] A review states that Th17/Treg dysfunction driven by metabolic changes is best documented in HT. Mechanisms in Graves' disease and Graves' orbitopathy are less complete. The metabolic-targeting agents tabulated (e.g. mTOR inhibition, AMPK activation) are supported mainly by animal and cell models, so this is hypothesis-level evidence. - PMID:42057030

[D | hypothesis] Targeting IL-17 in autoimmune thyroiditis is still experimental. Clinical evidence is very limited, results from the small studies are inconsistent, and there are safety concerns (candida infection risk, rebound on withdrawal). Whether IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors attenuate thyroid inflammation has not been confirmed in clinical studies. - PMID:41243116, PMID:42577425

[D | hypothesis] Case reports describe double heterozygosity (e.g., TSHR plus DUOX2) in patients with hypothyroidism, including onset after a normal newborn screen. They suggest digenic combinations may influence severity. Heterozygous variants may therefore be relevant beyond classic recessive models. - PMID:25928756

[D | hypothesis] Another PBMC study reports the opposite pattern: Th1 markers (T-bet, IFN-γ mRNA) decreased and Th17 markers (RORγt, IL-17) increased in HT, suggesting Th17 rather than Th1 predominance. This conflicts with the classical Th1-dominant model and is not tissue-based. - PMID:20696023

[D | emerging] TPOAb titre correlates with the degree of thyroid lymphocytic infiltration, and TPOAb is useful as a marker of underlying autoimmunity. However, a review states that its biological importance remains to be clarified. The data support TPOAb as a marker, not as a proven pathogenic effector. - PMID:10483258

[D | hypothesis] A case report describes a novel TSHR variant, p.C598R, in a father and daughter with subclinical hypothyroidism. It is called loss-of-function on in-silico analysis only. The abstract gives no ACMG classification, and the evidence is computational. - PMID:37622708

[D | emerging] A small case-control study (18 HT, 15 Graves' disease, 15 controls) found lower CD4/CD25 and CD25/FOXP3 percentages and lower absolute CD4/CD25/FOXP3 numbers in AITD overall than in controls. The absolute number was lower in Graves' disease than in HT. - PMID:41307767

[D | hypothesis] Mechanistic review material describes Treg dysfunction in HT, for example via T-cell miR-142-3p acting on Tregs through RAC1/ERK1/2. This is a mechanistic summary from a narrative review, and the sources provide no direct human functional data (such as suppression assays) to resolve whether Treg function is reduced. - PMID:42688475

[D | emerging] In one small Indian case-control study of adults with non-autoimmune, non-congenital hypothyroidism, heterozygous SLC26A4 variants were found in about 20% of patients. Some known variants (g.23034G>T and p.I455F) were also present in controls, and the authors propose that SLC26A4 variation may contribute to non-autoimmune adult hypothyroidism. This is an association from a single study. Control numbers and statistics are not given in the abstract, and replication is lacking. - PMID:28718179

[D | hypothesis] For autoimmune thyroid disease, small genetic studies suggest a possible link between SLC26A4 variation and Graves' disease or Hashimoto thyroiditis. These are non-South-Asian or unspecified populations, and most lack a replicated outcome link. Variant burden differed between Graves' and Hashimoto cohorts. A p.I300L variant was seen only in Graves' patients (n=3), and an intronic repeat haplotype was associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis (OR about 2). These are candidate-gene associations with unclear causality. - PMID:21045265, PMID:23280318, PMID:23452581

[D | emerging] Biallelic SLC26A4 variants in South Asians are well documented as a cause of deafness (DFNB4/Pendred syndrome). Where thyroid status was reported in biallelic Pendred cases (East Asian), thyroid hormone levels were largely normal, with goitre, thyroglobulin elevation or antibodies in some patients. The provided sources contain no adult South Asian data linking biallelic variants to hypothyroidism. - PMID:17697873, PMID:19287372

[D | hypothesis] Heterozygous SLC26A4 variants occur in about 4% of Chinese congenital hypothyroidism cohorts. Their pathogenic contribution is unexplained. Some variants impair membrane localisation or ion transport in cell models, and PS is rare as a cause of congenital hypothyroidism. - PMID:26886089, PMID:34545167

[D | hypothesis] Iodine record may modify the thyroid phenotype in SLC26A4-related disease. Regions with high iodine record are reported to have less PS-related goitre. This is a discussion-level observation from a case report and is not tested in adult hypothyroidism. - PMID:39359669

[D | hypothesis] Functional in vitro studies of a novel SLC5A5 missense variant (p.L562M) in a compound heterozygous patient showed reduced iodide accumulation. The reduction was attributed to defective plasma-membrane expression, with the mutant NIS retained in the endoplasmic reticulum. - PMID:39749016

[D | hypothesis] Several other novel SLC5A5 missense variants (D331N and S547R; Q263L and G350D; V59E) showed severely reduced or negligible iodide transport in vitro. For D331N and S547R, the reduction was linked to impaired NIS targeting to the plasma membrane. - PMID:10907989, PMID:31115276, PMID:39895319

[D | hypothesis] Non-missense SLC5A5 defects are also experimentally supported: an intronic variant causing exon 8 skipping, a synonymous variant causing exon skipping (minigene assay), and a 5'UTR variant reducing NIS translation efficiency. - PMID:21565787, PMID:34726525, PMID:35600585

[D | hypothesis] The pathogenicity of SLC26A4 missense variants is difficult to predict from conservation and population frequency alone. Functional studies, and some hypo-functional alleles, have been found to be coincidental findings in nonsyndromic EVA. In silico predictions can also disagree for the same variant, so a VUS should not be treated as pathogenic or benign on computational scores alone. - PMID:19017801, PMID:19204907, PMID:42387562

[D | hypothesis] The sources raise the possibility of a link between SLC26A4 and autoimmune thyroid disease. One case report advises thyroid antibody testing in patients with pathogenic SLC26A4 variants and suggests even nonpathogenic variants might influence AITD risk. This is hypothesis-level, and the patient's autoimmune status is unrecorded. - PMID:39359669

[D | hypothesis] A genomic study of familial thyroid nodular disease found a heterozygous SLC26A4 variant in a single affected individual, with loss of heterozygosity in tissue. The authors considered this a likely somatic second-hit mechanism that did not explain familial aggregation. This is weak evidence that a germline heterozygous SLC26A4 variant could be relevant to nodular thyroid disease. - PMID:42723469

[D | emerging] Genetic counseling is suggested for SLC26A4 variants because of autosomal recessive inheritance. The excerpt frames this for patients with hearing loss. Its relevance to a VUS carrier without hearing loss is unclear, although consanguinity in the paternal grandparents may be relevant to recessive risk. - PMID:39359669

[D | emerging] A homozygous DUOX2 missense variant was reported in an adult woman who was initially euthyroid, developed subclinical hypothyroidism in her forties and had a goiter since about age 20. This shows that biallelic DUOX2 variants can present in adulthood, but it is a single case. - PMID:18426362

[D | emerging] Several reports describe genetic hypothyroidism with delayed onset after normal newborn screening. These include IYD variants in adolescence and combined heterozygous TSHR and DUOX2 variants in early childhood. Normal neonatal screening therefore does not exclude a genetic cause. - PMID:25928756, PMID:42147080

[D | emerging] Heterozygous DUOX2 or TSHR variants show variable expressivity: some carriers have no obvious abnormality, others have transient or persistent mild hyperthyrotropinemia, and some develop later hypothyroidism. Modifiers such as a second variant or iodine record may influence this, so a single mild variant is not predictive of an adult-onset presentation. - PMID:16134168, PMID:25928756, PMID:32803677

[D | hypothesis] Reviews state that genetic testing in congenital hypothyroidism mainly helps long-term management (prognosis, monitoring intensity, timing of treatment-withdrawal trials) and rarely changes early levothyroxine decisions. Direct evidence that testing changes management in adults with first adult-onset hypothyroidism is not provided. - PMID:42170892

[D | hypothesis] In Slc26a4-null mice, iodine restriction did not reproduce a goiter or thyroid phenotype. This challenges the idea that dietary iodine alone drives the phenotype, and points to individual or other factors. - PMID:20834201, PMID:21689387

[D | emerging] One pediatric case report describes a girl with two pathogenic SLC26A4 variants, normal thyroid function tests and a positive TPO antibody. The authors suggest Pendred syndrome and Hashimoto's thyroiditis can coexist and that antibody status matters for follow-up. The report does not show that SLC26A4 variants cause autoimmune hypothyroidism. - PMID:39359669

[D | hypothesis] SLC26A4 expression differs by thyroid pathology: higher in Graves' disease and lower in Hashimoto thyroiditis, carcinoma and goiter tissue. The authors link this to autoimmune thyroid disease and thyroid function. This is tissue-level association and does not show that variants alter hypothyroidism risk. - PMID:21035230

[D | hypothesis] A Pendred syndrome case showed progressive goiter with normal TSH and normal iodine organification, suggesting some variants may affect the thyroid through mechanisms other than an iodine handling defect. This underlines the phenotypic heterogeneity. - PMID:20583162

[D | emerging] In Indian patients with TDH, exome sequencing found nine biallelic TPO variants in nine unrelated families, eight of them novel. Pathogenicity of the missense variants was supported by in vitro loss of enzyme activity and by computational structural analysis, not by a formal classification scheme. - PMID:38986456

[D | emerging] Three South Asian adolescents from unrelated consanguineous families were homozygous for the IYD c.301C>T (p.Arg101Trp) variant. They had goiter, primary hypothyroidism and negative thyroid autoantibodies, and normal neonatal screening. The authors state that consanguinity should raise suspicion of autosomal recessive causes of hypothyroidism, including dyshormonogenesis. - PMID:42147080
[D | emerging] Normal neonatal screening does not exclude a genetic dyshormonogenesis cause, because clinical presentation can be delayed. - PMID:42147080

[D | emerging] In consanguineous families, pathogenicity of TPO variants has been established by segregation with disease. This relied on homozygous disease haplotypes in affected children, heterozygous parents and absence from ethnically matched control chromosomes. - PMID:25241611, PMID:26777044

[D | hypothesis] Variant spectrum and frequency differ by ancestry. A Chinese TG cohort found one variant unique to the Asian population and many variants of unknown significance (VUS). In the gnomAD database, TPO variant types differ across populations, including South Asian, and many predicted-damaging variants are novel. - PMID:26777470, PMID:35995307

[D | hypothesis] Computational prediction identified 183 novel TPO variants in gnomAD that were not reported in the literature and are predicted to be deleterious. The estimated heterozygous carrier prevalence was 1:77. These are in silico predictions only. - PMID:35995307

[D | emerging] Genotype may be partly predictable from phenotype. In Sudanese families, low or undetectable thyroglobulin was associated with TG mutations and markedly higher thyroglobulin with TPO mutations. This is a hypothesis-generating observation from a small, geographically distinct cohort. - PMID:31867598

[D | hypothesis] TG mutations have also been reported in euthyroid simple goiter. Some patients with TG mutations may compensate and maintain thyroid hormone production when iodine supply is sufficient. This suggests that variable, mild or late-presenting phenotypes are biologically plausible, but the sources give no direct adult-onset evidence. - PMID:19509106, PMID:20093166

[D | hypothesis] Biallelic TG variants have been described in siblings with goitrous hypothyroidism recognised in adulthood (aged 25 and 31 at presentation). One sibling developed follicular-variant papillary thyroid carcinoma, and the authors suggested prolonged TSH stimulation may promote malignant transformation. This is a single case report on biallelic variants and does not show that heterozygous variants cause adult-onset disease. - PMID:20089614

[D | emerging] The Indian and Kashmiri PTPN22 studies in the sources concern rs2476601 and non-HT outcomes. The 1858T allele is rare in Asian Indians, and no association was found with Graves' disease in Kashmiris. – addresses HT or non-rs2476601 variants in thyroid disease. - PMID:16893384, PMID:30148088

[D | hypothesis] An Indian study of PTPN22 variants beyond rs2476601 (rs1217406, rs3789609) found a haplotype associated with lower rheumatic heart disease risk. This is not thyroid disease. - PMID:25273327
[D | hypothesis] A rare PTPN22 missense variant (p.Asn26Ser) segregated with HT in one Chinese family. It is a case-level observation with no functional proof and no South Asian data. - PMID:30384852

[D | emerging] p.R277X is a recurrent TG variant and a proposed mutational hot spot. Unrelated affected individuals did not share a common allele, so recurrence did not reflect a single founder. In one cohort, 33 of 96 TG alleles carried p.R277*. A p.R277X/p.R1511X combination recurred in Argentinian and Brazilian families on different haplotypes, so no founder effect was shown between those populations. - PMID:15769978, PMID:17911408, PMID:29275168

[D | emerging] Consanguineous families have yielded novel homozygous or segregating TG nonsense variants (p.Q630X and p.W637X in two consanguineous families; R768X in two sisters of consanguineous parents). This is consistent with autosomal recessive disease, in which homozygosity is expected in consanguineous pedigrees. The authors suggest NGS-based testing in primary CH cases. - PMID:23455760, PMID:23949896

[D | emerging] A second, partially independent Indian cohort (juvenile goitrous autoimmune hypothyroidism, Hyderabad) found increased DRB1*04 frequency. This is directionally different from the south Indian AITD study, where DRB1*04 was increased only in combination with the CTLA4 GG genotype. It is not a clean allele-level replication. - PMID:17588142

[D | emerging] The DQB1 and amino-acid study uses what appears to be the same south Indian cohort as the DRB1/CTLA4 study (HT=180, GD=55, 235 controls). It should not be counted as independent replication. - PMID:29307887

[D | emerging] Serum Tg in congenital hypothyroidism depends on the underlying defect: it was markedly increased in dyshormonogenic goiter, while patients with defective Tg synthesis or release had low basal Tg that did not rise after bovine TSH stimulation. A Tg value alone therefore does not define 'TG dyshormonogenesis' as a single pattern. - PMID:4036506, PMID:6715793

[D | emerging] Strongly positive anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies were used to confirm autoimmune thyroiditis in a case report, which supports antibody positivity as an indicator of an autoimmune cause. Antibody status is unrecorded for this patient. Whether negative antibodies point toward a non-autoimmune cause (such as a Tg defect) is not established in these sources. - PMID:42713188

[D | hypothesis] Very high serum Tg may interfere with measurement of anti-Tg antibodies in highly sensitive assays. A very high Tg could therefore mask or distort a TgAb result, which matters when both are measured together. - PMID:10670755

[D | emerging] RTHα is described as rare and probably underdiagnosed because thyroid function tests can be near-normal. No source quantifies how often it is found among adults with presumed primary hypothyroidism or with symptoms persisting on levothyroxine. - PMID:37469961, PMID:42843455

[D | hypothesis] Several sources suggest THRA analysis in patients with specific clinical or biochemical clues, such as low reverse T3, low FT4:FT3 ratio, anaemia or mild hypothyroid features not confirmed biochemically. This is an expert suggestion drawn from case series, not a guideline-endorsed testing threshold. - PMID:25670821, PMID:32349464, PMID:37469961

[E | hypothesis] IYD (DEHAL1) is described only as the enzyme that rescues and recycles iodide, and as one of the genes linked to thyroid dyshormonogenesis, with autosomal recessive and possibly dominant inheritance. The provided sources contain no experimental or functional data on IYD defects. - PMID:28648508

items: [A | established] Clinical practice guidelines consistently identify LT4 monotherapy as the standard of care for hypothyroidism. They do not support routine LT4+LT3 combination therapy; at most two European guidelines allowed it in certain circumstances as an experimental treatment. - PMID:26654514

[A | established] Meta-analyses of randomized trials show no difference between LT4 monotherapy and LT4/LT3 combination therapy in clinical status, quality of life, psychological distress, depressive symptoms or fatigue (low-to-moderate certainty). An earlier RCT likewise found no benefit of combination therapy for weight, lipids, symptoms or cognition. - PMID:14665656, PMID:29381251, PMID:34340589

[A | guideline supported] The guideline recommends OSA screening for high-risk individuals with typical symptoms, signs or relevant comorbidities. Hypothyroidism is listed as a relevant comorbidity, and anxiety appears in the same list. Routine screening is not recommended for people without high-risk features. - PMID:41820035

[A | guideline supported] STOP-Bang is the guideline-recommended screening questionnaire. However, questionnaires alone, without objective sleep monitoring, are not recommended for diagnosis. The Epworth Sleepiness Scale assesses sleepiness severity but should not be used to diagnose OSA. - PMID:41820035

[A | guideline supported] PSG is the diagnostic gold standard. HSAT is suited to suspected moderate-to-severe uncomplicated OSA but should not be used to rule out OSA or to diagnose mild OSA. - PMID:41820035

[A | guideline supported] If OSA is confirmed, PAP is first-line for moderate-to-severe disease (AHI ≥15), and lifestyle measures apply to all patients. The guideline advises cautious use or avoidance of sedative-hypnotics and other medications that may induce or exacerbate OSA. Follow-up should include monitoring for cardiometabolic, cognitive and safety risks. - PMID:41820035

[A | established] Levothyroxine monotherapy is the guideline-endorsed mainstay of hypothyroidism treatment. LT4+LT3 combination is not preferred until clear advantages are shown. - PMID:25617173, PMID:40622204

[A | evidence supported] In RCTs of subclinical hypothyroidism, LT4 did not improve survival, cardiovascular morbidity, quality of life or symptoms, though some lipid and cardiac function parameters improved. - PMID:17636722

[B | evidence supported] In blinded trials, patients more often prefer combination therapy (LT4+LT3 or desiccated thyroid extract) than LT4 alone. Preference is not matched by differences in measured quality-of-life outcomes, and in one trial it correlated with weight loss. - PMID:29381251, PMID:39290156

[B | guideline supported] Food delays and lowers levothyroxine tablet absorption, and keeping a time interval between the dose and food or interfering supplements is the recommended way to avoid this. She takes a tablet formulation (Euthyrox), so this applies to her. - PMID:25694412, PMID:33801406, PMID:39215906

[B | evidence supported] Morning and bedtime dosing are reported as equally effective in a systematic review, but a separate review describes inconsistent findings for bedtime versus pre-breakfast dosing. Bedtime dosing is presented as an option, mainly for people wanting to avoid food at the time of the dose. - PMID:25694412, PMID:33801406

[B | evidence supported] Other common interferers, which she is not recorded as taking but which a clinician may want to ask about, include calcium and iron supplements, magnesium, cow's milk, coffee and tea. Separating them from the levothyroxine dose is the usual remedy. - PMID:29589994, PMID:36171905, PMID:37384019, PMID:41221788

[B | evidence supported] Liquid and softgel levothyroxine formulations are reported to be less affected by food and some interfering substances than tablets. Switching formulation is one option described when tablet absorption is problematic. - PMID:33801406, PMID:39215906

[B | evidence supported] A 2018 systematic review/meta-analysis of three RCTs in women with SCH diagnosed in pregnancy found no significant benefit of levothyroxine on obstetric, neonatal or childhood IQ/neurodevelopmental outcomes. It concluded that trial evidence did not support treatment. - PMID:30196268

[B | evidence supported] A 2024 updated meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found levothyroxine associated with lower pregnancy loss in pregnant women with SCH, but no significant effect on live birth. The authors suggest benefit may depend on early prescription. - PMID:38676741

[B | evidence supported] In an RCT of hypothyroid patients already on levothyroxine and vitamin D, an 8-week multi-micronutrient supplement (selenium, zinc, magnesium, vitamins A, C, E) did not change TSH, fT4 or TPO-Ab versus placebo. It showed small effects on fasting glucose/insulin resistance and physical quality of life. The authors state that routine supplements other than vitamin D are not supported in hypothyroidism treatment. - PMID:39968472

[B | evidence supported] In a large RCT of older Australians, vitamin D3 supplementation did not significantly reduce incident hypothyroidism (defined by levothyroxine prescription). A possible effect in females was suggested but was not statistically significant. - PMID:37698908
[B | evidence supported] STOP-Bang at a cut-off of ≥3 has high sensitivity but low specificity in pooled analyses, and the certainty of the evidence is low. - PMID:26658438, PMID:34406554

[B | evidence supported] In a lower-prevalence general population, STOP-Bang ≥3 kept good sensitivity, but PPV was very low. Most positive screens in such settings are false positives. - PMID:26658438

[B | evidence supported] In adults with cardiovascular risk factors and in mixed high-risk clinic patients, STOP-Bang had high sensitivity. These validation cohorts were older, majority-male and of higher BMI. - PMID:30518441, PMID:33664122

[B | emerging] In an open-label RCT of 88 adults with well-controlled hypothyroidism, taking LT4 with breakfast (with a 15% dose increase in the trial protocol) achieved TSH stability comparable to fasting record. It also showed a trend toward better self-reported well-being, and most participants preferred the nonfasting routine. - PMID:41431302

[B | evidence supported] In a meta-analysis of 25 RCTs (1,735 patients), LT4 versus placebo increased FT4 and decreased TSH. In SCH it also decreased systolic blood pressure and total cholesterol. These are biochemical and surrogate outcomes, not patient-important outcomes. - PMID:32238664

[B | evidence supported] In RCTs, evening and morning LT4 dosing produced similar TSH changes. When TSH is persistently off target on oral tablets, ingestion routines can be optimized and alternative formulations considered. - PMID:32740045, PMID:40220082

[B | evidence supported] Evening and morning LT4 dosing produced no significant difference in TSH change in a meta-analysis of RCTs. Weekly dosing gave slightly higher TSH but still within the reference range. - PMID:40220082

[B | established] Levothyroxine treatment of clinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy is standard practice. In pregnant women with subclinical hypothyroidism, LT4 was associated with lower preterm birth, miscarriage, postpartum haemorrhage and low birth weight. - PMID:20614463, PMID:35523752

[C | evidence supported] Roughly 5-10% of patients who reach normal TSH on LT4 report persistent symptoms. The sources recommend checking TSH control, adherence, LT4 administration (fasting, timing relative to other agents) and absorption, and investigating non-thyroid causes such as other autoimmune conditions, anaemia and mental-health disorders. - PMID:29381251, PMID:33112818

[C | evidence supported] The treatment target for LT4 monotherapy is a TSH within the reference range plus symptom relief. Aiming for a particular point within the range, or adjusting therapy for a low T3, does not appear to improve outcomes. - PMID:33112818, PMID:37419564

[C | evidence supported] If T3 is ever added, careful monitoring for iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis is advised. In one trial, add-on combination produced over-replacement with TSH below the normal range, and in a network meta-analysis liothyronine increased adverse events versus placebo (very low certainty). - PMID:33112818, PMID:41838451

[C | emerging] In a large retrospective cohort, LT3-containing regimens were associated with lower dementia and mortality risk than LT4 monotherapy. This is an observational association, and the authors state confirmation is needed. - PMID:40579157
[C | emerging] Adding aerobic plus resistance training to LT4 improved quality-of-life and mental-health scores compared with LT4 alone in a network meta-analysis, at low certainty. - PMID:41838451

[C | emerging] The effect of dietary fibre on levothyroxine absorption is not fully understood. One review lists fibre among the agents that interfere with absorption, while another says its effect is not yet established. - PMID:19942153, PMID:28153426

[C | evidence supported] When absorption-impairing factors are present (for example gastrointestinal disorders), monitoring of TSH and free T4 is advised. Reviews also say many interactions can be avoided by separating the dose from the interfering substance. - PMID:28153426
[C | evidence supported] The Melbourne public hospitals consensus, endorsed by the Endocrine Society of Australia, recommends the following for pregnancy:
trimester- and assay-specific TSH reference intervals where available;
otherwise a TSH treatment cut-off of 4 mU/L irrespective of antibody status;
an on-treatment TSH target of 0.1–2.5 mU/L;
generally stopping levothyroxine after delivery for SCH treated in pregnancy. - PMID:30561039

[C | emerging] A narrative review reports that benefits on miscarriage and preterm delivery were seen mainly with first-trimester treatment and TSH mostly ≥4 mU/L. It also lists possible harms of treatment and cautions that treating every pregnant woman with TSH >2.5 mU/L is premature. - PMID:32975922

[C | evidence supported] In women with already-treated hypothyroidism, thyroid hormone requirement rises during pregnancy. Sources describe a 20–40% increase in requirement, or about 50% more glandular production, and state that most women on levothyroxine before pregnancy need a dose increase. - PMID:20463094, PMID:25288580

[C | evidence supported] In the THERAPY RCT, an empirical levothyroxine increase at pregnancy confirmation, of either two or three extra tablets per week, prevented first-trimester TSH elevation above 5.0 mIU/L. However, it frequently suppressed TSH below 0.5 mIU/L, significantly more with the three-tablet increase.
