items: athyreotic women;
women with prepregnancy TSH <1.5 mIU/L;
women on prepregnancy doses ≥100 µg/d. - PMID:20463094

[C | emerging] A small RCT found ongoing TSH-guided levothyroxine adjustment as effective as an empirical two-pill/week increase for keeping TSH within trimester goals. The empirical approach caused more first-trimester TSH suppression below 0.1 mIU/L. - PMID:28911144

[C | evidence supported] Monitoring: THERAPY recommended TSH testing every 4 weeks through midgestation, which identified 92% of abnormal values. A Danish retrospective cohort found TSH frequently out of range in early pregnancy despite monitoring, and recommended increased monitoring of women with hypothyroidism planning pregnancy. - PMID:20463094, PMID:25441726
[C | evidence supported] Safety:
Levothyroxine is a narrow-therapeutic-index drug, and small dose variations can change thyroid status.
Suboptimal adherence is common.
The FDA label lists uncorrected adrenal insufficiency as a contraindication. - DB:96b16a3165b01a96, PMID:37897184

[C | emerging] Intestinal absorption of oral B12 is dose-dependent. A narrative framework paper proposes that supplement intakes of 20 µg/day or less are unlikely to have pharmacological effects, and that 200 µg/day or more behaves like a drug. This is relevant when judging what the patient's supplement dose is meant to do. - PMID:39939550

[C | emerging] In a small human radiotracer study, co-ingesting 1 g ascorbic acid did not impair absorption of hydroxocobalamin and slightly increased cyanocobalamin absorption. This suggests that taking B12 with another vitamin is not necessarily a problem. It is indirect evidence only, because the patient's listed products do not include vitamin C. - PMID:7112085

[C | emerging] B12 forms differ in chemical stability. Cyanocobalamin is the most stable and has been used most in supplements. Methylcobalamin, hydroxocobalamin and adenosylcobalamin are less stable. A review also covers B12 stability in the presence of oxidants, reductants and other water-soluble vitamins, which concerns product formulation and storage rather than in-body interaction. - PMID:36615431

[C | emerging] A pediatric review lists medicines and conditions that impair B12 handling, including long-term proton pump inhibitors and metformin, colchicine and neomycin. Levothyroxine, vitamin D3, ashwagandha, protein powder and fibre powder do not appear in this table. That is an absence in a children's review excerpt, not evidence of no interaction. - PMID:42591473

[C | evidence supported] B12 status is best assessed with a combination of tests. Serum B12 alone is not completely reliable. Functional markers (methylmalonic acid, homocysteine) improve diagnostic accuracy in borderline cases. Deficiency typically shows low serum B12 with raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, while raised homocysteine also occurs in folate deficiency. - PMID:28360040, PMID:42591473, PMID:42633317

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of 57 human studies found that observational associations between selenium, zinc and iron status and iodine status were not confirmed by randomized controlled trials. - PMID:29596650

[C | evidence supported] In iodine- and iron-deficient populations, RCTs showed that giving iron with iodine improved thyroid function and volume more than iodine alone. Most human RCTs of selenium supplementation failed to show an effect on thyroid metabolism. - PMID:20172476

[C | emerging] Iodine record shows a U-shaped relationship with thyroid dysfunction. In iodine-replete or high-exposure settings, excess iodine more commonly precipitates hypothyroidism through impaired autoregulation. - PMID:41718360

[C | emerging] Iodine deficiency can occur even in iodine-sufficient countries, notably in vegetarians and people following low-salt diets. Selenium, vitamin A or iron deficiency may worsen the effects of iodine deficiency. - PMID:19594417, PMID:41718360

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews support assessing nutritional status as a complement to levothyroxine in women with hypothyroidism. They also state that most nutrient–thyroid evidence is observational and that diet-based strategies are not an independent therapy for autoimmune thyroid disease. - PMID:40728470, PMID:40843807, PMID:41798186

[C | emerging] The food matrix affects vitamin D3 absorption. In postmenopausal women, D3 bioavailability was higher with milk or water than with apple juice, and adding whey protein isolate did not improve it. This is relevant to how a protein powder or a drink taken with vitamin D3 might affect absorption. - PMID:36563435

[C | emerging] A 2-year RCT gave vitamin B12 (500 µg) and folic acid with vitamin D3 (600 IU) versus placebo plus the same vitamin D3. The excerpt shows no adverse effect on physical performance, grip strength or falls. It does not examine a B12-D3 pharmacokinetic or safety interaction. The vitamin D3 was given to both arms. - PMID:26412463

[C | hypothesis] A narrative review reports that antiepileptic drugs can enhance the metabolism of thyroxine and vitamin D3. This is not applicable to the patient's current medicines, none of which is an antiepileptic. It matters only if an enzyme-inducing anticonvulsant were ever added. - PMID:1959513

[C | emerging] A cross-sectional study of 100 hypothyroid patients found a high OSA prevalence on PSG. OSA was more frequent in treatment-naive than in treated patients, and the authors recommend OSA screening in hypothyroidism. - PMID:36412342

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review proposes STOP-Bang risk bands: 0-2 low risk and 5-8 high risk for moderate-to-severe OSA. Mid-range scores of 3-4 need additional criteria such as BMI >35 kg/m2. - PMID:26378880

[C | evidence supported] The sources contain no evidence that STOP-Bang screening itself improves patient-important outcomes. OSA treatment improves symptoms and quality of life, but its effect on cardiovascular events is heterogeneous. The guideline also recommends screening where OSA could raise driving or occupational accident risk. - PMID:41820035, PMID:42200975

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews state that women with known hypothyroidism should receive preconception care so that they are euthyroid from the onset of pregnancy, with a TSH target below 2.5 mIU/L. Optimising treatment of overt hypothyroidism is described as reducing adverse fetal and maternal outcomes. - PMID:32616466, PMID:39943743

[C | evidence supported] Reviews cite current guidelines recommending that hypothyroid women on levothyroxine who plan pregnancy adjust treatment to a TSH between the lower reference limit and 2.5 mU/L. The rationale is that requirements rise in pregnancy, and a lower starting TSH reduces the risk of first-trimester TSH elevation. - PMID:29706030, PMID:36013589, PMID:37024331

[C | evidence supported] The reviews describe an anticipatory levothyroxine increase once pregnancy is suspected or confirmed, with differing magnitudes cited. Subsequent titration is guided by TSH against trimester-specific ranges. Any dose change is a physician decision. - PMID:32616466, PMID:36013589

[C | evidence supported] Early gestation is described as a critical window of fetal vulnerability to maternal thyroid dysfunction. This is the rationale for achieving euthyroidism before conception rather than after a pregnancy is detected. - PMID:29706030

[C | emerging] Observational data question whether the strict TSH <2.5 mU/L preconception target improves outcomes. In 78 hypothyroid women, most did not reach the target, yet preconception and early-gestation TSH >2.5 mU/L was not associated with adverse fetal or maternal outcomes. A larger retrospective cohort of euthyroid women found no difference between TSH 0.5-2.4 and 2.5-4.6 mU/L. - PMID:23512388, PMID:37024331

[C | emerging] Thyroid autoimmunity status changes management considerations, and the supplied evidence on it is limited. The patient's antibody status is not recorded. Empirical levothyroxine in euthyroid TPOAb-positive women is not universally accepted, because high-quality RCT evidence is lacking and offspring side-effects are possible. Overall, the preconception thyroid evidence base is described as not consistent enough for fully evidence-based recommendations. - PMID:36013589

[C | evidence supported] Preconception counselling reviews list adequate iodine record as part of preconception thyroid care in most regions. The need for this should be assessed by a clinician. - PMID:36013589

[C | evidence supported] A review reports that reduced LT4 absorption is established and clinically significant when LT4 is taken together with calcium salts (carbonate, citrate, acetate), iron sulfate, proton pump inhibitors and several other agents. It states these adsorption-based interactions can be avoided by separating LT4 administration from the interfering substance. - PMID:28153426

[C | evidence supported] The same review identifies soybeans and coffee as having the greatest impact on reducing LT4 absorption. It states that the effect of dietary fibre on LT4 absorption is not yet fully understood. - PMID:28153426

[C | emerging] In 37 previously well-controlled patients whose TSH rose after starting coffee and/or tea within 1 h of LT4, advice to avoid coffee and tea for at least 4 h before and after LT4 (same dose) was followed by reduced TSH and increased T3/T4 at 3 months in all three groups. - PMID:36171905

[C | evidence supported] The sources support TSH (with free T4) as the monitoring marker when absorption-affecting factors change. The review advises monitoring TSH and free T4 during treatment of absorption-impairing GI disorders to avoid iatrogenic hyperthyroidism. A case report rechecked TSH 6 weeks after removing the interfering supplement. - PMID:28153426, PMID:34280893

[C | evidence supported] GI disorders such as celiac disease, atrophic gastritis, lactose intolerance and H. pylori infection may impede LT4 absorption. These are alternative explanations to consider if control remains poor despite separating supplements. - PMID:28153426

[C | evidence supported] Multiple reviews report a consensus/guideline position that levothyroxine therapy is indicated for subclinical hypothyroidism when TSH is persistently above 10 mIU/L. - PMID:15799214, PMID:22191793, PMID:23627903, PMID:31963883

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of 21 trials reportedly found no clinically relevant benefit of thyroid hormone on symptoms or prognosis in adult SCH. An independent panel (BMJ Rapid Recommendation) issued a strong recommendation against treatment, explicitly excluding women who are pregnant or trying to conceive and patients with TSH >20 mIU/L. - PMID:32134225

[C | evidence supported] TSH ≥10 mIU/L has been associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Patients with cardiovascular risk factors, especially younger ones, may benefit from treatment. - PMID:21983317, PMID:31963883

[C | evidence supported] Several sources identify factors that favour treatment of milder SCH: positive TPO antibodies (higher progression risk), goitre, symptoms, infertility, and pregnancy or contemplated pregnancy. There is consensus to treat SCH of any magnitude in women contemplating pregnancy. - PMID:15799214, PMID:22191793

[C | evidence supported] Over-replacement with levothyroxine is common and associated with atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis. TSH-suppressive doses (in thyroid cancer) were associated with increased cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. - PMID:22191793, PMID:31963883

[C | evidence supported] Treatment is monitored with serum TSH; one review cites a target of 0.5–2.0 mIU/L. A persistently elevated TSH despite an apparently adequate dose should prompt checks for adherence, malabsorption and drug interactions. - PMID:22191793

[C | evidence supported] SCH should be confirmed by persistent TSH elevation with normal FT4 on at least two occasions. Overtreatment is associated with early initiation and absence of confirmatory testing. In one withdrawal study of patients with an uncertain initial diagnosis, 61% were euthyroid 6–8 weeks after stopping levothyroxine. - PMID:31963883, PMID:42249773, PMID:42985925

[C | evidence supported] Positive TPO antibodies indicate increased risk of other autoimmune diseases, including pernicious anaemia, celiac disease, type 1 diabetes and Addison's disease. - PMID:31963883

[C | evidence supported] Levothyroxine monotherapy, titrated to keep TSH within the euthyroid reference range, is described as guideline-based standard-of-care treatment for hypothyroidism. - PMID:32740045, PMID:34553643

[C | evidence supported] In SCH, the cited double-blind RCTs show no improvement in symptoms or cognition when TSH is below 10 mIU/L. One review states treatment is generally not necessary unless TSH exceeds 7.0-10 mIU/L, and that the diagnosis should be confirmed on repeat testing, since many elevated TSH values revert spontaneously. Possible cardiovascular-event reduction under age 65 is suggested, but the systematic review judges benefits in younger patients to be hypothesis-generating. - PMID:34766382, PMID:42732446

[C | evidence supported] In treated patients with persistent nonspecific symptoms, narrative reviews report that targeting a particular TSH level or adjusting for low T3 does not seem to improve outcomes. Clinicians are advised to consider other diagnoses when TSH is normal. - PMID:37419564

[C | emerging] Adding liothyronine (LT4+LT3) lowered TSH and raised FT3 versus LT4 alone in a meta-analysis. However, most RCTs have not shown clinical benefit. Combination therapy is described as an option for selected persistently symptomatic patients only with careful monitoring. - PMID:32238664, PMID:35662440
[C | evidence supported] Age-specific TSH reference limits are reported: a 97.5th-percentile upper limit of 3.6 mIU/L under age 40, versus 7.5 mIU/L over age 80. - PMID:34766382

[C | evidence supported] Overtreatment with LT4 is associated with cardiovascular, cognitive and skeletal complications (hazard ratios 1.37-2.02). Iatrogenic over-dosing is the most common cause of subclinical hyperthyroidism, so the indication and dose should be reviewed regularly. - PMID:42768899

[C | evidence supported] Reproductive context: the American Thyroid Association is reported to recommend treating both subclinical and overt hypothyroidism with LT4 in lactating women. LT4 requirements may rise postpartum in Hashimoto's thyroiditis. - PMID:30000062

[C | guideline supported] Many treated patients fail to reach symptom relief and TSH control. An estimated 20-50% do not achieve optimal response on standard dosing and need ongoing dose adjustment and monitoring. - PMID:40622204, PMID:42278392

[C | evidence supported] Overt hypothyroidism is described as a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor. In subclinical hypothyroidism, the cardiovascular benefit of LT4 remains uncertain. - PMID:41996368

[C | evidence supported] Over-replacement should be avoided. Minor over-replacement risks cardiac events, chronic over-replacement may cause osteoporosis, and low TSH (subclinical hyperthyroidism) is associated with increased atrial fibrillation risk. Thyroid hormone must not be used for weight loss. - DB:056af987bb039dc6, PMID:16026104, PMID:41996368
[C | evidence supported] Dietary fibre, soy, coffee, papaya, iron and calcium can reduce LT4 absorption. LT4 is typically taken fasting, 30-60 minutes before breakfast. - PMID:42278392
[C | guideline supported] The ETA guideline lists over-the-counter whey and soy protein supplements as possibly interfering with LT4 bioavailability. - PMID:40622204

[C | emerging] In a pilot double-blind RCT in adults with subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4.5-10 μIU/L), 8 weeks of ashwagandha root extract significantly improved serum TSH, T3 and T4 versus placebo. Outcomes were laboratory surrogates only. - PMID:28829155

[C | emerging] A systematic review of herbal RCTs in primary hypothyroidism included only 4 trials (186 participants). Its ashwagandha data (rising T3/T4, falling TSH) come from a single trial, and the authors call for more rigorous methodology. - PMID:37013429

[C | evidence supported] In an 8-week RCT in 80 healthy adults, ashwagandha root extract produced no significant change in thyroid hormonal profile, haematology or biochemistry, and no adverse events were reported. - PMID:33338583
[C | emerging] Short-term adverse events in the subclinical hypothyroidism pilot RCT were few, mild and temporary, and no more frequent than with placebo. - PMID:28829155

[C | emerging] A narrative review reports trials showing reductions in stress biomarkers and improvements in sleep and mood with standardized extracts. It flags heterogeneity of extracts, small samples and possible CYP-mediated metabolic variability. - PMID:41356880

[D | hypothesis] Levothyroxine label safety: it is contraindicated in uncorrected adrenal insufficiency. A boxed warning states thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss, because doses beyond daily requirements may cause serious or life-threatening toxicity. - DB:96b16a3165b01a96

[D | hypothesis] DIO2 (Thr92Ala) polymorphisms have been proposed as a way to identify LT4 non-responders who might benefit from LT3, but this remains a research question without conclusive clinical evidence. - PMID:29381251, PMID:33112818

[D | emerging] A soy protein supplement taken right after levothyroxine was reported to reduce its absorption and raise the dose needed. This is one case report, in a patient needing TSH suppression after thyroid cancer. Reviews list soy among the foods with the greatest impact on absorption. The composition of this patient's protein powder is unknown, so it is not known whether this applies to her. - PMID:11421567, PMID:28153426, PMID:33801406

[D | hypothesis] Ashwagandha has reported thyroid-modulating effects, with one clinical study of hypothyroid patients (summarised in a narrative review) reporting normalised T3, T4 and TSH versus placebo. No source tested ashwagandha together with levothyroxine. A possible additive or confounding effect on thyroid tests is therefore unexamined and hypothetical. Ashwagandha could also confound the interpretation of her TSH and fT4. - PMID:42183570

[D | hypothesis] Translational data suggest that excessive iodine record may disrupt gut microbial short-chain fatty acid metabolism and favour a pro-inflammatory phenotype linked to thyroid autoimmunity. - PMID:41798186

[D | hypothesis] In a small pilot of healthy men, vitamin D3 at 1000 IU/day did not alter digoxin pharmacokinetics, which suggests no P-glycoprotein-mediated interaction. Plasma calcium rose modestly but significantly. This does not test levothyroxine, B12, ashwagandha or powders. - PMID:21477267

[D | emerging] In hypothyroid patients needing disproportionately high LT4 doses who used fibre supplements, withdrawing the fibre at a constant LT4 dose was followed by lower TSH or lower dose requirement. In vitro, wheat bran adsorbed LT4 in a dose-dependent, nonspecific way. - PMID:8636317

[D | hypothesis] Single case reports link protein supplements to impaired LT4 effect. For soy protein, temporal separation from LT4 allowed target hormone levels at lower LT4 doses. For whey protein, TSH normalised at 6 weeks after the supplement was stopped on the same LT4 dose; separation was not tested. - PMID:11421567, PMID:34280893

[D | hypothesis] A retrospective cohort reported that patients with higher dairy record were more likely to report inadequate preparation of LT4 record. The authors concluded that dairy affects LT4 absorption and dosing. - PMID:41955596

[D | hypothesis] Label safety: levothyroxine is contraindicated in uncorrected adrenal insufficiency. A boxed warning states it should not be used for obesity or weight loss, and supraphysiological doses can be toxic. - DB:57413f992de8a040

[D | evidence supported] Levothyroxine is contraindicated in uncorrected adrenal insufficiency. A case report describes persistently elevated TSH despite adherence that led to diagnosis of autoimmune adrenal insufficiency in a patient with autoimmune thyroiditis. - DB:056af987bb039dc6, PMID:42684977

[D | hypothesis] Selenium in Hashimoto's thyroiditis lowered TPO antibodies in some trials, but the evidence on clinical efficacy is incomplete. [D | hypothesis] In a propylthiouracil-induced hypothyroid rat model, ashwagandha methanolic extract improved thyroid hormones and oxidative-stress markers. This is a mechanistic hypothesis only. - PMID:31203475

[E | hypothesis] No high-certainty synthesis of LT4 effects on patient-important outcomes (mortality, cardiovascular events, quality of life) in SCH is available in these sources. The updated Cochrane review is only a protocol, with no results. - PMID:42985925

items: [A | established] LT4 monotherapy is the guideline-endorsed standard of care for hypothyroidism. Guidelines worldwide do not support routine LT4+LT3 combination therapy. - PMID:26654514

[A | established] LT4 monotherapy is the guideline-endorsed standard of care for hypothyroidism. Guidelines worldwide do not support routine use of LT4+LT3 combination therapy. - PMID:25266247, PMID:26654514

[A | guideline supported] Guidelines worldwide regard LT4 monotherapy as standard of care and do not support routine LT4+LT3 combination therapy; a minority allow it only in selected circumstances as experimental. - PMID:26654514

[A | evidence supported] Meta-analyses of RCTs show no consistent efficacy advantage of LT4/LT3 combination over LT4 alone for symptoms, quality of life, depression or fatigue, though patients more often prefer the combination. - PMID:34340589, PMID:39273168

[B | evidence supported] Adding LT3 to LT4 offered no advantage for persistent hypothyroid symptoms in the RCTs reviewed. Combination therapy is not recommended routinely. - PMID:29381251, PMID:39273168

[B | guideline supported] The ETA guideline permits LT4+LT3 only as an experimental approach, under specific conditions and specialist supervision. Two guidelines (ETA 2012, BTA 2015) allow this; the other guidelines in the review do not. The patient's eligibility cannot be judged because TSH, adherence and autoimmune status are unknown. - PMID:24782999, PMID:26654514

[B | evidence supported] Efficacy: randomised trials do not show that LT4+LT3 relieves persistent hypothyroid symptoms better than LT4 alone. Some patients nonetheless prefer combination therapy, and this preference is not explained by objective measures. The early positive result was not confirmed in later studies. - PMID:15928247, PMID:27982198, PMID:39273168

[C | evidence supported] Treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism is supported when TSH exceeds 10 mIU/L. For milder elevations, treatment is individualised and a wait-and-see approach is often advised. - PMID:22191793, PMID:31963883
[C | evidence supported] A raised TSH should be confirmed by repeat testing before the diagnosis of subclinical hypothyroidism is made, because many elevations revert to normal. - PMID:34766382

[C | emerging] Some guidance allows an experimental LT3 add-on trial only in selected, compliant, biochemically euthyroid patients after other causes of symptoms are excluded. It should not be used during pregnancy, and it carries over-replacement risks. - PMID:31354624, PMID:34543420

[C | evidence supported] Persistent symptoms on LT4 with a normal TSH may have causes unrelated to thyroid function, which should be investigated. Over-replacement is a recognised safety risk. - PMID:22191793, PMID:29381251

[C | evidence supported] In primary hypothyroidism, LT4 treatment is monitored with serum TSH against a stated target. In patients with persistently elevated TSH despite an apparently adequate dose, compliance, malabsorption and drug interactions should be checked. - PMID:22191793

[C | evidence supported] Levothyroxine absorption can be impaired by interfering drugs, foods and concomitant diseases. The sources list specific interfering agents, and the excerpt shows no direct mention of fibre powder, protein powder, ashwagandha, vitamin D3 or B12. - PMID:36412275

[C | evidence supported] Safety: small trials and reviews report possible harms from adding LT3. These include more patients with T3 above the upper limit, a higher resting heart rate, and more adverse events in an older crossover trial. Effects on bone resorption and cardiac effects are flagged but not established. Long-term safety is described as unknown or in question. - PMID:15928247, PMID:27982198, PMID:29381251, PMID:32636887

[C | guideline supported] Monitoring: the ETA guideline advises close monitoring on combination therapy, aiming to normalise TSH and fT4 and also the fT4/fT3 ratio. Suppressed TSH from over-replacement is a recognised issue in LT4 therapy generally. - PMID:24782999, PMID:31695677

[C | guideline supported] Persistent symptoms with biochemically adequate LT4 treatment may have causes unrelated to thyroid function. Reviews advise investigating these before attributing symptoms to inadequate thyroid replacement. - PMID:24782999, PMID:29381251

[C | emerging] LT3 monotherapy has limited, low-certainty evidence from crossover trials in women with persistent symptoms on LT4 (better fatigue and cholesterol on LT3 in one open-label trial). The guideline authors judged this to be at high risk of bias. - PMID:40699541

[C | evidence supported] Sources disagree on guidance for a trial of LT3 in symptomatic patients, but several support an individualised, monitored trial only after optimising LT4 and excluding other causes. - PMID:33112818, PMID:39625345

[C | evidence supported] Before any LT3 is considered, persistent symptoms on LT4 should be investigated for non-thyroid causes and for LT4 dosing, adherence, timing/food or drug interaction and malabsorption problems. - PMID:33112818

[C | evidence supported] Safety: RCTs of LT4+LT3 did not show clear or consistent safety problems, but adverse events are only narratively compared, and over-treatment is a recognised concern. A network meta-analysis reported more adverse events with LT3 versus placebo, at very low certainty. - PMID:34340589, PMID:39625345, PMID:41838451

[C | emerging] One large retrospective cohort reported lower dementia and mortality with T3-containing regimens than LT4 alone. This is an association from observational data and the authors state it needs confirmation. - PMID:40579157

[C | evidence supported] Normal free thyroid hormone and TSH concentrations establish euthyroidism when total T4 is abnormal because of transport-protein variation. The choice of free-hormone assay matters, because analog methods can give misleading results. - PMID:1422238

[C | evidence supported] When total T4 and TSH are discordant, thyroid hormone-binding protein abnormalities should be excluded before interpreting thyroid function tests. TBG deficiency and excess occur at measurable frequencies and can be inherited in an X-linked pattern. - PMID:15489553

[C | evidence supported] Initial work-up of an abnormal T4 or TSH in an outpatient includes a medication review and neck examination. Additional T4 or TSH testing follows, and protein-binding measures (T4-binding capacity or electrophoresis) can confirm a suspected congenital or acquired T4-binding abnormality. Euthyroid hypothyroxinemia or hyperthyroxinemia should be recognised so that inappropriate treatment is avoided. - PMID:7776719

[C | evidence supported] In levothyroxine-treated primary hypothyroidism, treatment is monitored by TSH. If TSH stays elevated despite an apparently adequate dose, adherence, malabsorption and drug interactions should be checked. Over-replacement is common and carries risks. - PMID:22191793

[D | hypothesis] DIO2 deiodinase polymorphisms are proposed as a mechanism and possible predictor of response to combination therapy. This is unproven and not clinically actionable. There is no genotype data for this patient. - PMID:29381251, PMID:39455510

[D | hypothesis] Analogue-based total T4 immunoassays can report values that depend on which binding protein carries the T4. Total T4 is underrepresented when T4 is TBG-bound and overrepresented when T4 is albumin- or transthyretin-bound, with substantial disparities between assays. - PMID:15687815

[D | hypothesis] Assay interference (such as heterophile antibodies) and TBG deficiency can produce thyroid test results that conflict with the clinical picture. Testing in two laboratories, with and without dilution, and measuring TBG helped resolve this in reported cases. - PMID:27483566

[D | hypothesis] Familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia and other inherited increased binding of T4 to serum proteins produce a high total T4 and a high free T4 index with a normal TSH and a normal true free T4. Affected patients are euthyroid and need no treatment, and the free T4 index can misrepresent the true free T4. - PMID:7937417, PMID:85873

items: [B | emerging] In a double-blind crossover RCT (n=75), LT4, LT4+LT3 and desiccated thyroid extract gave similar outcomes for the group as a whole. In the exploratory subgroup of the most symptomatic third on LT4, there was a strong preference for T3-containing treatment, with improved symptom, mood and visual memory scores. - PMID:34185829

[B | evidence supported] A GRADE-based meta-analysis of randomized trials found that adding liothyronine had minimal or no effect on fatigue and quality of life in hypothyroidism, which are the outcomes most relevant to this patient's symptoms. - PMID:30550536, PMID:33276704

[B | evidence supported] In a meta-analysis of RCTs, more patients preferred combination therapy (L-T4 + L-T3 or desiccated thyroid) than L-T4 alone. This is a preference outcome, not a measured improvement in symptoms. - PMID:39290156

[B | evidence supported] A systematic review of 20 studies found that LT4/LT3 combination therapy gave no advantage over LT4 monotherapy for persistent symptoms. This held regardless of cause, scale used, sex, LT4:LT3 proportions or timing. Participants were predominantly women, but age-specific results were not reported in the excerpt. - PMID:39273168

[B | guideline supported] Assay interference is a recognised alternative explanation when thyroid function tests are discordant with the clinical picture or with each other, and raised TSH can reflect analytical interference, TSH resistance, consumptive hypothyroidism or levothyroxine refractoriness. - PMID:37067253, PMID:42466561

[C | evidence supported] Central hypothyroidism may coexist with other pituitary hormone deficits. GH or ACTH deficiency can carry a risk of life-threatening hypoglycaemia. This is a safety consideration in the work-up of central forms, not a safety finding about TRHR modulators. - PMID:26416826

[C | evidence supported] A key unmet need is persistent symptoms in a minority of levothyroxine-treated patients despite normalised TSH. Standard LT4 may not restore thyroid hormone signalling in all tissues, and it also has dosing, drug-interaction and adherence difficulties. - PMID:36277721, PMID:37738506

[C | emerging] The most advanced alternative approach is combination LT4+LT3 therapy, with slow-release LT3 formulations under testing. The review reports trials showing safety and patient preference, but the sources do not establish it as standard of care. They also note unresolved questions about formulation regulation and safety and efficacy data. - PMID:36277721, PMID:37738506, PMID:43005807

[C | emerging] Absorption and bioavailability of oral LT4 are affected by interfering drugs, foods and diseases. Novel liquid and soft-gel formulations are designed to circumvent malabsorption, but study designs are flawed and the debate is ongoing. - PMID:36277721, PMID:36412275

[C | hypothesis] Peripheral (tissue-level) hypothyroidism, with impaired cellular thyroid hormone action despite normal serum T4, T3 and TSH, is proposed as an under-recognised cause of unmet need. Diagnosis is hampered by the lack of sensitive biomarkers of tissue thyroid status. Liver-selective thyromimetics such as resmetirom have been used in MASLD. - PMID:37738506, PMID:43005807

[C | evidence supported] Mendelian evidence: pathogenic THRB variants cause RTHβ, typically autosomal dominant via a dominant-negative effect. The biochemical signature is elevated thyroid hormones with non-suppressed TSH, i.e. reduced tissue sensitivity to thyroid hormone. This is not the same phenotype as primary hypothyroidism, so it does not establish THRB as a cause of hypothyroidism. - PMID:33868182

[C | evidence supported] If a THRB variant of uncertain significance were found, computational predictions alone should not guide clinical decisions. Family co-segregation and functional data are preferred. - PMID:33868182

[C | emerging] TSHR variants are among the genes found in a Chinese congenital hypothyroidism cohort (second most frequent after DUOX2). This supports TSHR as a genetically implicated gene in some hypothyroidism, but in newborns with variants in a small sample. - PMID:34539567

[C | emerging] TSHR is a validated autoantigen in autoimmune thyroid conditions, and structural work shows that stimulating and blocking autoantibodies can cause hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. This provides a mechanistic rationale for TSHR modulation in antibody-mediated hypothyroidism, but no source tests it. - PMID:35940204

[C | evidence supported] Safety signal from related TED therapy: teprotumumab (blocks IGF-1R, not TSHR) is associated with notable side effects such as hearing loss in about 30% of patients, plus high cost and relapse. It is a contextual safety concern for biologics near the TSHR/IGF-1R axis in a different disease. - PMID:40324443

[C | emerging] TYK2 small-molecule inhibitors fall into two binding-site classes: allosteric JH2 (pseudokinase) binders and JH1 ATP-site (catalytic) inhibitors. BMS-986165 (deucravacitinib) is the representative JH2 binder. - PMID:38904160

[C | evidence supported] If 'TG' means triglycerides, hypothyroidism is associated with raised total cholesterol, LDL-C and triglycerides. This is an association with, and a possible downstream consequence of, hypothyroidism, not evidence that modulating triglycerides treats hypothyroidism. A cross-sectional study also found higher TC, TG, LDL-C and HbA1c and lower HDL-C in hypothyroid than in hyperthyroid patients. - PMID:35038435, PMID:42969393

[C | emerging] THRA variants cause RTHα, a rare inherited condition with tissue-specific hypothyroid-like features without TSH elevation. Most variants are heterozygous and act through a dominant-negative mechanism. - PMID:42843455

[C | emerging] Levothyroxine is the only therapeutic intervention reported for RTHα. Earlier initiation is associated with better neurodevelopmental and growth outcomes, and established skeletal abnormalities are poorly reversible. No THRA-targeted modulator is described in the sources. - PMID:42843455

[C | emerging] Thyromimetics selective for THRB (liver-directed) are designed to spare THRA-dominant tissues such as heart and bone. Reported cautions are slight free T4 suppression, possible problems in people with low thyroid reserve such as subclinical hypothyroidism, and possible hypothalamic-pituitary effects. These data concern THRB-selective drugs for MASH, not THRA modulation, and are indirect safety context. - PMID:39420154

[C | evidence supported] Thyroid abnormalities are statistically enriched in individuals carrying pathogenic KAT6B variants compared with variant-negative patients with suggestive features. This is an association within a rare syndromic population, not evidence that KAT6B drives common adult hypothyroidism. - PMID:25424711, PMID:42923075

[C | evidence supported] A UK consensus statement says that, for some patients with confirmed overt hypothyroidism and persistent symptoms despite adequate levothyroxine and with other causes excluded, a trial of combined LT3/LT4 therapy may be warranted. This is a shared decision, and clinicians are not obliged to prescribe it. The statement also notes that trials have not shown benefit of combination therapy over monotherapy. - PMID:37272400

[C | emerging] A large retrospective cohort analysis (TriNetX), reported alongside a meta-analysis of hypothyroidism and dementia, found lower dementia and mortality risk with LT4+T3 than with LT4 alone. This is an association from observational data, subject to confounding by indication, and the authors state that confirmation is needed. - PMID:40579157

[C | emerging] A narrative review states that more than 20 prospective RCTs found LT4+LT3 safe and effective, with many patients not fully benefiting from LT4 reporting improved quality of life and cognition after switching. It also states that about 10-20% of patients do not fully benefit from LT4. - PMID:37738506

[C | emerging] A critical narrative review argues that symptom-based thyroid treatment risks missed diagnoses and that adjusting TSH targets or low T3 levels has not been shown to improve outcomes. The author does not favour adding LT3 pending better trials. - PMID:37419564

[C | emerging] The consensus and review literature suggests that earlier null trials may have failed to target the most symptomatic patients. Combination therapy is proposed only for selected patients, after other causes are addressed, with monitoring and continuation only if patient-reported quality of life improves. - PMID:35662440

[D | hypothesis] A small double-blind crossover study (n=45) found that carrying both DIO2 rs225014 and MCT10 rs17606253 variants was associated with a higher preference for LT4+LT3. Preference rose from 42% to 63% to 100% across groups carrying none, one or both variants. - PMID:28785541
[D | hypothesis] The clinical relevance of Thr92Ala may vary by racial background, and associations have not been reproduced in all populations. - PMID:30063552

[D | hypothesis] At least one crystal structure of the TYK2 JH2 pseudokinase domain has been reported, in complex with ATP-γS. A co-crystal structure with a small-molecule inhibitor is also mentioned, so structural data exist. The total number of TYK2 PDB entries is not stated in any supplied source. - PMID:26359499

[D | hypothesis] A pharmacovigilance analysis of budesonide/formoterol reported hypothyroidism as a distinctive signal in the Canadian adverse-reaction database (CVARD). This is a disproportionality signal from spontaneous reports and does not establish causation. It cannot be attributed to formoterol rather than budesonide, and it may reflect confounding by indication or by comorbidity. - PMID:41654451

[D | hypothesis] In mice, the beta2-agonist terbutaline induced thyroid colloid droplet formation and raised blood radioiodine levels, an effect reduced by propranolol. This suggests beta2-adrenergic receptors can mediate thyroid hormone secretion in rodents. It is preclinical, not human, and not a clinical recommendation. - PMID:239845

[D | emerging] In an authors' interpretation of beta2-agonist use in untreated thyrotoxicosis, the caution is based on clinical adverse reactions rather than altered serum thyroid hormone concentrations. The sources contain no analogous caution for hypothyroidism. - PMID:6127097

[D | hypothesis] The only direct evidence in an Indian population (36 non-autoimmune hypothyroid cases, 22 controls) found a non-significant adjusted association between rs2268458 and non-autoimmune hypothyroidism. - PMID:42605379

[D | hypothesis] A small Iranian study (60 hypothyroid, 20 hyperthyroid, 20 normal) reports that rs2268458 is associated with hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism and that the C allele may be a risk factor. The design and reporting are weak, so this does not count as robust replication. - PMID:36130976

[D | hypothesis] The Chinese TSH GWAS abstract highlights XKR4, FOXE1 and CAPZB as TSH loci. It does not mention TSHR rs2268458, so the sources provide no GWAS support for this SNP. Absence from an abstract is not proof of absence in the full data. - PMID:24852370

[D | hypothesis] A school-based Chinese pediatric study genotyped rs2268458 but reported no main-effect association with thyroid dysfunction. A subgroup signal (TT genotype with frequent kelp/laver record and subclinical hyperthyroidism) did not survive false discovery rate correction. - PMID:42797068

[D | hypothesis] First-in-class VHL-recruiting TYK2 PROTAC degraders built on an allosteric TYK2 inhibitor have been reported. They degraded TYK2 selectively over JAK1, JAK2 and JAK3 in Jurkat cell assays. - PMID:36414177

[D | hypothesis] A CRBN-recruiting TYK2 PROTAC (15t), based on an allosteric TYK2 inhibitor, has been reported with sub-nanomolar degradation potency in cells. It suppressed TYK2-mediated pathology in a murine psoriasis model without apparent toxicity. - PMID:40116635

[D | hypothesis] A review abstract states that the TYK2 inhibitor field includes TYK2 degraders alongside single-target and dual-target small-molecule inhibitors. Only the abstract was available, so no details on modalities, clinical status or non-PROTAC approaches can be drawn from it. - PMID:40782408

[D | hypothesis] An earlier JAK-family PROTAC design study targeted JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2. The abstract reports induced degradation of JAK1 and JAK2 only. It does not report TYK2 degradation, so it cannot be counted as a demonstrated TYK2 degrader. - PMID:32001089

[D | hypothesis] Clinical-stage PROTAC evidence in the supplied sources concerns other targets, such as the oral ER degrader vepdegestrant and topical androgen receptor degraders. Topical JAK-targeting PROTACs are described only preclinically. No TYK2 PROTAC clinical data are provided, and no non-PROTAC non-small-molecule modality for TYK2 is described. - PMID:41255358

[E | hypothesis] The provided sources contain no direct evidence on antibody, PROTAC/degrader, oligonucleotide or other non-small-molecule modalities against TYK2. Anifrolumab is described as an anti-IFNAR1 antibody acting on the upstream receptor, not on TYK2 itself. Antibody tractability for TYK2 (an intracellular kinase) is therefore not established here. - PMID:42328642

[E | hypothesis] – of the supplied sources report the frequency of TRHR variants (heterozygous or otherwise) in South Asian populations. The only TRHR-containing cohort in the sources is Chinese, and the excerpt gives no TRHR-specific carrier rate. - PMID:32319661

[E | hypothesis] No source provides human patient-reported-outcome data for sustained-release liothyronine plus LT4. SR-T3 is described as still in development (phase 1 completed, not approved, long-term data pending), so the question cannot be answered directly from these sources. - PMID:34543420, PMID:35662440, PMID:40851876

[D | emerging] A homozygous missense TRHR variant (p.I131T) was linked to central hypothyroidism in one child. Heterozygous relatives had isolated hyperthyrotropinemia. In vitro work showed reduced TRH binding and Gq signaling, so TRHR signaling is a plausible but rare genetic cause of central hypothyroidism. - PMID:28419241

[C | evidence supported] Central hypothyroidism may coexist with other pituitary hormone deficits. GH or ACTH deficiency can carry a risk of life-threatening hypoglycaemia. This is a safety consideration in the work-up of central forms, not a safety finding about TRHR modulators. - PMID:26416826

[D | hypothesis] In gnomAD-based estimates, presumed pathogenic TRHR variants are very rare (global carrier frequency about 0.059%). TRHR therefore contributes little to predicted congenital hypothyroidism prevalence compared with genes such as DUOX2. The sources give no South Asian-specific TRHR figure. - PMID:34200080

[D | hypothesis] In rats and thyroid cell lines treated with triclosan, TRHr expression was induced by p38 activation, and TPO was suppressed via the p38/TRHr pathway. This suggests that TRHR upregulation in thyroid cells could contribute to TPO suppression and hypothyroidism in this toxicant model. It is a potential theoretical safety signal for TRHR modulation, not demonstrated in humans. - PMID:29462796

[C | evidence supported] A key unmet need is persistent symptoms in a minority of levothyroxine-treated patients despite normalised TSH. Standard LT4 may not restore thyroid hormone signalling in all tissues, and it also has dosing, drug-interaction and adherence difficulties. - PMID:36277721, PMID:37738506

[C | emerging] The most advanced alternative approach is combination LT4+LT3 therapy, with slow-release LT3 formulations under testing. The review reports trials showing safety and patient preference, but the sources do not establish it as standard of care. They also note unresolved questions about formulation regulation and safety and efficacy data. - PMID:36277721, PMID:37738506, PMID:43005807

[C | emerging] Absorption and bioavailability of oral LT4 are affected by interfering drugs, foods and diseases. Novel liquid and soft-gel formulations are designed to circumvent malabsorption, but study designs are flawed and the debate is ongoing. - PMID:36277721, PMID:36412275

[C | hypothesis] Peripheral (tissue-level) hypothyroidism, with impaired cellular thyroid hormone action despite normal serum T4, T3 and TSH, is proposed as an under-recognised cause of unmet need. Diagnosis is hampered by the lack of sensitive biomarkers of tissue thyroid status. Liver-selective thyromimetics such as resmetirom have been used in MASLD. - PMID:37738506, PMID:43005807

[D | hypothesis] Regenerative approaches (thyroid scaffolds, ESC- or iPSC-derived follicular cells, organoids) have restored thyroid function in animal models only. Clinical translation has not been achieved. - PMID:27876515, PMID:36277721, PMID:37738506

[C | evidence supported] Mendelian evidence: pathogenic THRB variants cause RTHβ, typically autosomal dominant via a dominant-negative effect. The biochemical signature is elevated thyroid hormones with non-suppressed TSH, i.e. reduced tissue sensitivity to thyroid hormone. This is not the same phenotype as primary hypothyroidism, so it does not establish THRB as a cause of hypothyroidism. - PMID:33868182

[D | emerging] Common-variant case-control evidence in an Indian cohort: the minor allele of rs1505287 (A) was more frequent in hypothyroid patients, suggesting a risk effect, and the minor allele of rs4858608 (G) was more common in controls, suggesting a protective effect. Haplotypes H1 (A-T) and H4 (G-G) correlated with hypothyroidism. No association was seen with hyperthyroidism. - PMID:39921048

[D | emerging] A THRB intronic SNP (in9-G/A) was associated with higher serum TSH in Danish twins (a nominally significant association) but was not significant in the Rotterdam Scan Study. Other THRB and THRA SNPs showed no association with thyroid hormone levels. This is a TSH-level association in healthy people, not a hypothyroidism association. - PMID:18844476

[D | emerging] In a large 68-gene pathway association analysis, THRB polymorphisms showed only suggestive associations with TSH. These did not pass multiple-testing correction, whereas PDE8B (TSH) and DIO1 (FT4) did. - PMID:21367965

[D | hypothesis] An association between RTHβ and autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD) has been described, but causality is unclear. AITD can also confound the clinical diagnosis of RTH, and a THRB variant (G339S) found in a family with AITD had normal function and normal thyroid function tests. - PMID:23806029, PMID:33868182

[C | evidence supported] If a THRB variant of uncertain significance were found, computational predictions alone should not guide clinical decisions. Family co-segregation and functional data are preferred. - PMID:33868182

[C | emerging] TSHR variants are among the genes found in a Chinese congenital hypothyroidism cohort (second most frequent after DUOX2). This supports TSHR as a genetically implicated gene in some hypothyroidism, but in newborns with variants in a small sample. - PMID:34539567

[D | hypothesis] The intronic TSHR SNP rs2268458 was reported as possibly associated with non-autoimmune hypothyroidism in a small Indian hospital study. The adjusted association did not reach statistical significance. - PMID:42605379

[C | emerging] TSHR is a validated autoantigen in autoimmune thyroid conditions, and structural work shows that stimulating and blocking autoantibodies can cause hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. This provides a mechanistic rationale for TSHR modulation in antibody-mediated hypothyroidism, but no source tests it. - PMID:35940204

[D | emerging] Clinical TSHR-targeted therapy is early-stage and has been tested in thyroid eye disease, not hypothyroidism. A phase I trial of the TSHR-blocking antibody K1-70 reported favourable safety and tolerability, with a small sample. Blocking TSHR is the opposite of what hypothyroidism would require. - PMID:41728592

Needed to judge whether TSH is actually unstable and whether instability tracks dose changes or other factors.
Baseline TSH and free T4 at diagnosis (overt vs subclinical hypothyroidism)
These determine which guideline applies (SCH recommendation against treatment vs standard LT4 replacement) and the likelihood of successful discontinuation.
Evaluation of non-thyroidal causes of fatigue, anxiety, cramps and sleepiness (e.g., B12, vitamin D, sleep assessment)
Symptoms attributed to thyroid dysfunction often have non-thyroidal causes. Recognising this avoids inappropriate dose escalation.
Current on-treatment TSH and free T4, and timing of blood draws relative to levothyroxine and supplements
Needed to judge whether her persistent symptoms (fatigue, dry skin, cramps, sleepiness) reflect inadequate replacement or non-thyroidal causes.
Verified supplement list and doses (ashwagandha, protein and fibre powders, vitamin D3, B12)
Diet and drugs may alter thyroid function test values. The medication entries are model-extracted and unverified.
Imaging report details for the L4-L5 disc compression
It would show whether imaging is concordant with symptoms. Imaging findings may not correlate with symptoms.
Thyroid control (recent TSH and free T4) and whether fatigue, muscle cramps and daytime sleepiness are linked to hypothyroidism
These symptoms could affect exercise tolerance and adherence; the sources do not address hypothyroidism.

Guidelines stress accurate diagnosis. Aetiology informs prognosis and monitoring, and her autoimmune status is unrecorded despite a family history of thyroid di

Current and recent TSH and free T4 values, and the dose-change history since 2025-04
Determines whether under- or over-replacement could explain fatigue, anxiety, cramps, dry skin or sleepiness.
Current TSH and free T4 levels and thyroid antibody status
Untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism was associated with higher OSA prevalence, and poor thyroid control could itself explain fatigue and sleepiness.
Timing of levothyroxine dosing relative to fibre powder, protein powder, vitamin D3, B12 and ashwagandha, and verification of these medicati
Co-ingestion may impair absorption. Ashwagandha is not covered in the supplied sources and may affect thyroid function.
Pre-treatment serum TSH and free T4 values (at diagnosis, before levothyroxine started in 2025-04)
Needed to tell primary overt, primary subclinical and central hypothyroidism apart, and whether baseline TSH was above or below 10 mU/L.
Time of blood draw relative to the levothyroxine dose and to supplements (fibre, protein, vitamins)
FT4 can be transiently higher after a dose and absorption can be altered by fibre or protein, affecting FT4/FT3 interpretation.
Ashwagandha product, dose and start date relative to TSH changes
Natural products may directly modulate thyroid function, which could confound TSH results.
